#2802. California attorney general issues Nvidia subpoena in probe of China chip diversion

California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China in contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said.

The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that is being investigation for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China.

"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement.

"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.

Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair. The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.

#2801. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2800. Hiroshi Nanami: The magical left foot of Shizuoka who controlled time and space on the pitch

A visionary maestro of the J.League's golden era, Hiroshi Nanami used his sublime left foot like a compass, guiding Júbilo Iwata and the Samurai Blue to historic heights while proving that football's ultimate truth lies in controlling the tempo of the game.

At a time when modern football began to obsess over distance covered and pure physical power, Hiroshi Nanami stood as a serene, brilliant antithesis. He was a playmaker who did not need to run aimlessly because he could roll the entire pitch in the palm of his hand with a single, casual swing of his left foot. As the undisputed metronome of Júbilo Iwata and the iconic number 10 of the Japan national team, his elegance shaped a golden age of Japanese football.

His journey took him from the quiet fields of Shizuoka to the historic canals of Venice, and finally to the grand stage of the 1998 FIFA World Cup. Across his decorated career, he earned a legendary reputation as a master tactician who elevated the intelligence of everyone around him. Even today, his legacy remains a shining reminder that soccer is not just a game of speed, but a canvas of infinite, artistic possibilities.

Born on November 28, 1972, in Fujieda, a historic football hotbed in the Shizuoka Prefecture, Hiroshi Nanami's destiny was carved out on the pitch from an early age. Fujieda was a city where football was treated with immense reverence, and youth players were expected to possess immaculate technique. He honed his craft at the prestigious Shimizu Shogyo High School—a legendary academy that produced some of the country's finest technical players—before refining his game at Juntendo University.

In 1995, the promising midfielder officially signed with Júbilo Iwata, immediately establishing himself as a permanent fixture in a star-studded starting eleven. His rookie season was nothing short of explosive, as he brought a rare, calculated calm to a league that was often frantic and chaotic. Operating as a deep-lying playmaker, he possessed a maturity that defied his youth, consistently picking out defense-splitting passes with millimeter precision.

His sublime left foot did not escape the attention of Italian legend Salvatore "Totò" Schillaci, who shared the dressing room with Nanami at Júbilo Iwata and raved about him to the Italian press: "Here in Japan he is one of the best. He does everything with his left. His specialties are assists... and free kicks, then: implacable. He reminds me of Giuseppe Giannini."

Between 1996 and 1998, Nanami became the undisputed heartbeat of Júbilo Iwata, leading them to a J1 League title, a J.League Cup, and the prestigious Asian Club Championship. His domestic dominance was absolute, earning him three consecutive J.League Best Eleven selections and cementing his status as the nation's premier midfielder. On the international stage, he famously inherited Japan's heavy number 10 shirt, orchestrating the nation's historic first-ever qualification for the FIFA World Cup in 1998.

At the World Cup in France, Nanami played every single minute in Group H, going head-to-head with legendary global superstars. He fought valiantly in the midfield against Juan Sebastián Verón and Javier Zanetti in a narrow 1-0 defeat to Argentina, before battling Croatia's Aljoša Asanović and Robert Prosinečki in Nantes. Against Jamaica in Lyon, his creative passing helped unlock the defense, allowing his teammate Masashi "Gon" Nakayama to score Japan's historic first-ever goal on the World Cup stage.

By the summer of 1999, European scouts were thoroughly enamored with Nanami's sublime technical style. Serie A club Venezia FC, looking for a worthy replacement for Álvaro Recoba, signed Nanami on a high-profile loan deal. Venetian club president Maurizio Zamparini proudly introduced his new Japanese star to the Italian media with grand expectations:"Nanami has the same class as Recoba."

Nanami's time in the floating city was a challenging battle against a highly physical, defensive Italian league, resulting in just one goal (scored against Udinese) in 24 appearances as Venezia suffered relegation. Yet, the Shizuoka maestro chose to look at his Italian adventure through a lens of profound gratitude rather than disappointment. Upon his return to Iwata in late 2000, he reflected:"An experience in Italy is more important than money."

Upon returning home, Nanami immediately reached his absolute career peak at the 2000 AFC Asian Cup in Lebanon. Playing every single minute of the tournament, he scored three crucial goals, guided Japan to a spectacular championship, and was rightfully crowned the tournament's Most Valuable Player (MVP).

This continental triumph set the stage for Júbilo Iwata's most legendary tactical experiment in 2001: the revolutionary "N-Box" formation. Conceived by manager Masakazu Suzuki to shorten running distances and maximize possession, the system placed five midfielders in a tight die-like "five" pattern, with Nanami at the absolute center. Flanked by Toshiya Fujita, Daisuke Oku, Takashi Fukunishi, and Toshihiro Hattori, this setup allowed them to pass the ball at dizzying, high speeds.

Reflecting on the sheer difficulty and ultimate genius of the system, former teammate Takashi Fukunishi revealed:"At first, everyone said it was impossible during training camp... it was always crowded where Nanami was, but because he was there, we could possess the ball anywhere."

The relentless physical demands of elite football eventually caught up with the elegant playmaker. In 2001, Nanami suffered a severe knee injury that effectively ended his international career after 67 caps and 9 goals. The injury robbed him of his sharpness, forcing him to rely entirely on his positioning and spatial awareness to survive on the pitch. Though he returned to help Júbilo Iwata capture another J1 League title in 2002 and the Emperor's Cup in 2003, his physical capabilities were permanently compromised.

He spent his final years searching for the old magic on brief loans at Cerezo Osaka and Tokyo Verdy, before returning to Júbilo Iwata for one last emotional chapter. In November 2008, dogged by chronic knee pain and realizing he could no longer perform at his own high standards, Nanami officially announced his retirement.

After hanging up his boots, Nanami naturally transitioned to the dugout, bringing his immense tactical intellect to the managerial realm. He returned to save his beloved Júbilo Iwata as manager in September 2014, successfully guiding them back to the J1 League in 2015. He also had a managerial stint with Matsumoto Yamaga before taking on his current, highly prestigious role as an assistant coach for the Japan national team under Hajime Moriyasu.

His tactical acumen and emphasis on elite, world-class standards continue to shape the next generation of Japanese stars. National team midfielder Daichi Kamada recently shared how Nanami's modern coaching methods have elevated their play:

"Mr. Nanami showed us videos of how the world's top players dribble past defenders and the timing of their shots, so we can progress further... Since Mr. Nanami has pointed it out, I think everyone can be more conscious about achieving it."

Hiroshi Nanami's legacy is not just one of trophies, but of a rare, artistic footballing philosophy. In an era that increasingly prioritizes physical metrics and athletic power, he remains a legendary symbol of how a beautiful mind and a golden left foot can command the beautiful game.

#2799. Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich takes blame for ugly touchdown drought

It has been a long nine quarters for the Jets offense, which hasn't scored a touchdown since the Nov. 1 loss to the Raiders in Las Vegas.

Few have felt the impact of the drought more than offensive coordinator Frank Reich.

"It starts with me,'' Reich said Thursday. "I'm the offensive coordinator. I — and we as a staff — have to put players in position to do what they do. We've got a very talented group. We need to do a better job coaching [and] the players need to do their part in executing and making plays."

The Jets have been held to eight Jason Sanders field goals since finding the end zone against the Raiders.

"We know we need to put more points on the board, whether it's in the red zone or whether we're farther out, we still want to be explosive,'' Reich said. "It's been nine quarters. Believe me, I feel every play of that nine quarters."

Offensive coordinator Frank Reich speaks to the media before Jets practice on Nov. 19, 2026, in Florham Park, N.J. Bill Kostroun for NYPost

Among the criticism of the Jets offense has been an inability to get the team's playmakers involved enough on offense.

"When your record is what it is and you go nine quarters without scoring a touchdown, that's what we're here all hours of the day trying to get right,'' Reich said. "We're working hard to get that right, and I'm confident we will."

Geno Smith (ankle) was limited in practice Thursday, but was on the field during warmups and has said he expects to play.

If Smith can't go, Cade Klubnik would be called upon again after filling in for Smith in Sunday's loss to the Bills.

Klubnik — who went 11-for-20 for 137 yards and one interception and was sacked three times in his NFL debut — was asked what he thought after having some time to watch film.

Quarterback Cade Klubnik runs up field during the Jets' Week 10 blowout loss to the Bills at MetLife Stadium. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura

"There were some good things,'' Klubnik said. "I made some good throws with confidence, and I was happy with some of my checks and my presence was calm."

Perhaps most importantly, he didn't feel overmatched. His teammates agreed he looked the part, which tells the fourth-round pick out of Clemson that he's headed in the right direction.

"I think it showed my preparation has been good,'' Klubnik said. "I'll be able to keep that going, whether I start or not [this week]. It feels good because I didn't finish the game and come home and say the next morning, 'I wish I did something completely different.' The process was good, but always needs to be fine-tuned."

Add Demario Davis to the chorus of people praising rookie David Bailey, who has 7 ½ sacks and five forced fumbles just nine games into his career.

"He's had unreal progression,'' Davis said Thursday of the No. 2 overall pick. "To be at the top of the league in sacks and pressures is impressive.''

And Davis has also liked what he's seen in other aspects of Bailey's game, like his ability to affect attempted screens and deflect passes.

"He's able to do all facets,'' Davis said. "You wouldn't know he was a rookie."

Andrew Beck, a fullback, has kicked off 10 times as the Jets look for an advantage in their coverage game, using him as a potential added tackler.

Special teams coach Chris Banjo noted that since teams are still adjusting to the new kickoff rules, "the challenge as coaches is to find that extra edge …"

Wide receivers Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle/hip) and Isaiah Williams (ribs) didn't practice.

#2798. APEC final day in photos: Trump, Xi and Putin shake hands; Takaichi kept at a distance

World leaders including the U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin gathered Thursday for the second day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, ahead of a historic trilateral meeting between the U.S., Russia and China later in the day.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva kicked off Thursday's agenda after China's President Xi Jinping's welcome note. Georgieva said that artificial intelligence and energy supply shocks had accelerated global inflation in many economies, calling for monetary policy tightening.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was met with another cold reception. She spent several minutes trying to talk to Xi who did not appear to respond with no interpreter present.

Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Xi earlier in the day. The president praised Xi's leadership and said Washington was negotiating deals with several major APEC economies.

In their first in-person talks in over a year, Trump told Putin that "We've known each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start," referring to Putin as a "friend."

The three leaders are due to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting later Thursday, with the Middle East conflict, Russia's war in Ukraine, trade and artificial intelligence likely on the agenda. Expectations for the historic three-way meeting to yield any concrete outcome remain low.

The summit will conclude Trump's whirlwind Asia trip, after which the American president will return to Washington, D.C.

#2797. LSU president orders RJ Luis benched amid SEC expulsion threat

The RJ Luis Jr. drama came to an inevitable and ignominious end Thursday, Nov. 19, as the LSU guard is to be benched by Will Wade at the behest of LSU President Wade Rousseau after playing in one game on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Luis, who played under the protection of a court order, scored 11 points for the Tigers in his season debut against Louisiana-Monroe, which ended in a 79-67 LSU win. Luis was added to the roster Tuesday, Nov. 17, with Rousseau saying in a statement:

"LSU is a member institution that will act in accordance with that order. The conference has confirmed it will do the same and has stated in writing that it 'will abide by the terms of the preliminary injunction while it remains in place and will not impose penalties or fines on LSU if (it) places Mr. Luis on its men's basketball roster."

'Really gross': Dan Hurley rips NCAA basketball eligibility crisis, blames coaches

Toppmeyer: Greg Sankey once ruled college football. Now, he's losing grip on SEC

In a course reversal Thursday, Rousseau said: "In my role as President of the LSU System, after further review, I have instructed LSU Men's Basketball Coach Will Wade to not play RJ Luis."

In a statement, Luis' lawyer Elliot Abrams said there were threats of expelling LSU from the SEC if Luis continued to play.

"The SEC's decision to threaten a member with expulsion if it plays an eligible student-athlete is reprehensible and seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him," Abrams wrote in a statement to USA TODAY Sports.

District Attorney Tony Clayton, another of Luis' attorney's, told The Daily Advertiser, part of the USA TODAY Network, that Luis told him to give up the fight.

Luis declared for the 2025 NBA Draft and was in the Jazz and Celtics organizations, but joined a lawsuit to get another year of eligibility after being waived before the start of the 2025 season.

Wade didn't elaborate on his decision to play Luis after Wednesday's game.

"I'm going to refer to our university's statement from yesterday," he said. "I'll be happy to answer any questions about how he played, but going to refer in terms of anything about his eligibility and rostering him to the university's statement yesterday.

"Everybody who played tonight is eligible."

LSU went through this same situation with football, when Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris were cleared to play by the courts, added to the roster, and ultimately later removed. Expulsion talks arose during that time as well.

#2796. Arizona women’s basketball escapes upset bid by New Mexico State

The New Mexico State Aggies have size and they know how to use it. They pushed the Arizona Wildcats in Tucson on Thursday evening, but the home team escaped with a 62-55 win.

"It's about just finding a way to get it done, and we did that today," said Arizona head coach Becky Burke. "Not pretty by any means. An ugly, grind-it-out game, but I think this was really good for us to to be down, to have faced adversity, for it to be low scoring and to still grind it out and win. Every game's had a different identity. Every game's kind of had a different story, and this one's no different. But that's a really good basketball team. I think he came in and built an entire new roster from overseas, and they're big and they're physical and they play well together."

Rebounding and points in the paint had the Aggies up by three at halftime. They outrebounded Arizona 21-6 in the first half, including 8-1 on the offensive boards. They also beat the Wildcats in points in the paint 30-16.

NMSU did it despite having leading scorer Raina Tomasicka go 0-0 from the floor, commit four fouls, and turn the ball over five times. Tomasicka came in averaging 19.5 points in 24.8 minutes per game.

"She was the huge focal point of our game plan," Burke said. "She got in foul trouble, which helped. She only played 15 minutes. I'll just be pessimistic. We also made one of her teammates look like a first team All-American. But I am proud of how he defended 24, especially down the stretch when they put her back in the basketball game. I thought they just tried to go to her instead of what was actually working to beat us. So I actually thought that was to our benefit when she came back in the game, and we were able to hedge those ball screens and be disruptive with her."

The player who looked like a first team All-American was Lilyana Fontcha, the Aggies' 6-foot-4 center. She dominated on the boards and in the paint, ending with a double-double of 21 points and 10 rebounds. Seven of her rebounds came on the offensive end, where NMSU crashed hard. She also had three assists and two steals without committing a turnover.

In the last game against Oregon State, Burke played Gerda Raulušaitytė and Breanna Williams together for an extended period of time in the third quarter. That was Arizona's best quarter and ended up being critical in an overtime victory.

This time, Burke waited until the fourth to play two bigs together. First, it was Raulušaitytė and Williams. When Williams picked up her fourth foul, it was Raulušaitytė and Priyanka Ponnam.

Once again, it was the best quarter by the Wildcats and the worst quarter for their opponent—especially Fontcha. After going 9 for 14 and grabbing nine rebounds through the first 30 minutes, the Aggies' center was 1 for 3 with one rebound in the final 10 minutes.

It was the only quarter when Arizona was able to keep up on the boards. They tied the Aggies 8-8 over the final 10 minutes after being outrebounded 32-14 through the first 30. NMSU still ended up with a 40-22 advantage in the rebounding column.

The Aggies also ended with a 44-30 advantage in paint points, although that imbalance was reduced by an even 14-14 battle in the second half.

"I probably should have went to it sooner now that it looked a little bit better," Burke said. "I mean, I'm always just thinking of what's going to give us the best chance to win and what's going to bode well for us. I actually didn't love it with Bre and Gerda today like I did the other day. But I thought Pri came in, and you have to guard Pri on the 3-point line, and I think that's something that was a little bit different, and that was our reasoning in bringing her in because they had a great game plan. They tried to take us out of transition, they tried to pack the paint, and they did that to an extent, but obviously we were able to execute when it mattered."

While Ponnam only took one shot and didn't score, her defense was on point as she helped keep NMSU from going to the bucket quite as effectively. She had one rebound and one steal in just under seven minutes.

In addition to using a combination of Ponnam and Williams, Burke also played Makayla Presser-Palmer more in the second half. Williams played just five minutes in the first half and Presser-Palmer was on the floor for only nine. Williams and Ponnam combined for 15 minutes in the second half and Presser-Palmer stayed on the floor for all 20.

"First half, I just wasn't really locked in," Presser-Palmer said. "Second half, I knew I had to turn it up, especially because we were down. I just had to get on the defensive end and offensive end, and it just worked out."

Arizona was also able to get to the free throw line with regularity. More importantly, the Wildcats were able to hit their free throws. That task has been a challenge for them in their early games, but they went 21 for 24 against the Aggies. Ten of those free throws came in the fourth.

"We've been shooting a lot of free throws, like a lot of reps a day," said guard Puff Morris. "But just today before the game, that was one of our goals and something that we wanted to pay attention to going into the game. So I think that's something that was mindful and we executed."

Morris was the offensive hero of the day. The diminutive guard had 17 points on 6-of-10 shooting. She went 2 for 5 from the 3-point line and 3 for 4 from the free throw line. She added three rebounds, one assist, and three steals.

Morris came up especially big down the stretch with 10 points in the fourth quarter.

Presser-Palmer was the other Wildcat to get into double figures. She had 11 points. While she only went 2 for 8 from the floor, she was a perfect 7 for 7 from the line. She grabbed four rebounds and one steal.

Like her teammate, Presser-Palmer's biggest contribution was in the second half. She scored all 11 of her points in the second half. Six of those points and three of her four rebounds came in the final quarter.

New Mexico State was not intimidated by the opponent or the Arizona crowd. The Wildcats went up by three early in the first quarter, but the Aggies came back to take a one-point lead on several occasions. When the final 10 minutes were over, Arizona had a slim 15-14 advantage.

It's not uncommon for a mid-major team to come into a Power 4 arena and compete for a while before going away. NMSU didn't go away.

The Aggies took a lead at 8:57 in the second quarter and started to pull away. They pushed the lead out to nine at the 7:26 mark.

NMSU had another nine-point lead at 28-19. Arizona went on a 9-0 run to tie it with 3:15 left in the half. Two straight buckets by Fontcha put the Aggies back up by four. The lead was three when halftime came.

"A character check and a competitiveness check," she said. "Like, you need to come out for the next 20 minutes and decide how competitive you want to be, how spicy you want to be, how tough you want to be. I mean, they beat us in every toughness category the entire first half, and I thought we beat them in the toughness categories in the second half."

The two teams played fairly evenly in the third quarter. They each scored 13 points, but that left the Aggies with a three-point lead heading into the final 10 minutes.

That's when Arizona locked in. They forced four turnovers, all coming on steals. That allowed them to get out and run.

Raulušaitytė grabbed one of her five rebounds with 5:59 to go in the game. Presser-Palmer converted on the other end to give Arizona its first lead since 9:31 in the second quarter. The Wildcats never trailed again.

Morris followed Presser-Palmer's make with five straight points.

NMSU started fouling with 31 seconds on the clock and a four-point deficit. Presser-Palmer hit two free throws and Morris hit one of two to account for the final score. The Wildcats and their fans could finally breathe.

"We probably won't be scheduling them next year," Burke joked.

Freshman guard Simba Finley did not play for Arizona after getting hit in the face against Oregon State on Sunday.

"I believe, if all things go well, like they should, she should be back for Vandy," Burke said.

Arizona plays No. 11 Vanderbilt on Monday, Nov. 23 at 3 p.m. MST in Jacksonville, Fla.

The declines in Asia come after the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% overnight following Anthropic's highly anticipated Wall Street debut.

Williams will be re-evaluated on Saturday, so there's a chance that this is the last game he misses before returning. That would be nice, as the Dubs are really missing his offense off the bench.

Out — Jimmy Butler III (right ACL repair surgery)Out — Moses Moody (left patellar tendon repair surgery)Out — Kristaps Porziņģis (not with team)

Same news as always with this group. But we're pushing through the season, which means Butler and Moody are getting closer to returning.

Questionable — LJ Cryer (left low back soreness)

Cryer has stepped into a large role — a starting role, even — with Curry and Williams injured. His three-point shooting is critical for the Warriors when Curry is out, so hopefully he's able to play tonight despite the back issue.

The former Warrior has been a revelation in his second season with the Grizzlies, after injuries cost him most of his first year with the team. Despite entering the season averaging just 9.3 points per game, Jerome has positively exploded for 25.4 points, while also dishing 5.3 assists. He scored 28 points when these teams met in October, but will miss his fourth straight game.

Out — Zach Edey (left ankle injury management)

The Warriors are getting a little bit of a gift with Edey's absence, as they struggle to contain size. Edey is one of the largest players in the NBA, and had 10 rebounds and two blocks in the last game against the Warriors, despite only playing 22 minutes.

Out — Scotty Pippen Jr. (lumbar disc herniation)

Pippen's been dealing with a back issue for a while now, as this will be his 11th consecutive absence. Hopefully he's back on the court soon.

Out — GG Jackson II (left 5th metatarsal fracture)

Jackson was having a solid fourth season, but suffered an injury last week that will cost him a few months. He's expected to be re-evaluated sometime around the All-Star break.

Out — Richie Saunders (right knee surgery)

Saunders, who was drafted 32nd overall in June, tore his ACL in February, so he's likely still a ways away from making his NBA debut.

Beef Stew has been solid in his first season in Memphis, averaging 10.9 points despite playing less than 20 minutes per night. He's only grabbing 3.3 rebounds, but even so, his size could be an issue for the Dubs.

#2792. AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

When Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career. It appealed to people who enjoyed getting into the weeds of code, tracking down bugs and building programs from scratch.

It's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC. But the arrival of artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace, with AI tools now part of the daily work of every software engineer she knows. In a 2026 Stack Overflow survey, 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool.

As AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have. Rodgers has always loved the sense of accomplishment that comes from piecing together different parts of code to find a solution, particularly when she's spent days, or even weeks, trying to fix a stubborn bug.

"The sense of joy and fun that I used to experience by having a challenge and then having to work that out, it's been removed somewhat," she said. "Now you can sometimes do it in a few prompts, and it's great — but it's a breadcrumb of joy, not a full meal of joy."

Rodgers is not alone in feeling nostalgic about the not-so-old days. Software engineers have taken to social media to describe missing their old way of working, when they could get into a flow state with code for hours at a time.

Still, AI tools can be useful and have lowered the barrier to entry significantly. "It's becoming an industry where a lot of people have been able to thrive who wouldn't necessarily have been able to thrive 10 years ago, five years ago, even three years ago," Rodgers said.

It's also important that the core skills engineers have traditionally learned on the job are not lost, she said. AI tools and internet services can go down unexpectedly, and engineers still need to know how to investigate problems and work through solutions themselves.

"The sorts of skills that we were taught years ago are kind of being lost because [engineers are] having to just churn work out," Rodgers added.

The job itself is changing, too. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might previously have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon. The hardest part of that, he said, is "having the judgment to decide which of those are any good."

"The [AI] agents are spitting out so much code that [engineers] haven't read it all anymore," Broadhead said. "It used to be you'd build up a sense of comfort and awareness of how the whole code base was structured, but now the whole thing changes all the time."

Joshua Wöhle, CEO of London-based AI training company Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who don't.

The industry used to talk about "10X engineers," he said, who were dramatically more productive than their peers. Now, AI is widening that gap even further to produce "100X engineers."

Wöhle believes companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who can get the most out of it. But he also understands why some engineers might struggle to adapt.

The people who once excelled at the job were often those who loved writing and working through code, he said, and those are not necessarily the current top performers.

"That's the grief that is very, very real," Wöhle said. "The thing you love doing is no longer the thing the company should be paying for, to a degree, because it's no longer adding the value to the company that it used to."

But not every engineer sees the move away from hands-on coding as a bad thing. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and CEO of London-based virtual office company Hoxton Mix, told CNBC that AI gives developers more time to tackle interesting problems. He views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision.

"The important thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgement is needed," Sees said. "We'd be silly to think AI gets everything right, and I know I get a lot of satisfaction out of proving and spotting where it has gone wrong."

Even so, Sees worries about what happens to the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned. Those tasks are "where you learn lessons and build scar tissue," he said, and companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process, rather than a shortcut.

For Rodgers, what matters is having control over how she uses the technology. As a self-employed developer, she can use AI to automate the parts of a project she finds tedious, while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself.

She believes there's something important about working through a difficult problem rather than immediately outsourcing it to technology. Friction and discomfort, she said, are vital parts of the human experience.

"As humans, we need to feel accomplished in something and part of accomplishment requires challenge," she said. "Unless we are able to work that through in so many different aspects of life, then you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side."

#2790. Seth McGowan Injury Update: Colts RB Hurt vs. Texans

INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Seth McGowan #20 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball against the Dallas Cowboys during the third quarter at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images)

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) hands the ball to running back Jonathan Taylor (28) during a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars on November 1, 2026, in Jacksonville, Florida. Getty

The Indianapolis Colts were already having a rough evening. They'd allowed a field goal late in the first half to allow the Houston Texans to go up 17-3.

And then on the ensuing kickoff, rookie running back Seth McGowan took a big hit and was slow getting up with an apparent injury.

The Colts have been giving McGowan more work on offense in recent weeks, but he has retained the kickoff return duties that he first impressed in starting with his Week 1 NFL debut.

McGowan had already returned one kickoff up near midfield on Thursday night when he began to ran back this late-half kick, and he took it up the right sideline to try and gain ground and set up points before the half.

GettyINDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA – NOVEMBER 08: Seth McGowan #20 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball against the Dallas Cowboys during the third quarter at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images)

McGowan was approaching the 30-yard line when he was clotheslined by a Texans defender.

The left arm of the tackler caught McGowan up high, near his facemask, and appeared to give McGowan's whole body a jolt.

While the replay made it look like a potential head injury, when McGowan made his way off with trainers, he was grabbing at his right leg, a bit like he had hurt his hamstring.

The Colts ran just one more play before halftime, so there was no way to know whether McGowan's injury would hold him out in the second half or not.

GettyJACKSONVILLE, FL – NOVEMBER 01: Quarterback Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts hands off the ball to runningback Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second half of the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images)

McGowan had pushed his way into somewhat of a timeshare with star RB1 Jonathan Taylor, but if McGowan has to miss time, Taylor should get the lion's share of the work going forward.

The Colts' other active running back on Thursday night is D.J. Giddens, who was a 2025 fifth-round pick but has been leapfrogged this season by the 2026 seventh-rounder McGowan.

With the Colts down 17-3 at the half, they'll likely have to throw a lot in the second half regardless. Both Taylor and McGowan can make an impact as receivers, too, if the Colts need to go that route — and if McGowan is healthy enough to return to the game.

#2789. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2788. Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need,' but analysts warn of volatility

Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday gave markets a much-needed boost after weeks of weakness, though analysts warned that the stock could remain volatile in the coming weeks.

Share of the Claude maker opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 per share, 17% above the IPO price. The offering raised $81.3 billion through the sale of 980 million shares — surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO on record.

Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as "foaming at the mouth" for the offering, with allocations "impossibly low," underscoring the strength of demand.

"Anthropic's IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, adding that markets have been "depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks."

Still, U.S. equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20, S&P 500 down 2.02% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 2.19%.

Artificial intelligence and technology stocks initially rose thanks to the IPO, but the gains faded as "profit-taking spread across AI-related stocks," said James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers.

While the initial pop was not surprising for such a highly anticipated listing, investors should avoid "chasing the IPO," Walser said.

She expects the stock to come under pressure in the coming weeks as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang testifies before the U.S. Senate, potentially reviving concerns around the AI sector.

"The shares remain highly volatile," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan.

Walser said that any weakness around the time of Huang's testimony could offer an entry point for investors interested in Anthropic, adding that she remains bullish on the OpenAI rival over the long term.

"For investors, it's going to become a blue-chip stock like Google," Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."

He added that U.S. technology valuations are at ridiculously low levels relative to the "crazy amazing innovation" coming out of California.

Morningstar's Khan struck a more cautious tone, warning investors against getting swept up in the enthusiasm around Anthropic, advising them instead to step back and "carefully" assess the company as a long-term business.

That will depend on Anthropic's ability to scale enterprise adoption, continue improving its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services in the AI ecosystem, he said.

"We remain confident that the firm will be able to execute on all three fronts," Khan added, setting a $92 fair value estimate for the stock.

Walser stated that Anthropic is "extremely important for the overall AI story" as the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public.

Its listing gives public-market investors their first direct test of how a major standalone AI model developer will be valued and perform outside the chip sector. Meanwhile, rival OpenAI could follow with an IPO sometime in 2027.

"This IPO is the show me moment for the AI story," Walser said, as much of the stock market's AI narrative has so far centered on chipmakers.

#2787. U.K.-India trade deal faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxes

Within months of taking effect, the India-U.K. trade deal is facing an early test, as New Delhi resists extending preferential tariffs to bulk Scotch whisky imports.

Duty on bulk Scotch whisky imports was expected to be slashed to 75% then gradually to 40% over 10 years as per the trade agreement. However, a Reuters report Thursday said that India now plans to levy a 162.5% duty on these imports, higher than the 150% in place before the trade deal.

While India's commerce ministry did not respond to CNBC's request for comments, experts said that authorities in India classify bulk Scotch as a raw material and claim the preferential tariffs accorded in the deal apply only to imported bottled Scotch.

Amid the confusion over tax rates, thousands of liters of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi are stuck at Indian ports, according to Reuters.

"Ministers are urgently working with the Government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal," a U.K. government spokesperson told CNBC.

Distillers in India use bulk Scotch in their own locally blended whisky brands. As a result, Indian tax authorities are classifying bulk Scotch as "compound alcoholic preparations" which do not qualify for the preferential rate, said Sohrab Bararia, partner and leader of global trade at Grant Thornton Bharat.

Meanwhile, distillers argue that "genuine Scotch whisky" does not cease to be whisky merely because it is imported in bulk containers or used later for blending and bottling in India, Bararia said.

After three years, including 14 rounds of rigorous negotiations, India and the U.K. finalized the deal last year, which is expected to boost bilateral trade by 25.5 billion pounds ($34 billion) per year by 2040.

Officials from Diageo and Chivas Brothers had cheered the trade deal and underscored its importance for Scotch and Scotland.

"India is the world's largest whisky market by volume, so Scotch was always going to be one of the biggest prizes for the UK in this deal," said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.

Instead of simply exporting bottled whisky, bulk scotch exports offer British producers long-term ties with companies in India, deepening their stake in the South Asian country's domestic alcoholic beverage industry, Bhattacharya said.

In the global spirits markets, while the U.S., Europe, and China are facing volume contraction, ageing populations, and shifting social habits, nearly 100 million new consumers will be of legal drinking age in India over the next five years, Indian brokerage HDFC Institutional Research said in a report in September.

The alcoholic beverage market in India is dominated by Indian-made foreign liquors (IMFL), as per the report. IMFL refers to alcoholic beverages produced in India by combining local spirits often with imported malts and flavorings.

Greater access to bulk Scotch stocks at competitive prices helps Indian distilleries to improve blending quality for premium whisky products while maintaining cost efficiency, experts said. However, the latest dispute poses a major threat to these operations.

The lack of preferential tariffs on bulk Scotch could have "substantial" financial implications for importers, Parth Shah, partner at Deloitte India, told CNBC. "This could particularly affect Indian manufacturers who have invested in domestic blending and bottling operations using imported bulk Scotch whisky," he added.

Diageo-owned United Spirits, Pernod Ricard and Indian firms Allied Blenders and Radico Khaitan own and market some of the popular whisky brands in India.

Companies and industry bodies, the International Spirits and Wine Association and Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies, did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

A spokesperson for one of the whisky makers told CNBC that industry bodies were in talks with the commerce ministry to "represent adherence to the India-UK FTA." The person did not wish to be identified as they fear it could lead to a potential backlash from regulators.

"The lesson for the EU and other partners negotiating with India is that securing a headline tariff reduction is only half the battle," Bhattacharya of Maplecroft Verisk said, adding that partners need to pay close attention to whether "concessions translate into actual market access."

#2786. 49ers’ George Kittle Gets Real on Vikings Defense Before Week 11

The San Francisco 49ers offense is coming off a 46-point performance against the Dallas Cowboys defense in Week 10. However, racking up 46 points against the Minnesota Vikings might be a little more challenging.

Minnesota only allowed 10 points in their Week 10 win over the Green Bay Packers and have only allowed two teams to score over 20 points on them this season. As a result, the Niners offense will be in for a major challenge.

Ahead of the Week 11 game between the 49ers and Vikings, George Kittle spoke to the media to share his thoughts on Minnesota's defense.

"Coach Flores, that defensive staff and those players, you can just see they play with so much confidence," Kittle told reporters on Nov. 19. "I think that's the biggest thing. Their offense has been kind of struggling throughout until last week when they got Kirk back, but their defense has just been humming and humming and humming."

The Vikings will be bringing the pressure and looking to repeat their eight-sack and four-takeaway performance as they made life challenging for Packers QB Jordan Love in Week 10.

Moreover, the Minnesota defense leads the league with 37 team sacks, so 49ers QB Brock Purdy will have to prepare for the pressure he'll be facing. Kittle notes that typically, a defense this late in the season can begin to show weaknesses for opposing offenses to attack.

However, that's not the case with the Vikings' defense, as their only weakness to this point was not getting enough offensive help, leading to their two losses.

"Usually, when you're going against a team that is the No. 1-ranked defense through the first couple of weeks of the season, they might get exposed once," Kittle added. "They haven't been exposed one time. They're really good on third down. They make everything chaotic.

"What I personally see from this year, as opposed to other years, is that they're as confident as they were two years ago with Sam Darnold, when they won 14 games. They're just so confident in their scheme and their abilities to hit people, make plays, and make you mess up. They play without hesitation. It's really cool to see. Hopefully, it's fun to play against, but that remains to be determined."

Meanwhile, 49ers general manager John Lynch recently explained how much responsibility falls on Purdy's shoulders to read opposing defenses and keep the 49ers offense operating smoothly, a challenge that awaits him against the Vikings.

"Lots of times, a couple plays are called, and it's Brock's job to identify what they're doing defensively and get us in the right call. He does that seamlessly, and a lot is put on him," Lynch said during a Nov. 19 appearance on KNBR. "I just can't say enough about Brock. Brock can play on time and rhythm, and he can also create and make things happen, as we saw the other day.

"You saw all of it on full display. He's playing at an incredibly high level, and it's just really what we've come to expect. He's having an unbelievable season, and he knows the challenge he'll have this week against Minnesota."

#2785. There are worse backup plans than Beaux Limmer

The starting center for the Los Angeles Rams, Coleman Shelton, is expected to miss four to six weeks with a severe hamstring injury.

He will be replaced by Beaux Limmer, who watched Shelton take his job following a painful end to his Limmer's rookie season.

At one point, Limmer looked like a draft steal. LA swiped the former Arkansas Razorback in the sixth round. He went on to start 14 games and play 1,000 snaps as a rookie, including in the divisional round game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

2025: What do the Rams truly have in Beaux Limmer?

And that is where Limmer's reputation quickly shifted from draft steal to a problem that needed upgraded. On the final two plays of an all-important playoff matchup, Limmer left Jalen Carter unblocked for quick pressures on Matthew Stafford. The result? Two incomplete passes and the Rams flying back to Los Angeles with their heads slumped in defeat.

As a consequence, the Rams prioritized a reunion with Shelton in free agency. Limmer was a nice surprise. He could return to the starting lineup one day. But center is an important position and growing pains for a young player could have jeopardized the remaining window of Stafford's career.

It's a full-circle story. The truth is there are worse backup plans than Limmer. He's capable. In front of him is an opportunity to grab the starting job. This time he might not let go.

Shelton has been an above average starter for LA. Left guard Steve Avila missed the most recent game against the Cardinals.

Limmer earned the start at left guard. When Shelton came out, backup Dylan McMahon lasted nine plays before suffering a significant injury of his own. Limmer slid inside. Bill Murray came in at left guard.

According to Pro Football Focus (PFF), Limmer played 76 snaps and earned a near-elite pass blocking grade of 88.8. He did not allow a single pressure. The run game was also marked at a plus level with a grade of 70.4 for a net offensive grade of 75.5. For comparison, that edges out Shelton's season offensive grade of 74.7.

Limmer is 25 years old. He wasn't a finished product as a rookie. If what he put on tape through 1,000 snaps in 2024 was enough for us to be excited then, it would be foolish to write him off as a future starter moving forward. The Rams have a surplus of players they must re-sign over the next couple of offseasons. Limmer is under contract through 2027.

Limmer holding onto the starting job for the remainder of the season and proving he deserves the job in 2027 would be a welcome development for the Rams.

#2784. Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon

While investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut, a very different IPO is making waves in Europe: Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the operator of one of the world's most famous geothermal spas.

Blue Lagoon Corp. raised roughly 14.3 billion Icelandic kronur ($110 million) through the offering, valuing the Icelandic geothermal spa operator at about $787 million, according to the company's investor presentation.

The Blue Lagoon traces its origins to 1992, when Blue Lagoon Ltd. was founded to study the water in the Blue Lagoon, an open-air pool of warm, milky-blue water set in a black lava field in southwestern Iceland. It grew into a business spanning a spa, hotels and skincare made with ingredients from the lagoon.

Shares will trade under the ticker "BLUE" on one of Europe's smallest stock exchanges, Nasdaq Iceland Main Market, part of the Nasdaq Nordic group, which also operates exchanges in Sweden, Denmark and Finland.

"Wellness is the new luxury, and we know that the wellness economy is growing faster than the economy as a whole, so we have tailwind from that," CEO Sigríður Margrét Oddsdóttir told CNBC on Thursday.

"Now is the right time for us to list," she added. "We are a company that thinks long-term, we have a clear vision for the next decade, and being publicly listed gives investors the opportunity to participate in our journey."

The company's operations are centered on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, where, as well as the Blue Lagoon geothermal spa, it runs the Silica Hotel, the Retreat luxury hotel and spa, and the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant.

It also operates the Kerlingarfjöll Highland Base and Hrauneyjar properties in Iceland's highlands, and sells Blue Lagoon-branded skincare products internationally.

The 34-year-old company has averaged 11% annual revenue growth over the past decade, and next year is expected to be a record, with revenue growing by more than half, Oddsdóttir said.

The company plans to use the raised capital to fund expanding its existing properties, acquiring businesses, and developing new destinations.

In total, nearly 4,000 subscriptions were received in the initial public offering, worth about 15.3 billion kronur, about 7% more than the total size of the offering, the company said, citing strong demand from smaller investors, including retail investors.

Iceland's relatively small stock market had just 27 companies on its main exchange at the end of 2025, according to Nasdaq. The market is dominated by banks, seafood companies and other domestically focused firms.

The global wellness industry reached $7.5 trillion in 2025, up 8.9% from the previous year, according to the Global Wellness Institute. Spending on thermal and mineral springs grew 10.4% over the same period, with the institute forecasting annual growth of nearly 10% for the sector through 2030.

Tourism accounted for nearly 9% of Iceland's GDP in 2025, and is growing, according to Statistics Iceland. The country welcomed around 2.3 million international visitors that year, with the U.S. as its largest source market.

#2783. Zak Brown explains why McLaren keeps selling F1 cars before they race ahead of 2027 auction

McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown has explained why the Woking outfit is selling its Formula 1 cars at auction before they have even turned a wheel, saying the alternative is leaving them hidden away.

McLaren will auction its 2027 car, the MCL41, with RM Sotheby's in Abu Dhabi on 9 December, three days after the season finale. A chassis used by either Lando Norris or Oscar Piastri will be offered with a 2027-specification Mercedes power unit.

It follows last year's sale of this season's car, the MCL40A, which went for a staggering $11.48million at RM Sotheby's Abu Dhabi sale last December. It was the first time an F1 car had been sold before it had raced.

The buyer will not receive that car until 2028, because of rules designed to stop rivals getting access to a team's intellectual property, and was offered a 2025 show car to display in the meantime.

Asked in the team principals' press conference in Las Vegas about the thinking behind the sales, Brown said it made more sense than locking the cars away.

"Yeah, the other alternative is you leave them all on shelves under wraps, which is a shame. We have a great automotive business, we have a very passionate fan base, and we have a certain part of our fan base that has a passion to collect cars," Brown said.

Brown, a keen car collector himself, said last year's buyer had been able to follow their car all season.

"And so last year with Sotheby's, we sold '26 cars and someone had the ability to come on the journey, watch their car race, win some races. And so we're going to do that once a year at least. That's our intention," he said.

McLaren's 2026 car has won three races this season, all with Norris, in Hungary, the Netherlands and Brazil. The team currently sits fourth in the constructors' championship with 398 points, 17 points behind Red Bull in third.

This year's winning bidder will get a tour of McLaren's Woking headquarters before the 2027 season, the chance to meet Brown, Norris and Piastri, and an invitation to the team's 2027 launch.

Brown said the sales gave a small group of fans an experience that would otherwise not exist.

"We have a nice business. We've done 35 track cars of our Le Mans car, so for us it's about experiential opportunities for those fans of ours that are in a privileged position to be able to own Formula 1 cars. Otherwise, we make four or five cars a year and they end up stacking up on a shelf, and that's no good for anybody," he said.

#2782. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2781. Senate passes BAAJA permitting reform bill backed by AI, energy sectors

The Senate on Thursday passed a long-sought bill to ease the nation's environmental permitting laws and overhaul electrical transmission regulations, a crucial step toward boosting construction for the energy and technology industries.

Senators voted 62-33 to pass the bill, which split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

The vote offers a window into the fissures forming in the Democratic Party as it prepares to assume full control of Congress in January and tries to address the affordability crisis that catapulted it to power.

More Democrats voted against the permitting measure than voted for it. Still, more than a dozen — including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. — voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes to get the bill across the finish line.

"It's going to be legislation that's really going to make the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters on Thursday before the vote. Gallego supported the measure.

The bill's Senate passage is a key step to it becoming law, but it would also need to clear the House before heading to President Donald Trump's desk.

Democratic supporters of the bill touted its cost benefits as a win after they ran campaigns on affordability, and pointed to a massive glut of clean energy the bill could bring onto the grid. Opponents lamented rollbacks to the nation's bedrock environmental protection laws favored by the fossil fuel industry and Republicans, and warned the measure could offer carte blanche authority to the data centers undergirding artificial intelligence.

"No big, bipartisan bill is going to be perfect for everyone, but we have a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Working people can't afford to wait another few years for us to get this done," Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said in a statement to CNBC.

Heinrich brokered the agreement with his counterpart Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, along with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

"Earlier this month, Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," he said.

Getting to a final vote was acrimonious. Senators amended the package in the weeks leading up to the vote to address concerns from Native American tribes, which objected to changes in their participation in permitting.

"I'm not going to sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told reporters Thursday about the push for his amendment, which would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands.

Clean energy and fossil energy groups both cheered the bill's passage in the Senate.

As negotiated, the bill would benefit both renewables and fossil fuels. Artificial intelligence and the broader tech industry also stand to benefit — despite the bill's provision forcing hyperscalers to pay for upgrades to the grid — as power-hungry data centers demand more electricity.

The American Clean Power Association, a group that represents renewables, said it was "a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices."

The American Petroleum Institute, which represents the oil and gas industry, called the bill a "major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure."

Renewables would benefit largely from the bill's electricity transmission component, along with measures aimed at blocking Trump from cancelling already-permitted wind and solar projects. New solar and wind projects are often bottlenecked by a lack of transmission able to deliver power to the grid.

Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040. Natural gas exports would rise 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy. Greenhouse gases would be reduced by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040.

"A lot of Democrats are involved and supportive in this deal because expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy," said Rob Gramlich, the founder and president of Grid Strategies, an energy consulting group. "Republicans are maybe less interested in that benefit, but they do care about economic growth and serving new large loads. And I think members on both sides of the aisle are pretty well aware that we're doing much less grid investment here in the U.S. compared to other countries."

Gramlich added that "you can't get to 60 to 80% of our grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity."

However, the Natural Resources Defense Council was among the opponents.

"The House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers," the organization said in a statement. "Lawmakers should oppose this bill and try again next year to pass legislation worthy of the American people, not for the fossil fuel industry and data center companies."

The bill now heads to the House, where Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. Trump also supports the deal.

But as in the Senate, Democrats are expected to be divided.

"Democrats promised to lower bills, cut pollution, and protect ratepayers," said Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a longtime champion of permitting reform. "Voters are giving us a chance to show we mean it. BAAJA does all three. We should pass it before the end of this Congress."

House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, D-Calif., meanwhile, urged Democrats to say no to the permitting bill.

"Don't believe the lie that this terrible bill, exactly as drafted, is the last, best and only chance to ever do permitting reform," he said. "We can produce a better deal."

#2774. Bears-Lions Thanksgiving audience will be huge — and it could have been even bigger

Last year, both of the early Thanksgiving Day games broke the prior record for NFL regular-season audience size. This year, the all-time record of 57.2 million from the Chiefs-Cowboys game is likely safe.

With one small tweak to the schedule, it perhaps wouldn’t be.

In 2025, Packers-Lions attracted an incredible 47.7 million viewers. This year, the looming battle between the 7-2 Bears and 7-2 Lions should approach (if not match . . . if not beat) that number.

The problem is the second game. The 2-7 Eagles are in soft-tank mode. The 4-6 Cowboys have disintegrated into defensive disarray. While it will still attract a very large audience given the captive audience and the usual Thanksgiving routines, it likely won’t approach 50 million.

While the NFL has granted a permanent hammerlock to the Lions and Cowboys for the traditional Thanksgiving afternoon games, a simple tweak would have set the stage for Bears-Lions to break 50 million — and perhaps to threaten last year’s record.

Here’s the idea. Why not install flexibility to flip the start times of the afternoon games?

It’s no different than the usual Sunday-afternoon flex, like the one that happened this weekend when Steelers-Eagles moved from 4:25 p.m. ET to 1:00 p.m. ET and Jaguars-Giants slid to the higher-profile slot.

On Thanksgiving, the late-afternoon game always does better than the early one. In some years, the Lions game could be viewed as more attractive than the Cowboys game. This year would be one of those years.

It’s something to consider. Getting an annual Thanksgiving Day game doesn’t mean owning the window. And given the NFL’s current willingness, on and after Week 12, to flex from Sunday to Thursday or Sunday to Monday, why not reserve the right to acknowledge that, for the two afternoon games on Thanksgiving, the “best” one should be played in the higher-profile slot?

#2764. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.
