#2755. Karl-Anthony Towns letting his Knicks play speak loudest in face of uncertainty

MINNEAPOLIS — In his own words, this should be an uncomfortable situation for Karl-Anthony Towns.

Regardless, it's produced some of the best basketball of his career.

Before the season, when Towns still was publicly pushing for a contract extension from the Knicks, he said he wanted his long-term future settled "so I can feel as comfortable as possible." Without a new deal, he said, "there's no comfortability to be had."

Karl-Anthony Towns rises up for a rebound during the Knicks' win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026, in Toronto. NBAE via Getty Images

That new deal, of course, never materialized, as the Knicks shut down all extension negotiations for the season while navigating owner James Dolan's mandate to stay under the second apron. It left Towns in that uncomfortable situation.

He's responded by making a loud statement to Knicks brass with his play.

"I got a job to do, at the end of the day," Towns said before the team's game against the Timberwolves on Thursday. "I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what's best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I'm just here to do my job."

Towns entered Thursday night's game averaging 21.2 points, 3.9 assists and a league-high 14.1 rebounds while shooting 54.5 percent from the field and 40.0 percent from 3-point range.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a pass while being defended by Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

He has been by far the most consistently strong performer through the Knicks' rocky first few weeks of their championship defense.

He's shown no signs of letting that discomfort affect him. If anything, it is fueling him.

"I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates," Towns said. "So, that's all I really think about."

Towns' standout performances came just as he returned to Minnesota, where he spent the first nine years of his career.

He didn't want to opine Thursday about whether winning a championship with the Knicks validates the move for New York and means it won the blockbuster trade with the Timberwolves, which sent Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo back to Minnesota.

But at this point, it's a clear Knicks win.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a move on Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. Dan Hamilton-Imagn Images

But it doesn't make being back any less emotional for Towns, who still has a painting of him and his mother and father hugging that the Timberwolves gifted him. They were the last team he played for before his mother passed away during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"I still have so much love for this place," Towns said. "It doesn't go away. I think it's actually grown as I've been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she's in high school. It's a different part of life, but it's a part of life that I really enjoy."

Thursday was the third time Towns returned as an opponent. But it was the first time as a champion.

"It's always great to be home and to be back here," Towns said. "Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it's special to be back. Obviously, it's bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven't seen an NBA championship here. But it's great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here."

#2752. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2751. Research moves closer to identifying CTE in living patients

The ability to detect CTE only through autopsies prevents football players from knowing whether they have it during their careers. Work continues to change that.

Via ESPN, a pair of studies published by The Journal of the American Medical Association show that a new blood test could detect advanced stages of CTE in a living patient.

A study from Boston University and Banner Health was based on blood drawn from a small sample of former players during their lifetimes. Autopsies performed after they died showed that they had CTE. The researchers then found a marker for CTE based on the levels of a specific type of protein in their blood.

“I’m cautiously optimistic that we can really understand this finding and move it forward in the next five years or so,” Dr. Michael Alosco, one of the authors of the study, told ESPN. Alosco described the test as a “game changer.”

The study applies only to advanced stages of CTE.

“We are still in the discovery phase and it’s a small sample size,” Alosco said in a statement released regarding the study. “But if future studies validate these findings, this blood test will allow us to detect CTE with a high level of accuracy and open the doors to clinical trials and treatment.”

The ultimate goal remains developing a test that would show any degree of CTE in a living patient. It would allow football players to know whether they already have CTE, and possibly the extent of the disease.

Football players would first have to decide whether they want to know if they have CTE and, if they do, whether they will keep playing.

More broadly, football leagues at every level would have to decide whether players would be prevented from participating if they have CTE.

The development of a test to diagnose CTE could also lead to research aimed at identifying potential treatments for it.

Where the work leads will be determined over time. And the knowledge acquired by football players will allow for informed — if not complicated — decisions as to whether they will choose to keep playing, and whether they will be medically cleared to do so.

Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson commented publicly on Thursday for the first time since suffering a season-ending torn ACL in his right knee.

In an Instagram post, the two-time Pro Bowl defensive end pledged to come back from his injury stronger than ever and to never again jump up to celebrate a big play.

"I honestly can't believe it," Hutchinson wrote in his post. "I've jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me. But even something like this won't hold me back."

"Two things I know for sure," he added. "1. I always come back stronger. 2. That's the last time I go airborne."

Hutchinson injured his knee on the Lions' first defensive series during their matchup in Munich with the New England Patriots on Sunday.

Following a sack of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, Hutchinson jumped in celebration and landed awkwardly on his right leg. The star pass rusher immediately fell to the turf and quickly grabbed his right leg, gesturing to the front of his right knee.

Maye reportedly suffered a fractured ankle on the sack, though the Patriots have yet to confirm that injury. Yet Patriots coach Mike Vrabel sounded as if a return was possible for the quarterback this season, likely depending on whether surgery is required.

The Lions went on to a 35-10 win. With their fifth consecutive victory, Detroit improved its record to 7-2 and is tied with the Minnesota Vikings for first place in the NFC North. New England dropped to 5-5 after losing three of its past four games.

Hutchinson finishes his 2026-27 season with six sacks and 24 total tackles in nine games. He was also credited with one pass defended and one forced fumble.

The torn ACL is the second season-ending injury that Hutchinson has sustained in his five NFL seasons. During the 2024 season, he suffered a broken fibula and tibia in his left leg during a Week 6 win over the Dallas Cowboys. Hutchinson recovered to play in all 17 games last season, compiling 14.5 sacks.

#2745. Sunderland at Villa Park: Can the Lads Spring a Surprise?

Villa Park is one of the classic English football grounds, instantly recognisable as one of the best in the game.

As a football fan, it's one of the stadiums that is well worth a visit and, despite our ropey away record this season, I can't wait to make my second visit to this corner of Birmingham.

Villa are having an interesting season. After failing to score in their first three games, they haven't lost since 12th September and are picking up points in the league and on the continent.

Their last game at Old Trafford was utter madness, and Villa managed to blow a two-goal lead twice against a Manchester United side managed by Michael Carrick for the first time.

As we welcome Sunderland, we're probably moderately optimistic that we'll continue our unbeaten league run. With just a single point on the road this season, you can see why.

Historically, we've also got a poor record at Villa Park, but one of our few wins is always one that sticks with me because it was our first Premier League away win under Roy Keane. It came the day before my birthday – which is 23rd March – showing just how dire we'd been away from the SoL up to that season.

Phil Bardsley was the last Sunderland player to score a winner at this ground, in a 1-0 win in 2011, which really dates how long it's been since we returned from Villa Park with maximum points.

After another international break, the lads will hopefully be raring to go again and will play a bit better than we did after the last one. Some of our players went away; most stayed behind this time, which is probably for the best given our less-than-impressive start to the campaign.

Every game is hard in the Premier League, especially when we've made it easy for the opposition on too many occasions this season, and a trip to Villa Park will be no exception. I can't wait to be back watching the Lads and to make this second trip to this famous old stadium.

It can't be any less entertaining than my first visit, which ended 0-0, with Craig Gardner being sent off and Nicklas Bendtner having a perfectly fine goal ruled out for offside. In all fairness, a 0-0 draw on this occasion would be a great result and would keep us on the path of improvement.

Saturday is the start of another brutal run of games, which includes trips to Liverpool and Milan and a cup quarter-final. It's hard to decipher whether it's one of the easier games, as, having already lost to two of the newly promoted teams, none of that seems to necessarily matter.

Yet Villa are a team that can ship goals, and we've kept two clean sheets in our last three league matches. Is this clutching at straws and being glass-half-full? It certainly is.

My glass is probably even closer to being full because Saturday is an away day I can get to, and one which is just up the road from my Midlands flat. I'll be full of optimism until 3pm – then will come the stress, but I'll have had a few beers by then, so it's all good.

He looks so good upfront; his hold up play is coming on leaps and bounds and he's a genuine threat. Defences are definitely scared of him and that provides opportunities around him as a result. I love Wilson Isidor but feel we haven't given him a fair chance so far.

We need to be more adaptable in our build up so that we can use his pace in the channels or behind defenders. Perhaps we should also consider using two of our wingers at the same time before I'm sure Chemsdine Talbi, Nilson Angulo, Malick Fofana and Jocelin Ta Bi could all cause problems for the opposition.

Xhaka will be a miss as I still think his impact on the side when he's in the middle of the park can be significant given how young some of the players are.

That said he's lost a little of his spark in recent games and it's likely that Régis Le Bris will go with more pace in the middle. Given that we look best when we close with intensity and counter at pace, fresh legs at this stage of the season might be a bonus given the amount of games in the run up to the new year.

Brobbey has been immense and gives us so much when he's on his game, and the opposition centre backs are normally both focused on the big man. We had this problem with Ross Stewart — a catalyst for the team but with a season ticket to the treatment room.

Wilson Isidor is likely to start and if so, we need to play to his strengths and recognise we can't expect him to hold the ball up.

It means a different shape and style when we have the ball, and we need to bring in a decent striking option in January.

Xhaka needed a rest irrespective of the injury, and this is a great chance for the team to build from the Chelsea performance, and to progress options for longer time life without him.

It'll mean we need to be creative to rotate our midfield between the Premier League, Europe and the cups, but sometimes injuries bring opportunities for the team and certain players and I hope this is one that we benefit from.

The other side of the story is that without Brobbey, we're reliant on a hungry but immature contribution from Timur Tuteriov, and the pacy but less effective leading of the line from Wilson Isidor.

That said, Brobbey has been immense but a little inaccurate with chances of late — which is potentially down to his frequent visits to the physio's room.

We'll miss him massively in terms of his hold up play and physicality but we have a squad for a reason, and again if this gives Isidor a run of games supported by Tuteriov, who knows? We may see a couple of people down the pecking order grab the chance too.

Losing Xhaka provides a superb opportunity for Jules Ahoka to nail down a starting spot.

It's too early to judge whether the loss of Xhaka allowed us to play with the handbrake off against Chelsea. Does this make the players braver and less scared to make a mistake? He'll still be a voice around the dressing room and the training ground and will no doubt give us some tactical advice, too. We should certainly play with a bit more energy and pace through the middle.

We've already seen the drop off without Brobbey and missing someone with such unique physical output will leave a gaping hole in any team.

When we're so used to playing a certain way with Brobbey, it's not just a case of flipping the switch and instantly playing a different way. With that said, Wilson Isidor seemed to enjoy games against the Villa last season, and teams may not be set up to play against without having Brobbey to defend against.

Timur Tuteriov should still be full of confidence and we can still cause teams problems but the onus is on Régis Le Bris to make us more potent in attack and set us up to get attacking players involved in and around the eighteen-yard box to give us more threats across the park.

Given Jules Ahoka's remarkable rise to prominence, I feel that Xhaka's absence — although not ideal in terms of robbing us of depth as well as the experience he brings — can be dealt with.

If the DR Congo international and his teammates can raise their games to match the demands of Aston Villa and beyond, I think we can perhaps start to develop a style of play based on greater dynamism and forward motion in midfield. It'll also enable our captain to rest up, recover and possibly get back to somewhere near his most effective after an underwhelming season so far.

Xhaka's form has long been a concern but for the moment, we need to adapt, get on with things and place our faith in the likes of Ahoka, who looks perfectly suited to this level, it must be said.

However, trying to cope without Brobbey — a player that, had he been standing on the bow of the Titanic in 1912, the iceberg that caused the great ship to founder would've thought "To hell with this. I'm not messing with him. I'll find another ship to sink" — will be far more challenging, and I'm not entirely convinced we will.

Are Wilson Isidor and/or Timur Tuteriov going to bully defenders, hold the ball up, bring others into play and draw fouls with the same kind of potency as the Dutch striker? Unlikely, although slightly paradoxically, Isidor is a more composed and natural finisher than Brobbey and can certainly score goals at this level, as we've seen previously.

Bringing the best out of him will demand a new approach; for Sunderland to play at a higher tempo and for the likes of Enzo Le Fée to spot his runs and slide the ball into gaps for the Haitian international to run onto.

This was showcased at Villa Park last season when Isidor drew us level at 3-3, and if he gets the opportunity to impress in Brobbey's absence, I hope we don't try and deploy him as a clone of the former Ajax striker, but that we play to his strengths and attempt to get him into the heart of the action as often as possible.

More questions for Régis Le Bris to answer. Let's hope he can.

Unfortunately for Sunderland, I don't think you can put a positive spin on either of these injuries.

Whilst Xhaka has struggled for form this season and is perhaps in need of a break, his influence on the squad behind the scenes as well as on the pitch is no secret.

With an already threadbare midfield, Xhaka's absence will heap further pressure on those who are available, giving those in the middle little respite before the gruelling slog of the December and January fixtures.

As for Brobbey, yet another period on the sidelines is good for neither the team or for himself, especially given how crucial his physicality is when Sunderland play at their most effective.

With open-play goals for the Lads being as rare as hens' teeth this season, losing Brobbey's presence is undoubtedly a blow. This is perhaps exacerbated by Wilson Isidor's tendency to score in bursts and if Isidor can't hit the ground running over the coming weeks, further concerns will arise in Brobbey's absence.

Opportunities will of course come to those on the fringes, wth Jules Ahoka, Timur Tutierov and Juan Angulo standing to be beneficiaries of such absences in terms of increased game time, and whilst many will be relaxed on the prospect of Ahoka receiving further minutes, the same may not be said for others given the precariousness of our league position.

All in all, this is a case of two bad injuries at a bad time for us — at a time when our backs already feel firmly up against the wall. The only real hope we have is that in during trying times is when we usually see the best of Régis Le Bris.

#2732. Buccaneers at Lions: Thursday injury report for Week 11

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers received some encouraging news Thursday as they continued preparations for their Week 11 matchup against the Detroit Lions.

After missing Wednesday's practice, quarterback Baker Mayfield (foot/right thumb) returned to the practice field Thursday as a limited participant. It's a positive development for the veteran quarterback, whose availability for Sunday has been in question since suffering a foot injury against the Chicago Bears.

Mayfield revealed Thursday that the injury occurred early in the game against Chicago during a scramble that resulted in a completion to running back Kenny Gainwell. He played through the discomfort for the remainder of the contest.

When asked about his readiness to play against Detroit, Mayfield responded, "I feel ready."

While his return to practice is certainly encouraging, the Buccaneers are expected to make a determination on his availability Friday. Rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels remains the next man up should Mayfield be unable to play.

Unfortunately for Tampa Bay, safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (ankle) missed his second consecutive practice, while outside linebacker Yaya Diaby (knee) remained limited.

Wide receiver Chris Godwin Jr. and running back Bucky Irving were added to Thursday's injury report as non-participants, while defensive lineman A'Shawn Robinson was limited. All three received rest designations.

Cornerback Josh Hayes (knee), tight end Cade Otton (thumb) and left tackle Tristan Wirfs (toe) remained full participants.

For Detroit, there were no changes to its injury report from Wednesday. Center Cade Mays (ankle) remained sidelined, while six players, including cornerbacks D.J. Reed (hip) and Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (shoulder), remained limited. Safety Kerby Joseph (knee) was once again a full participant.

Both teams will release their final injury reports Friday, with much of the attention in Tampa Bay continuing to surround Mayfield and whether he will be healthy enough to lead the Buccaneers' offense Sunday in Detroit.

#2730. Lakers vs. Kings Preview: Time to start another winning streak

After witnessing their nine-game losing streak come to an end, the Lakers (13-3) have the opportunity to get back in the win column on Friday against the Sacramento Kings (1-13). This is considered an NBA Cup Game for both teams under Group C.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers vs. Sacramento Kings

Nobody is more disappointed in the Lakers' losing streak ending than the team themselves. After Wednesday's loss to the Utah Jazz — where they put up their worst offensive game of the season — head coach JJ Redick and Luka Dončić were pretty bullish on not bringing up the fatigue card despite this being their third game in four nights.

That alone says a lot about this team's character and their determination to be the best they can be, night in and night out. It's what makes the upcoming match against the Kings quite interesting because we're going to see how the Lakers bounce back, especially with the added stakes of an NBA Cup Game.

On Friday, Los Angeles will see a Sacramento team that has lost seven games in a row. That means the Kings could come into this matchup either very hungry for a win, struggling to find their footing or perhaps a little bit of both. Maybe playing on the road will help these Kings because they just finished a disastrous 0-7 homestand.

Ideally, the Lakers shouldn't need Dončić to score 40 points again in this one because it would nice to see a collective team effort win. In their last meeting against the Kings, when the Lakers came away with a 13-point win, we saw arguably their best defensive effort of the season. Hopefully, we see that same level of intensity again because the Lakers could use as convincing a win as possible to keep their NBA Cup hopes alive.

If it's not too much to ask, perhaps an 11-point win or more, so the purple and gold can climb to second place, with the hope that the Warriors lose their remaining NBA Cup games as well. That would set the Lakers up as the wildcard team in Group C.

The Lakers need to make sure that Darius Acuff Jr. — the only bright spot for the Kings so far this season — doesn't go off. Same goes with a microwave scorer like Zach LaVine and even Domantas Sabonis, who combined for 37 points last time. That was the same L.A. team that lost the rebounding battle (46-36), which can't happen again.

It would be nice to see a bounceback performance from Walker Kessler, who struggled mightily against the Jazz last Tuesday. Same goes with Sandro Mamukelashvili, Colin Sexton and Jake LaRavia, who need to provide some scoring to ease off the pressure on Dončić and Quentin Grimes.

If the Lakers regain their offense and play like the team that had just won nine straight games, then they should be able to take care of this one. Let's see if they can start another winning streak by defeating the Kings on Friday.

The Kings have struggled to close out games, which could work in the Lakers' favor. Ideally, L.A. won't need a clutch-time performance but if it comes down to that, they should be able to capitalize.

The Kings also don't guard the 3-point line very well. In their previous game against the Phoenix Suns, the latter shot 44% from deep.

On to the injury report, only Austin Reaves (left heel contusion) is out.

As for the Kings, Ben Simmons (right Achilles tendon repair) and Maxime Raynaud (right patella subluxation) are out. Precious Achiuwa (left lower leg contusion) is doubtful, while De'Andre Hunter (left hip soreness) is questionable.

#2728. Mauricio Pochettino: Man United squad’s surprise first impression of new boss

Manchester United are embarking on a fresh journey under their new manager Mauricio Pochettino, who took charge as Michael Carrick's replacement at Old Trafford on Wednesday.

With the team languishing in 18th place in the Premier League table after 10 games, having managed just one win, the Red Devils decided to part ways with the English manager last week.

Pochettino, who was most recently in charge of the United States Men's National Team, was identified as the ideal candidate to get the Premier League giants out of troubled waters.

The Argentine met his new squad following his arrival at Old Trafford and even oversaw his first training session at the club ahead of the fiery game against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, 22 November. A fresh report now sheds light on the players' first impression of their new manager.

Mauricio Pochettino Managerial Career Stats

According to the Manchester Evening News, United players who have already interacted with Pochettino believe he will be a demanding manager. The report states: "The MEN understands that Manchester United players who Mauricio Pochettino has spoken with have been left with the impression that he will be demanding to work under."

The report, though, acknowledges that there is a general excitement about the future among the players, adding: "However, there is a general feeling of excitement for the future under the current crop of players."

Pochettino is well versed with the rigours of the Premier League, having spent time at Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea.

The Argentine has managed close to 294 games in the English top flight, registering 150 wins, 70 draws and 74 defeats. While he had a mixed spell at Stamford Bridge, the 54-year-old remains highly regarded for his work with Spurs, having transformed the north London side into one of the best in the league.

United's performances this season have lacked intensity at times, while they also appear to be low on morale. There remains a belief that the team is close to salvation but is faltering at the final hurdle.

The football under Carrick has been impressive at times, but it has not been to the standards that the Englishman set last season. United have struggled to score as well as keep clean sheets this campaign.

They have also lacked control in the middle of the park, despite investing over €150 million on Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba over the summer.

Perhaps the biggest complaint has been their lack of fight on the pitch at times, which is something Pochettino must address immediately. The Argentine's preference for high-intensity attacking football could just be the solution to the Red Devils' woes.

#2723. San Antonio vs. Los Angeles, Final Score: Spurs outlast Clippers in 124-112 win

It didn't take long for the Spurs to get back on the winning track. The Silver and Black didn't amaze, but they took care of business at home against a shorthanded Clippers team. The 124-112 score might suggest that it was a comfortable victory, but it was mostly a close game in which the more talented squad simply stepped on the gas late to close it out.

The Spurs, facing an inferior opponent after the loss to the Pistons but missing Dylan Harper, didn't look as dominant as it would have been ideal to start the game. The pace wasn't great, and neither was the decision-making for most of the first half. Defensively, they had good stretches but also moments in which they allowed dribble penetration without much resistance or left shooters open. It wasn't the strong bounceback many were hoping for, but because of their tremendous talent, they managed to lead by 14 points at one point in the second quarter.

Unfortunately, the lead disappeared as the bench had one of its all-too-familiar poor runs. In all fairness, however, the second unit wasn't the only reason why the home team only led by three at the break, as the starters didn't return with the energy required to pull away. Some good moments showed the high ceiling the Silver and Black have, but it wasn't a particularly inspiring first half. The Clippers deserve credit for capitalizing on the at times lackadaisical and downright sloppy play from the Spurs, but a lot of San Antonio's wounds in the opening two frames were self-inflicted.

In the second half, the visitors went from simply being opportunistic to actively hurting the Spurs on the offensive end. The threes were falling, and they were not afraid to hunt mismatches, using Brook Lopez in the post, especially in the third quarter. Ty Lue's guys were confident after coming back to make it close earlier and put themselves ahead on the scoreboard with more consistent play, while San Antonio relied on individual stretches of greatness from different players. Castle had it going as a scorer, Devin Vassell made some defensive plays, and even some of the bench guys got in on the action.

A legitimate blowout was out of the question after three quarters, but the Spurs have been good at elevating their play when they need to throughout this season. It's been enough for them to beat lesser teams, and it happened again against the Clippers. It wasn't the prettiest of games, something that has also been a trend this year, but San Antonio did what it needed to. As the minutes passed, the Silver and Black got a double-digit lead, and they didn't squander it late. Hopefully, it will be the beginning of another long win streak.

As expected, Mitch Johnson started Julian Champagnie in place of Dylan Harper, out with a hip injury. The Fox-Castle-Vassell-Champagnie-Wembanyama unit started most of last season and outscored opponents by over 17 points per 100 possessions, so it should be fine. Still, there were some moments early when the lack of a third ball handler seemed to bother San Antonio. The turnovers piled up as some players, especially Stephon Castle, often forced the issue. The Spurs will miss Harper, which was expected.

Devin Vassell continues to be cold in the outside shooting department (3-for-16 in the last four games), but as usual nowadays, he made an impact elsewhere. Hopefully the shooting touch returns soon.

Carter Bryant was the first guy off the bench for the Harper-less Spurs. In the second half, Jordan McLaughlin got the call. Mitch Johnson is experimenting with his rotations and trying to find guys that can replace Harper's athleticism and ball-handling. We might see different players get minutes depending on what the team needs on any given night.

The second unit has been getting a lot of flak, mostly deserved, for their play early in the season, but they were huge for the Spurs on Thursday. They brought a lot of energy to a game that sometimes lacked it, at least from San Antonio's side.

Brandon Ingram, the big piece going back to the Clippers in the Kawhi Leonard trade, was out with an injury. The other player Los Angeles received in the transaction, Gradey Dick, wasn't all that effective in limited minutes. The Clippers' major summer move had little effect on the result of this one.

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI provided the Spurs' broadcast with the perfect excuse to show one of the best photos ever: the 99 team playing StarCraft together after winning the title. Look at those magnificent nerds.

The Spurs will host the Pelicans on Saturday. New Orleans will be in the second game of a back-to-back after playing the Thunder on Friday.

#2721. Louis Saha Backs Régis Le Bris Amid Sunderland’s Tough Spell

Interview brought to you by https://www.casinohawks.com/

Former Sunderland striker Louis Saha believes Régis Le Bris has earned the backing of the club's hierarchy, insisting there is little reason to be concerned about the Frenchman's ability despite the challenges currently facing the Black Cats.

Le Bris has enjoyed a remarkable start to life at the Stadium of Light, guiding Sunderland back into the Premier League before helping establish the club in the top flight and secure European qualification.

However, competing domestically and in Europe has brought additional demands, with injuries, defensive inconsistencies and questions over Sunderland's attacking options contributing to a more difficult spell.

Speaking about where he would rank Le Bris among current French managers working across Europe's top five leagues, Saha was full of praise for his compatriot.

"Régis Le Bris is definitely an up-and-coming French manager. I think he's done really well," Saha explained.

"Promotion is always a tricky moment because of the challenges that you face across a long season, even for the bigger clubs.

"They've done pretty well to not only maintain their place in the top flight, but also get to Europe. And now it's obviously a bigger challenge because you could be playing well in Europe, winning two games is impressive for them."

Saha acknowledged that the Premier League can expose weaknesses in a squad, particularly when options in attacking areas are limited, but believes Sunderland's recent difficulties should be viewed in that context.

"But the Premier League is where you get caught, especially if you don't have options up front. So the recent results are down to maybe some injuries, defensive instabilities, and stuff like this.

"I think that's why he still has the backing of this board. They know it's a tough moment, but it's nothing to worry about in terms of Le Bris and how good he is as a manager."

Saha also discussed the international prospects of Sunderland pair Nordi Mukiele and Enzo Le Fée, with both players having ambitions of representing France on the biggest stage.

While missing out on a potential World Cup call-up would have been disappointing, the former Manchester United and Sunderland forward believes there could still be opportunities for the pair under national team manager Zinedine Zidane.

Saha highlighted Zidane's willingness to look beyond the most established names when making his selections, suggesting that playing outside the traditional top leagues will not necessarily prevent players from earning international recognition.

"It's hard for Nordi Mukiele and Enzo Le Fée, but what is a great opportunity for them both is that they have a national manager who isn't only picking players from the top flight who are well known by him.

"Zidane has proved that he's also looking at players in the second division [of Germany]. That's the case for one player who's been called up, so I think the two players from Sunderland can definitely have their chances."

Saha's message to the Sunderland duo was straightforward: continue performing and make the most of the opportunities presented by playing European football.

"They have to keep going. And obviously, it's easier when you play in Europe and show your quality on the biggest stages."

Saha also offered an interesting assessment of Sunderland's current striking options, with Brian Brobbey, Wilson Isidor and Timur Tutyerov all providing different possibilities for Le Bris.

The former Black Cats forward believes it is understandable that Sunderland have become increasingly reliant on Brobbey, particularly because of the Dutchman's ability to lead the line independently.

His physical presence, hold-up play and finishing provide Sunderland with an important focal point, especially when the team are under pressure and need an outlet.

"It's totally normal that there is going to be a reliance on Brian Brobbey because he is able to play that role alone, providing that focal point. He gives you that extra second to resettle, especially when you are under pressure. And he's a good finisher.

"So definitely, when Sunderland are struggling to create chances, he's got the ability to convert straight away. I think it's definitely a big plus having Brobbey."

However, Saha also believes Brobbey and Isidor could operate together, with the latter offering a different dimension through his movement and ability to exploit space behind opposition defences.

"But they also complement each other because if you look at the style of Isidor, he's someone who runs in behind when he's got space.

"So I think they can play together in the same team at the same time. It's just a matter of timing."

Saha suggested that Le Bris is currently prioritising greater stability throughout the side, particularly in midfield and defence, before looking to make the most of his attacking options.

"When you are under pressure, the manager tends to always look for security. Having this setup and a better structure in midfield and defence, I think it's a moment where Le Bris is looking for that stability before relying on what was done last year."

Ultimately, Saha believes Sunderland have three complementary attacking options who can offer different qualities depending on the opposition and circumstances of a match.

"Those strikers are very complementary, so let's hope they can carry on how they're doing in Europe."

For Le Bris, the challenge will be finding the right balance between restoring consistency in the Premier League and continuing Sunderland's impressive European adventure.

But Saha's assessment offers an encouraging endorsement of the manager, his current squad and the direction of the club under his leadership.

#2716. Warriors finish winless road trip with lopsided loss to Grizzlies

It turns out that Steph Curry is pretty important to the Golden State Warriors success. When the Dubs head out on a five-game road trip just over a week ago, they did it with an eight-game winning streak and all the momentum in the world. And then, just a few minutes into the five-city trip, Curry suffered an oblique injury, and a few hours later, the Warriors lost to the Houston Rockets. What followed was brutal: a 38-point loss to the San Antonio Spurs, a 21-point defeat at the hands of the New Orleans Pelicans, a 22-point loss to the upstart Dallas Mavericks, and finally, on Thursday night, a 28-point loss to the surprisingly great Memphis Grizzlies.

The silver lining, if you're into that sort of thing, is that the Warriors looked the best that they have since Curry was injured, despite losing 126-98. The execution was the best it had been in a while, but ultimately, an astounding lack of shooting did the Dubs in.

As had been the case in all of the other Curry-less games, the Warriors got off to a comically slow start. They trailed 5-0, and then 8-2, and Steve Kerr's first timeout came when the Warriors trailed 13-4 just a few minutes in, as the team was racking up the turnovers. Even the good news was bittersweet: Charles Bassey scored the first seven points for Golden State, but also collected three quick fouls.

Still, the Warriors were executing well … mostly. They couldn't resist turning the ball over, with eight giveaways in the first quarter alone, but they were creating things on offense and getting good looks. Unfortunately, the good looks weren't falling, and they weren't able to do much on defense. Even with a nice run to end the opening frame, the Warriors trailed 31-24 after the first.

The Grizzlies came out firing in the second quarter, and quickly led 43-29 with an astonishing 21 points off of turnovers. That, combined with the Warriors' inability to make seemingly any jump shot, made it clear that unless there was a serious reversal of fortunes, the Warriors would not be winning. And there was, unfortunately, no reversal of fortune.

Memphis was turning Golden State's turnovers and missed shots into offens of their own, and used a 14-1 run to turn the game into a blowout at 47-30. But Golden State's response was impressive. The defense really stepped up late, and put the clamps on the Grizzlies with some of their best possessions in the past week (low bar, I know). That led to some much better offensive possessions, with the team getting significantly more aggressive to make up for the unsuccessful shooting. After trailing at one point by 18, the Warriors ran off a 10-0 run, and thanks to a strong defensive stand to end the half, only trailed 55-47 at the break. They had only made three shots from beyond the arc, they had no players in double figures, and Yaxel Lendeborg had yet to make a field goal, yet somehow they were in the game.

It wouldn't last long. For the third quarter in a row, the Grizzlies started the third hot, and quickly pushed the lead comfortably into the double digits. It felt like the Warriors were so close to playing well, but just couldn't quite get over the hump. They would execute well but miss shots, and then they would follow it up with some impressive individual plays supplemented by poor execution. The third quarter was ultimately defined by a distinct lack of easy shots … even when they scored, they simply couldn't get anything easy, and labored over every possession, good or bad. They still couldn't make any threes, and they still had too many turnovers, though credit where it's due: the energy and effort level didn't fade a bit, from opening tip until final buzzer. But energy and effort were no match for talent and execution, and the Grizzlies took a 92-73 lead into the final frame.

From there, it was just window dressing. The Grizzlies again were on fire to start the quarter, and quickly pushed the lead well into the 20s, making it clear that there would be no miraculous comeback for the Dubs. Both teams emptied their benches fairly early, as Memphis rolled to a 126-98 victory, their second win of the season against Golden State.

The Warriors had a serious talent deficit, playing without not just Curry, but also Draymond Green, Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Brandon Williams. Charles Bassey led the way with 16 points, and also grabbed 13 rebounds for a double-double, while Will Richard had another strong game off the bench, scoring 15 points and playing excellent defense. But Yaxel Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski once again struggled to carry the offense with Curry out, with the former scoring 11 points on 3-for-11 shooting, and the latter 15 points on 5-for-12 shooting. While Lendeborg struggled on offense, he played a good defensive game, and finished with eight rebounds, seven assists, one steal, and two blocks.

For Memphis, Jaylen Wells (22 points and seven rebounds on 8-for-10 shooting) and rookie Cameron Boozer (16 points, six rebounds, and five assists on 6-for-6 shooting) starred in a total team effort. But the biggest discrepancy, as it has been for much of the road trip, was the shooting. Golden State shot a miserable 5-for-29 (17.2%) from deep, while the Grizzlies went an excellent 15-for-35 (42.9%). That, along with 22 turnovers, is how you lose by 28 points.

#2714. OTD (20/11/1999): Sunderland Left To Rue Missed Chances As Liverpool End Unbeaten Home Run

The 1999/2000 season was quickly becoming one of Sunderland's greatest in recent times, with the team sitting pretty near the top of the table after a hugely impressive start to the season, whilst a year-long unbeaten home record remained intact.

Not since 21st August 1999 had Peter Reid's Sunderland tasted defeat in the FA Carling Premiership, but that run would come to an end when Liverpool came to town on this cold November day, with young striker Michael Owen continuing his rise to fame as England's great new hope.

Truthfully, this was a game that Sunderland could – and most certainly should – have won given the number of chances they created. The fearsome duo of Niall Quinn and Kevin Phillips had a hatful of opportunities throughout the game, whilst the away side had their goalkeeper Sander Westerveld to thank for a number of incredible saves, one of which was a particularly sensational effort to tip Phillips' header over the bar with Liverpool 1-0 up.

After the game, Peter Reid had very few complaints about his side's performance but rued their uncharacteristic lack of ruthlessness in front of goal, given their success thus far in the season.

"We didn't stick them in. If you don't take chances you don't win games."

The first half was largely characterised by our lack of conviction in front of goal and, whilst Niall Quinn had Liverpool defender Sami Hyypiä all over the place, the Irishman was consistently failing to capitalise on the opportunities that came his way and was guilty of spurning the best chance we created in the opening half.

The Republic of Ireland international muscled his way into the penalty area and chipped Westerveld, only for Rigobert Song to clear off the line.

His strike partner Phillips was not faring much better, and these missed opportunities were all the more disappointing given how much Liverpool struggled to bring their own star striker, Michael Owen, into the game during the first half.

Things didn't get much better for our attackers as the second half got underway, with Nicky Summerbee's inch-perfect cross being headed just wide by Phillips. With yet another chance going begging, Reid must have been wondering whether it was going to be our day and, against the run of play, the aforementioned Owen finally got his break.

A long ball upfield left Owen and Darren Williams in a footrace and, with Williams looking somewhat hapless and clumsy in his attempts to deal with the bouncing ball, the England striker nipped in ahead of him before dinking the ball over Thomas Sørensen to round off what was a brilliant solo goal.

The goal certainly aggrieved the home support, perhaps in part due to Owen's rather overzealous celebrations, but it was a real kick in the teeth given the performance we had put in with little to show for our efforts.

Reid opted against making any changes in response to the goal, but his side continued to plug away, with Phillips' aforementioned glancing header looking destined for the back of the net had it not been for Westerveld's heroics.

Quinn also went agonisingly close with another header, but with five minutes remaining, Liverpool put the game to bed and, in doing so, brought Sunderland's impressive unbeaten home run to an end.

Patrik Berger made sure of the points with a powerful finish following a run and cross from substitute David Thompson, who was inexplicably allowed to run free by Michael Gray, the Sunderland full-back appearing to slow to a complete stop after Thompson had cleverly evaded him.

Whilst the manner of the defeat was frustrating, perhaps the biggest compliment you could pay Peter Reid and his players was the fact that Sunderland supporters were leaving the Stadium of Light feeling somewhat aggrieved at having lost to a team of Liverpool's calibre.

After all, it was only a matter of months since we had been playing our football in the second tier, yet here we were, going toe-to-toe with one of the biggest clubs in English football and coming away wondering how on earth we hadn't taken all three points.

There would be plenty more memorable afternoons to come in a season that would ultimately see Sunderland finish seventh in the Premiership, but this was one of those occasions where the scoreline did little justice to the quality of the Sunderland side Peter Reid had assembled.

#2708. Puka Nacua's suspension arises from diversion program

The NFL’s statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn’t specify the reason for it. Further information provided by the league makes the basis for the ban clear.

It comes from Nacua’s entry into a “diversion program,” related to the incident that triggered a civil lawsuit alleging (among other things) that he bit a woman on New Year’s Eve.

In September, we explained that Nacua had begun the steps required to complete a diversion program, which happened without Nacua entering into a formal agreement to do so. It’s one of the unique facets of California law; namely, California gives some defendants the ability to embark on the steps to comply with a diversion program without the kind of express deal that would have automatically triggered review under the Personal Conduct Policy.

The approach ultimately didn’t avoid the NFL scrutiny.

The suspension of Nacua for three games, with the acknowledgment from the league that failure “to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program” will result in “additional and more substantial discipline,” means that the mere commencement of the process of compliance, even without an express agreement with prosecutors, was enough to get the process rolling.

It also led to a negotiated conclusion that entails Nacua being suspended for games he otherwise would have missed, due to his status on injured reserve. While it all looks convenient at best and fishy at worst, it represents the outcome of a bargain aimed at resolving the situation without full-blown activation of a process that would have entailed a formal hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, the person jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association to hear the evidence and to issue a preliminary decision.

Karl-Anthony Towns of the New York Knicks drives to the basket against the Minnesota Timberwolves on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. NBAE via Getty Images

The Knicks led by 12 entering the fourth quarter and were quickly up by 16 after Tyler Kolek's four-point play to start the quarter. But the Knicks proceeded to miss their next 13 shots and saw their lead dwindle to four.

It appeared they had stabilized a bit when Karl-Anthony Towns' driving layup and Mikal Bridges' subsequent 3-pointer put them back up by nine.

But Towns, after review, was given a technical for flopping for trying to get a foul called on Rudy Gobert. A free throw, a Gobert alley-oop and an Ayo Dosunmu 3-pointer later, and the Knicks led by just three. Towns was then called for an offensive foul and Mikal Bridges badly missed a jumper on the Knicks' next offensive possession.

New York Knicks guard Miles McBride (2) and Minnesota Timberwolves forward Jaden McDaniels reach for the ball on Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt

But the Timberwolves couldn't find a quality shot in between and never got closer than that three-point deficit. LaMelo Ball badly missed a potential game-tying 3-pointer with under 10 seconds left, and the Timberwolves weren't able to foul the Knicks after they corralled the rebound.

Despite the ugly finish, it meant the Knicks closed their four-game road trip 3-1 before heading back to New York.

Towns had 17 points at halftime, and Jalen Brunson erupted for 14 points in the third quarter. It appeared the Knicks would cruise to an impressive win over a quality opponent.

But Towns went 1-for-5 in the fourth quarter, while Brunson went scoreless in the quarter. As a team, the Knicks went 2-for-14 and scored just 12 points in that fourth quarter.

"I wanted to put on a show for these fans," Towns, returning to Minnesota as an opponent for the third time since the Knicks' blockbuster trade, said. "In the second half I didn't shoot well, I ain't gonna lie to you."

#2699. Vikings explored all options before deciding to stay in Minnesota this week

As Sunday’s Mexico City game between the Vikings and 49ers approaches, one of the big issues is the decision of the 49ers to spend the week at altitude in Colorado Springs while the Vikings opted to stay in Minnesota.

On that point, multiple 49ers players have claimed that the Vikings tried to secure the Air Force Academy facility at Colorado Springs, but the 49ers had beaten them to the punch.

The Vikings, we’re told, explored all options — including going to Air Force Acadamey facility and going to Mexico City early. They ultimately decided to implement a plan premised on staying in Minnesota as long as possible.

Obviously, the Vikings could have figured out something that would have allowed them to spend the week somewhere that would have allowed for full acclimation. There are other practice facilities in Colorado. And, again, early arrival in Mexico was always a possibility.

The issue has likely become a focal point of the days preceding the game because of the dramatically different approaches used by the 49ers and Rams before their Week 1 game in Australia. San Francisco went early; the Rams arrived late. And the 49ers stunned the Rams, 27-7.

In that case, it was about time and distance traveled. Here, it’s the same time zone, and the flight is roughly four hours — not much farther for the Vikings than a trip to Seattle, San Francisco, or L.A.

Teams that play in Denver don’t spend the week in Colorado. And while the altitude results in more sideline shots of players with oxygen masks during games, no one ever says, “Well, that team lost to the Broncos because they weren’t acclimated to the altitude.”

The Vikings-49ers game won’t turn on that. If the 49ers win, it will be because they were the better team during those 60 minutes of clock time. And, if the Vikings win, it won’t be because they someone cracked the code on playing at altitude.

#2697. C.J. Stroud, Texans take care of business vs. cratering Colts: TNF winners, losers

If you tuned in to stream the Houston Texans vs. Indianapolis Colts on "Thursday Night Football" to kick off Week 11 of the 2026 NFL season ... we're sorry for you. Hopefully you had the good sense to log out early.

If not − or if you're looking for a (very quick) recap − the Texans unsurprisingly put the Colts down in a 26-3 romp, though one that should give Houston added relevance moving forward.

But while we wouldn't suggest one of the worst games of the season will have massive ramifications across the league's landscape, there are certainly going to be some ripples. Your winners and losers from "TNF" on Nov. 19:

Four days after what could eventually prove a seismic collapse at Cleveland, the Texans improved to 4-6 and jumped up to ninth place in the conference − two games (and a tiebreaker) behind the Browns for the AFC's final wild-card berth. Still, Houston's schedule does have the potential to continue vaulting this team past some of its collapsing conference brethren.

An efficient night for Houston's QB1, who launched three TD passes and once again looked like the linchpin of this team. Stroud, who turned down an extension in the offseason, could find the market renders him the league's top-paid player in a few months ... if this keeps up.

If you were smart − or obsessed − you steered clear of football in Houston in order to start running roughshod in Vice City (don't catch any strays, Dolphins). We wish we'd been there to join you, getting fresh tags on that boosted Lambo.

Playing for the first time in nearly six weeks after recovering from a groin injury, the veteran tailback had his best outing in a Houston uniform, rushing for a season-high 107 yards on 26 carries. And a balanced offense − meaning a sustained running game for a team that's had one 1,000-yard rusher since the start of the 2020 season − could really make this team dangerous if it finds its way into the postseason field, especially given how a ground attack would reduce the need for Stroud to carry the offense.

The NFL's sack leader was a menace, adding to his league-best total (11½) with one takedown of Colts QB Daniel Jones while getting four licks on him Thursday. Houston's All-Pro pass rusher should very much be in this season's Defensive Player of the Year conversation, regardless of how the Texans finish.

You guys are so lucky you were liberated from Indianapolis prior to the league's trade deadline.

Houston broke out its new, predominantly (Liberty) white Nike "Rivalries" uniforms for prime time. Meh? Make no mistake, the team put a lot of thought into the threads and tying them into Houston's culture. But not sure they're going to make many non-Houstonians clamor for Ka'imi Fairbairn jerseys.

The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Heading into a mini bye, worth wondering if QB2 Anthony Richardson, who mopped up in Houston, gets a shot to play more in the coming weeks.

Whether Steichen is fired next year or retained, he won't be out of work for long − but hopefully he gets a reasonable chance to showcase his ability to generate offense by playing with a full deck in 2027.

The AFC teams most at risk of getting left in the also-ran dust if the Texans get a full head of steam. Beware, too, Browns ... though your margin is pretty cushy right now.

#2696. Avary Cain's breakout performance carries Oregon women past Fairfield

Coming into the year, Avary Cain was expected to take on a much greater offensive role for the Oregon women's basketball team than the one she had last winter.

A former five-star prep recruit who began her career at UCLA, Cain has made her presence felt on the defensive end during the early portion of the season but struggled to get going offensively.

Oregon's final home game of November, though, served as an offensive coming-out party for the talented junior.

Cain scored 23 points on 9-for-12 shooting, including 4 of 6 from 3-point range, to help the Ducks (6-1) to a 96-71 win over Fairfield (3-2) Nov. 19 at Matthew Knight Arena in Eugene. That smashed her previous career high of 13 points, which came last March against Maryland.

"I think my teammates did a really good job of finding me," Cain said. "I think it just all starts with them. It felt really good getting my confidence back there on the court."

Coming into the game, Cain averaged just 5.7 points per game on 34% shooting.

But she caught fire in the first quarter, pouring in 11 points and canning all three of her 3-point attempts to give the Ducks a 32-20 lead at the end of the period.

"Honestly, I think this was the best game we've played this year," Oregon coach Kelly Graves said. "We came out right from the tip and got after it. Offensively, we were on point. ... It was one of those games where things were working. Defensively, (Fairfield) are a tough team to guard. I thought we did a great job tonight defensively as well."

Katie Fiso poured in a team-high 27 points on 12-of-16 shooting to lead five Ducks in double figures. Fiso also dished out eight assists. Ehis Etute scored 12 and grabbed 10 boards for her sixth double-double of the year.

"If we keep getting that kind of production up and down the lineup, we're going to be tough to guard," Graves said.

As a group, Oregon shot 13 of 29 from downtown and scored 40 points in the paint.

Brooklynn Haywood was the lone Oregon bench player to log double-digit minutes. Each of the Ducks' starters played at least 30 minutes.

Graves said that was, in part, because "no lead is safe" against Fairfield, which reached the NCAA Tournament after winning the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference Tournament last year.

Graves also had his squad's upcoming schedule in mind.

"That starting group, they were firing on all cylinders. ... We have a whole week before we play our next game," Graves said. "So, I knew they were going to get a lot of rest."

The Ducks now head to Mexico for the Cancun Classic, where matchups with Maryland Eastern Shore (Nov. 26), Colorado (Nov. 27) and Georgia (Nov. 28) await.

Jarrid Denney is a sports reporter for The Register-Guard. He can be reached at jdenney@registerguard.com or on X @jarrid_denney

#2695. Jack Ham will return to Penn State radio booth following medical emergency

Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Ham announced he will return to the Penn State radio booth on Saturday, two weeks after a medical emergency.

Ham, a color analyst for the Penn State Sports Network since 2000, was transported to the University of Washington Medical Center during pregame of the Nittany Lions’ Nov. 7 game. He missed Penn State’s game against Minnesota last week.

I’ve spent a lot of Saturdays in Beaver Stadium, first on the field and then up in the booth,” Ham, 77, said in his statement. “I’ll be back alongside Steve [Jones] this weekend, and there’s nowhere else I’d rather be.”

Jones treated Ham at the scene, saving his life, according to Penn State coach Matt Campbell. Ham remained in the hospital several days before returning to Pennsylvania on Saturday.

“I’m feeling good, and I owe a great deal to the people who took care of me and stood by me through all of it,” Ham said.

Ham was a six-time All-Pro with the Steelers, with whom he won four Super Bowl championships. He also made eight Pro Bowl appearances. He earned All-America honors at Penn State in 1970.

He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and the College Football Hall of Fame two years later.

#2694. Russell Westbrook shows there’s no hard feelings in Los Angeles with heartfelt statement

Russell Westbrook spent four seasons in Los Angeles.

Russell Westbrook hands out Thanksgiving meals in Los Angeles. Instagram/@whynotfoundation

This holiday season, Westbrook has kept a close connection to the Los Angeles community.

Three years ago, Westbrook and the Clippers opened a community basketball court at Jesse Owens Park in South Los Angeles where he grew up. On Thursday, Westbrook returned to his hometown to hand out Thanksgiving meals and groceries.

Not long before Westbrook joined the Clippers, his 18-month tenure with the Lakers featured a fractured relationship with superstar LeBron James, locker room tension and organizational fallout.

But the franchise moved on and so did he.

Russell Westbrook hands out Thanksgiving meals. Instagram/@whynotfoundation

In August, the 2016-17 MVP announced his retirement after 18 seasons in the league. It was a shocking decision given many of his former teammates believed Westbrook could have continued his NBA career.

While Westbrook's time with the Lakers seemingly ended in dramatic fashion, it's evident he still holds the city near to his heart.

#2688. Rapid Recap: Trail Blazers 124, Bucks 114

In a game with plenty of highs and lows, the Milwaukee Bucks lost to the Portland Trail Blazers 124-114. On the second night of their back-to-back, the Bucks came out lethargic, but frankly, so did the Blazers. Portland gave Milwaukee plenty of chances to blow the game open, but they refused to take them, and in the end, Portland's vets knew what to do when the game was on the line. On the positive side, Nate Ament dropped a career-high 18 points on 6/11 shooting, while the Blazers were led by old friend Damian Lillard, who scored a season-high 33.

Early on, this looked like a game where the Bucks were on the second night of a back-to-back and the Blazers were deep into a road trip, with intensity lacking on both sides. Tyler Herro looked rough, losing the ball and even missing free throws. Thankfully, Nate Ament was the spark, scoring seven of the first nine points as the Bucks took an early lead. Without Deni Avdija, the Blazers looked considerably less dangerous offensively but still stayed close thanks to their defence as they kept forcing turnovers. Of course, it didn't help that the Bucks, yet again, couldn't make a free throw to save themselves, going 2/7 (!) in the opening quarter. And to top it all off, Gary Trent Jr. went for one of his signature steal attempts on the final play and missed, leaving Scoot Henderson open for three to give his team a 24-21 lead—really disappointing stuff.

It was more of the same bad Bucks basketball to open the second: more turnovers, missed free throws, and bad fouls as the Blazers quickly upped their lead to double digits, 32-22. Thank goodness for Nate Ament, though, who poured in a quick five points—paired with triples from Tyler Herro and Kel'el Ware—to reduce Milwaukee's deficit to just one at the six-minute mark as they went on a 12-4 run, down 40-39. Both teams traded leads for the next few minutes, with Brayden Burries really starting to get in his bag, nailing a catch-and-shoot three and following it up with a smooth deceleration move in the lane for the and-one. The Bucks finally played with some verve as Kasparas Jakucionis began to make his mark, nailing a transition three and a put-back as the home side took a 55-47 lead with 3:30 to play. Of course, Scoot Henderson, who was shooting 20.0% from three coming into the game, went 4/4 in the first half as Portland closed on a 15-3 run to take a 60-58 lead into halftime.

The Bucks started the third with great energy on both ends. They opened with a perfectly run post-entry play where Herro got the ball off a screen for a three; then, a few plays later, Burries stole the ball, and Herro drained another three—this time from the corner—Bucks up 68-63 after two minutes. Portland brought Jrue Holiday in to stem the tide, and, like clockwork, the Blazers responded with a 15-2 extended run. Yep. HOWEVER, the Bucks didn't go quietly as the second unit came in and offered a real spark, cutting the deficit back to three with a few minutes remaining. Crucial late plays from Jakucionis and Rollins put the Blazers up 96-92 after three.

After playing his first minutes of the season last night and making a great impression, Caris LeVert opened the fourth with an elite defensive play, stealing the ball from Dame and converting on the and-one. #2686. Shane Steichen on Daniel Jones remaining the starter: "We'll evaluate everything"

As the Colts continue to struggle offensively, they continue to cling to quarterback Daniel Jones.

Asked by reporters after the 26-3 loss to the Texans whether Jones will remain the starter, coach Shane Steichen said, “We’ll evaluate everything.”

The No. 2 quarterback is 2023 top-five pick Anthony Richardson. On Thursday night, he got a garbage-time drive in the fourth quarter. The three-and-out, which started at the Indianapolis 39, consisted of Richardson running for two yards and throwing two incomplete passes.

It was Richardson’s second appearance of the season; in Week 8, he got a couple of mop-up drives when the Colts trailed the Jaguars, 42-7.

At some point, Richardson deserves a real chance to play. How much worse can the Colts’ offense be?

The Colts were outgained by the Texans, 354 yards to 167. They converted one of 11 third-down tries. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes, for 144 yards, no touchdowns, and an interception.

There’s a business reason that points to the Colts eventually getting Jones off the field. His contract has a $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027. It vests in March. They’ll inevitably bench Jones to keep him from getting an injury that would keep the Colts from releasing him before the injury guarantee converts to a full guarantee.

That’s what the Giants did to Jones two years ago. He then requested, and received, his release.

The same thing could be happening, sooner rather than later, for Jones in Indianapolis. Which means that he could be available to another team.

That possibility highlights the Colts’ decision to not trade him for whatever they could get. And maybe they tried.

Maybe, in the end, his availability in trade is what helped the Vikings keep the Raiders’ asking price for Kirk Cousins to a third-round pick.

And maybe, in the end, the Vikings will have a chance to add Jones to the depth chart while showing Carson Wentz the door.

#2685. Damian Lillard scores season-high 33 points in first game vs. Bucks post-injury, leads Trail Blazers to win

The Portland Trail Blazers made the trek to Milwaukee last year to play the Bucks. Damian Lillard was present, even though he was sitting out the entire 2025-26 campaign — his first season back with the Trail Blazers — as he recovered from the Achilles tear he suffered while playing for the Bucks in their 2025 first-round playoff series.

Fiserv Forum aired a video tribute to Lillard amid that November 2025 meeting, and the nine-time All-Star received a standing ovation after it played that night.

Thursday marked the 36-year-old guard's first time taking the court against Milwaukee since his injury and his two-season stint with the Bucks. Lillard was subdued talking about the matchup in the lead-up to tip-off, but he came away with his best performance in 624 days.

March 5, 2025, was the last time Lillard had a 30-point game. He scored a season-high 33 points on Thursday in a 124-114 victory over a reeling and rebuilding Milwaukee (1-15).

Portland (10-5) bounced back after dropping consecutive games to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Lillard once again received a warm welcome from Bucks fans. Milwaukee ultimately waived him to sign center Myles Turner in the summer of 2025. The Bucks are still paying Lillard after they decided to stretch the remaining $113 million on his contract.

So, on Thursday, Milwaukee fans watched their team lose its 12th straight game and Lillard shoot 10 of 18 from the field, including 5 of 12 from the beyond the arc.

Plus, another former Bucks player, Jrue Holiday — part of Milwaukee's NBA championship team in 2020-21 — put on a show of his own. He logged 22 points, 7 assists and 4 steals.

Holiday stepped back to hit a crucial jumper with about 5 ½ minutes to go. Another 36-year-old guard, Holiday went on to help the Trail Blazers create separation late, even coupling a steal with a layup.

Portland also got 27 points and seven rebounds from a much younger member of its backcourt: Scoot Henderson.

Meanwhile, the Bucks fell again, a day removed from facing Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time.

Milwaukee had four players score 15-plus points this time out. Tyler Herro led the way with 19, Kasparas Jakučionis and Nate Ament had 18 apiece and Ryan Rollins chipped in 15. Turner, notably, was out with a shoulder injury.

The lead changed hands incessantly on Thursday. Herro drew the Bucks within one at the 3:18 mark in the fourth quarter. The Trail Blazers, though, scored the final nine points, with Lillard netting the last two at the free-throw line.

#2684. Colts surrender 26 unanswered points as Daniel Jones benched in blowout road loss to Texans

Houston, the problem here is the Indianapolis Colts offense is broken and has not reached the end zone in 17 consecutive drives. In their final primetime appearance on Thursday Night Football, the Colts surrendered 26 unanswered points in a 26-3 blowout loss to the rival Houston Texans.

Outside of the opening drive, there was nothing left from this depleted offensive unit. Backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr. relieved Daniel Jones for the final eight minutes of regulation. Richardson trucked Texans' linebacker Jake Hansen on his first snap for a minimal two yards, then nearly delivered Houston an interception before another anticlimactic three-and-out ended his night.

The Colts were poised to establish an early offensive rhythm after rookie Seth McGowan returned the opening kickoff to the 40. Jones found receiver Ashton Dulin wide open on a sit route against Houston's zone coverage, allowing the speedster to bounce outside and race to the sideline for 25 yards. McGowan followed with a tough run up the middle for eight yards, then Jonathan Taylor was patient enough to let a hole develop and surge forward to move the chains.

Texans' defensive tackle Logan Hall blew up McGowan's next run in the backfield, then Jones was forced to throw the ball away on third down. The Colts settled for an early chip shot as kicker Spencer Shrader connected on a 34-yard field goal to give Indianapolis its lone lead.

The Texans opened with a promising drive, but a forced pass ricocheted into an early break for the Colts. C.J. Stroud's throw bounced off the helmet of rookie safety AJ Haulcy before it tipped off Cam Bynum's hands and back into Haulcy's grasp for his first career interception.

Indianapolis could not have asked for a better start as Jones recognized the underneath coverage, went through his progressions and fired a dart down the sideline to receiver Quez Watkins for a 26-yard completion to march right back into Houston territory. The drive stalled after a dropped pass by Taylor was followed by a pass deflection from Hansen, then All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson chased down Jones and forced him to get rid of it out of bounds. The Colts intended to settle for a kick near midfield, but Shrader's 56-yarder was shanked wide left.

Despite taking a hit to his right bicep from Colts' defensive back Kapena Gushiken, Stroud stepped up into the pocket and launched a missile down the right sideline to receiver Nico Collins, who elevated over cornerback Justin Walley to haul in a 42-yard touchdown and put Houston ahead 7-3 late in the first frame.

The Colts' next possession unraveled inside of Texans' territory after receiver Anthony Gould took a bubble pass through a hole on the field side for 31 yards. Jones' next pass would have been picked off if Texans cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. weren't out of bounds. On the first play of the second quarter, Jones tossed up a meatball sub into double coverage to avoid the sack and was picked off by cornerback Kamari Lassiter over rookie Deion Burks.

Jones finished 12-for-27 for 144 pass yards and one interception, the sixth straight game he's thrown an interception. Shane Steichen has continued to rely on the eighth-year veteran, despite leading the NFL with 15 turnovers and never finishing a single game with more touchdowns than turnovers this season.

The Texans mounted a pair of long drives in the second quarter as Stroud shared the wealth with five different pass-catchers. Facing third-and-2 from just outside the red zone, Stroud delivered a perfect post to Kayshon Boutte near the goal line. Boutte rose over cornerback Kenneth Harris to secure the contested 24-yard touchdown catch, extending Houston's lead to 14-3 midway through the second quarter.

The Texans were able to capitalize on a choice to send Shrader out for a 62-yard field goal attempt, which was blocked by Hall to seize possession inside Colts territory. Houston leaned on its run game to drain most of the remaining clock before settling for a 27-yard chip shot from Ka'imi Fairbairn to take a 17-3 lead into halftime.

The stampede found some life to start the second half as defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore rushed past the left guard to corral Stroud from behind and secure his team-high fifth sack this season, sending Houston behind the sticks. Houston would avenge the hit on Stroud after a precision punt pinned Indianapolis inside its own 5-yard-line as Anderson rushed inside of right tackle Matt Goncalves to sack Jones in the end zone for a safety.

The Texans took advantage of the short field as Stroud connected with Tank Dell on three consecutive throws for a combined 27 yards to breach the red zone. Houston's offensive line gave Stroud a full seven seconds to scramble outside of the pocket, find tight end Marlin Klein near the pylon for a 13-yard TD that capped off a 12-play drive to seal the first home win for Houston.

The Colts could never get their rushing attack in any rhythm, held to just 38 rushing yards on 17 attempts. The rookies continued to impress on the defensive side as C.J. Allen led the game with 16 tackles, while Haulcy forced the takeaway to terminate Houston's opening drive.

Indianapolis (3-8) enters its bye week for Thanksgiving, with 10 days to prepare to host the New York Giants (5-3-1) at Lucas Oil Stadium on Nov. 29.
