#2683. Jeremiah Conwell's 3 TD passes lead Brennan over Weslaco in second round

Brennan coach Stephen Basore knew Weslaco was going to try to chew clock and limit the Bears' offensive opportunities.

He's used to opposing teams taking that approach. With the Panthers playing keep away, Brennan had to make each possession count.

They weren't perfect, but the Bears did just enough offensively as senior Jeremiah Conwell threw for 219 yards and three touchdowns, leading Brennan past Weslaco 31-15 Thursday at the Dub Farris Athletic Complex in the second round of Class 6A Division I playoffs.

"We scored when we had to. We got stops when we had to," Basore said. "It was a short game because they were obviously burning time early in the game, and pretty much the entire time.

"Again, we have to respond to that. And I thought generally we did. A late blown coverage makes it look a little tighter. Weslaco played a great game. I'm really impressed with those guys and how hard they play. They had a great plan."

Brennan began its opening drive on the 50-yard line. Four plays later, the Bears were in the end zone. Conwell hit senior Jaylin Kelly on third down for a 17-yard gain and found him again wide open on the next play for a 27-yard touchdown.

Weslaco responded with a 26-yard field goal from senior Ricardo Zuniga.

Early in the second quarter, Brennan extended its lead with a 58-yard passing touchdown from Conwell to senior Aiden Martin. The play began with a direct snap to Bears running back Jayshawn Mitchell. The junior passed the ball back to Conwell, who found Martin streaking open downfield for the score.

"I know I got some guys. They can play," Conwell said. "Jaylin Kelly and Aiden Martin, they're both really good. I know if I get the ball in their hands, they're going to make some plays and score."

Weslaco pieced together a 17-play drive that took over nine minutes off the game clock. But the Bears held, and the Panthers capped the drive with a 25-yard field goal from Zuniga.

Brennan, aided by a 36-yard connection between Conwell and Kelly, added a 30-yard field goal from Axton Parra with two seconds left before halftime to extend the lead to 17-6.

The Bears came out of the half and quickly moved into the Panthers' red zone. On first-and-10 from the 9-yard line, Conwell and Martin connected for their second touchdown to put Brennan ahead 24-6 with 8:21 remaining in the third quarter.

On the ensuing Panthers' possession, Zuniga drilled a 32-yard field goal, his third of the night.

With 9:04 remaining in the game, Brennan began its drive at the Weslaco 30-yard line. A 15-yard rush and a 6-yard catch from junior Nicholas Oliver Jr. set up the Bears' final score of the day.

Mitchell, Brennan's touchdown leader on the year, punched in a 5-yard score with 6:04 left on the clock.

Panthers junior David Perez scored their final points of the season with a 4-yard rushing score.

Brennan players tackle Weslaco's Andres Mandujano during the Class 6A Division I second round playoff game at Farris Stadium in San Antonio, Texas on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Brennan defeated Weslaco 31-15. (Katina Zentz/San Antonio Express-News)

Brennan moves on to face the winner of Lake Travis and Steele in the third round. The Cavaliers and Knights play Friday in a rematch of a non-district game that was called in the third quarter and ruled a tie because of inclement weather.

Regardless of the opponent, the Bears will have their hands full next week.

"It's the same as every week," Conwell said. "We compete. We study as much as we can, get our bodies and minds right. It's nothing new."

#2682. Clippers vs. Spurs takeaways: Victor Wembanyama adds to highlight reel

Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs remain the standard in the Western Conference and will continue to get everyone's best shot this season.

The Spurs served as a tough test for the Los Angeles Clippers. They gave the Spurs their best shot in a 124-112 loss in San Antonio on Thursday, Nov. 19. Wembanyama led the game with 32 points and 11 rebounds for the Spurs.

It was a bounce-back win for San Antonio, which had a 12-game win streak snapped against the Detroit Pistons earlier in the week.

The Spurs were missing Dylan Harper, who was out with a hip rotator strain, on Thursday. He avoided serious injury but is expected to miss at least a week.

Here's some takeaways from Thursday's game:

Wembanyama can simply do things that others can't.

His latest example came with 3:36 left in the fourth quarter against the Clippers on Thursday. Rui Hachimura's missed shot was rebounded by Stephon Castle, who threw the ball right down the court to a wide-open Wembanyama.

While Wembanyama could've dunked the ball, he seemed to settle for a jump shot inches from the rim.

Wembanyama laughed when asked about the play and stated that dunking has led to a blister on his hand.

"I'm not going to lie, I've had this blister forever and it's killing me," Wembanyama told reporters after the game. "Every time I dunk, it kills me. … It's actually so painful."

While the Clippers still have a lot of work to do if they want to be in a position to compete for a play-in spot later this season, coach Tyronn Lue's team showed some promise and potential against the West's best on Thursday.

L.A. shot the ball well for most of the game and kept the game close behind the effort of veterans Darius Garland and Brook Lopez. Both scored 23 points each.

Garland's had high-scoring performances early this season, but turnovers have been a problem for the guard. He managed to limit his mistakes Thursday, having just one turnover on a big stage against the Spurs.

Max Strus went 5-for-10 from the field, including 5-of-9 from the 3-point line for 18 points.

Clippers center Yanic Konan Niederhauser made his season debut. The second-year player was dealing with a right foot Lisfranc injury and was limited to 11 minutes against the Spurs due to a minutes restriction. He went 1-for-4 shooting and finished the game with two points, three rebounds and a steal. He did find himself in foul trouble with a team-high five personal fouls.

While the Clippers will have to figure out the center rotation following Niederhauser's return, Lue has encouraged Isaiah Jackson to stay ready.

"Nothing (Jackson) has done wrong," Lue said before the game. "You want to try to reward him for what he has done since Yanic has been out. We will see how the flow of the game goes."

Jackson shot 3-for-5 from the field, finishing with six points, four rebounds and three steals in nine minutes of play. He also recorded two blocks against Wembanyama, once at the rim and the second at the 3-point line at the end of the third quarter.

San Antonio managed to get the best of one of Los Angeles' NBA teams, but a meeting with the other still looms.

The Lakers will head to San Antonio next week for an NBA Cup showdown. The Spurs sit at the top of the NBA Cup Group C standings with a 2-0 record. The Lakers are third after splitting their first two games.

A win for the Lakers would not only place them in a tie for the top spot in the group but also provide a glimpse at where things stand in the conference.

The Lakers are tied with the Spurs and LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers for the best record in the league at 13-3. Los Angeles has played well throughout November but had its nine-game winning streak snapped against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

The upcoming Spurs-Lakers matchup will provide a glimpse at two of the league's early MVP front-runners on the court together. Luka Doncic is averaging a league-leading 38.1 points per game along with 7.6 assists and 7.0 rebounds. Wembanyama is averaging 28.4 points, 12.0 rebounds and a league-best 4.1 blocks per game.

#2681. History, hunger and headline bills - why Price is box office

It won't be the biggest fight that comes to Cardiff over the next few weeks.

But that doesn't mean Lauren Price's latest ringwalk into history shouldn't be seen as a main event in its own right.

The Welsh capital is about to become boxing's first city, the eyes of the world preparing to focus on the Principality Stadium and the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

Less than half a mile down the road, and three weeks before the circus comes to town, Price takes on Czech challenger Michaela Kotaskova at the 5,000 capacity Utilita Arena.

There will be fewer fans, less fuss and frenzy, but more than just pride at stake.

Price, in only 10 fights, already has three of the four major world titles to her name in the welterweight division, after a perfect start to her professional career.

The remaining belt is on offer on Friday, and thus the opportunity to become the first Welsh fighter to achieve 'undisputed' status.

Not even the iconic Joe Calzaghe managed that - the last great fighting pride of Wales who himself went from headlining the arena where Price fights to selling out the stadium down the road.

"People think I'm off my head wanting to fight at the Principality," the 32-year-old said after weighing in for her fight with Czech-born, Vienna-based Kotaskova.

"But I feel I've got a whole nation behind me."

The journey, says Price, keeps on getting bigger. Victory on Friday may see another arena bout in February, but stadia are in her thoughts for the summer.

Cardiff City Stadium has been mentioned, as has Cardiff Arms Park the venue where, in 1995, Naseem Hamed was crowned world champion at the expense of Cardiff Cinderella Man Steve Robinson.

It is part of the plan for promoter Ben Shalom.

"We want to bring the big nights here, can we get the big stadiums and can we create history with Lauren," Shalom detailed.

"Not just as a one-off, but we want to bring stadium fights to Cardiff regularly.

"That's what the building blocks have all been about.

"I was worried initially that having the fight on the Friday we wouldn't have the same number of supporters. It's been bigger. I've never seen the level of sales for someone at this stage of their journey."

Price fighting to be Wales' first undisputed world champion

Edwards' world title aim to join Welsh boxing greats

Fury v Joshua fight faces objections over 3am finish

More than 80,000 fans witnessed Katie Taylor bow out from boxing at Dublin's Croke Park in September [Getty Images]

Yet while Price's journey to tonight's fight is likely to pass the alluring outline of the Principality Stadium, a venue that could arguably provide greater inspiration is a few hundred miles west.

Settling into newly married life – something she says has added to her happiness at home and hunger at work - Price watched from the sofa as the trail-blazing Katie Taylor sold out Dublin's 83,000 capacity Croke Park for her final fight two months ago.

Is Price able to become that level of main event?

"She has the opportunity to go and prove that," argued Shalom.

"Don't forget, Katie is 10 years Lauren's senior, but the journey has been similar with the Olympic gold and having a nation behind her.

"Look at where Lauren is now, headlining already. We can see from the trajectory that's the goal - and it's a realistic goal."

Indeed, it's hard to ignore some of the shared stories between the two. A talented amateur having played international football for their country before putting on the gloves, flying the flag of a smaller nation, taking on all comers.

Partly because of the path forged by Taylor, Price has headlined earlier than Ireland's 2012 gold winner and scooped up more titles at this stage of her career.

And Price's visibility on terrestrial broadcast – this fight her third screened by the BBC – is very much part of a plan to build the brand into something bigger. After all, how better to become a household name than to be available to watch in every household?

Hence there is no envy at not being an undercard fighter on that Fury-Joshua bill, not when she has her own fans to consider and cultivate. An outstanding boxer with a standalone support, a main eventer in her own right.

But what she needs, as Taylor found with A-list adversaries such as Amanda Serrano, is a dance partner.

As a glance at the grudge match due to be held at the Principality Stadium will remind, big-stage boxing needs its rivalries.

Because of her quality, Price has dismissed all opponents without time to build one.

She goes into her 11th fight having only dropped a handful of rounds, a badly cut lip in her last defence against Stephanie Pineiro in April providing Price the opportunity to dig deep and "learn lessons".

She believes she is getting better and seems more confident, certainly looking more at home in the professional world of ticket-selling and soundbites than she did when she first hung up the amateur gloves after her 2021 Olympic success.

But the step up in class – and in stardust – lies elsewhere.

Five-weight champion Claressa Shields looked a possibility but talks broke down when Cardiff was not an option in a two-fight proposal. Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer fight each other at light-middleweight next month, Mayer giving up the WBO welterweight belt Price now eyes in the process.

Michaela Kotaskova has only been beaten once in 15 professional fights, losing on points to Chantelle Cameron in April [Getty Images]

Even Kotaskova admits she was surprised to receive the call to face Price, believing the four are the elite out on their own – although not without warning the home fighter that "nobody's perfect".

Kotaskova believes she saw weaknesses in the Pineiro fight that can be exploited to cause a shock.

The 35-year-old should not be taken lightly, her only professional defeat coming at the hands of Cameron after 10 three-minute rounds at light-middleweight in April.

But she is not surprised Price is looking to the future given her class - and Price is comfortable with being ambitious.

"I think I've showed a level in boxing to justify that, and you have to have plans.

"I believe in myself and I believe I get that win on Friday - and then I want to know when I'm boxing next."

A question for Shalom to answer, and he is not afraid to state his own belief that Price has the capability to hit heights never seen before in women's boxing, saying the vision at the beginning was to lay foundations for Price to become the greatest.

"I think people will naturally want to see Lauren Price kick on and do what we say she's going to do - beat everyone in the sport. Win every belt. Win at every weight division," Shalom said.

"Claressa Sheilds, for me, is the greatest female currently in world boxing in what she has done and her legacy," he added.

"I think Lauren is the only one that can challenge her. She has a background and a fan base to be respected and we really believe can take the throne."

Price was among Welsh sporting royalty at Thursday's weigh-in when Wales rugby great Sir Gareth Edwards turned up to show his support.

Likewise, she has lent her support to other Welsh boxers who gain exposure and a big-show opportunity on Friday's undercard.

But, make no mistake about who the main event in Cardiff is right now.

In fact, Price has the chance to make sure it's undisputed.

The boxer who lost 45kg and fought depression to chase a dream

#2678. Rockets' Marcus Smart suspended three games for punching Warriors' Charles Bassey during in-game scuffle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA has suspended Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart for three games for "throwing a punch that made contact with the face" of Golden State Warriors big man Charles Bassey, the league announced on Thursday.

The incident came late in the third quarter of Wednesday night's game in Houston. After Smart and Bassey got tangled up on the other end of the floor, Smart chased Bassey down and threw a punch at his head area. They were quickly broken up from there, and Smart was eventually ejected from the game with a flagrant-2 foul. Despite his absence, the Rockets went on to win the game, 115-108.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What triggered the incident? "I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

Bassey, on the other hand, blamed Smart for what happened. "He's been playing dirty the whole game," the Warriors big man said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Charles Bassey on Marcus Smart throwing a punch at him: “Fake toughness.”“I don’t think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game.” pic.twitter.com/ZxbgvUDeY9

As for what sort of words were exchanged between Smart and Bassey? "He said something to me," Bassey explained. "He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Smart is no stranger to NBA discipline. He has 12 ejections, nine fines (excluding flopping and technical foul fines) and two suspensions across his 13-year career. Now, the 9-3 Rockets will be without a key guard for the next three games, but fortunately for them, their next three opponents are all below .500: the Utah Jazz, Washington Wizards and Miami Heat.

#2677. Donald aims for England T20 chance in Australia

From Gorseinon cricket club in Swansea to some of the most famous grounds in Australia.

That is the journey England's latest Welsh batter Aneurin Donald is preparing to complete when the T20 five-match series starts against Australia on Saturday.

Donald made his England debut in the home three-match series against Sri Lanka but this represents a step up.

It is 12,000 miles between the Swansea suburb and the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) where the first game is being played.

It is a journey that has taken many years since starting at his local cricket club.

He originally came down with his father Andrew to watch the local rugby club but became hooked on cricket.

"Gorseinon means so much to me," said Donald, speaking to the BBC at the Welfare Ground where the two clubs are based.

"My family and friends are so involved down here and I spent so much time there growing up as a kid, playing rugby and cricket.

"I try and get back there as much as I can. It's the lifeblood of the community and the reason I got the chances I did.

"The basis that I gathered here, the time and energy I spent training in the winter got me on the rung to professional sport and now an international cap."

England's Donald ready to savour Welsh homecoming

The one-lane indoor net, now called the Alan Jones indoor cricket centre after Gorseinon's other England batter, helped shape Donald's talent.

"That one little indoor net lane we had is probably the big reason as to why I've made it as far as I have," said Donald.

"It was a little tin shed with probably a five yard run-up where my brother [Gafyn] used to bowl into the middle of my bat.

"It was a massive part of my career now."

Those nets included training when others were relaxing.

"If I had to put one thing down in my junior years and what separated me was probably coming down and training and being able to use that little indoor shed," said Donald.

"My dad installed a belief in me if I was training on a day nobody else is, you have added that little extra, whatever time of year.

"We used to go down every week and I can remember training on Christmas Eve.

"It was freezing cold and I remember being wrapped up in scarves and there was ice on our breath."

While the Donalds were freezing inside, outside honing his kicking skills was a Wales rugby icon who also started his sporting journey at Gorseinon.

"We used to see Leigh Halfpenny kicking for hours on end and it's probably a reminder that work ethic is what makes great players like him great," said Donald.

"I can't compare my career with his but I took inspiration from seeing him out there."

Aneurin Donald's family were on hand to watch him be presented with his first England cap before the opening Vitality T20 International Series match against Sri Lanka [Getty Images]

Donald's dedication has had to be matched by his resolve.

His road to international cricket proved longer than most, having to recover from two serious knee injuries.

After starting his career with Glamorgan, he moved on to Hampshire and Derbyshire, where he has established himself as the explosive specialist short form batter he now is.

His England recognition came later than most at the age of 29 with his his three T20 appearances against Sri Lanka in September.

There was a game on Welsh soil in Cardiff after his debut in Southampton where he was awarded his cap by England consultant Kevin Pietersen in front of his parents and girlfriend Heather.

"That was the one moment I will never forget," said Donald.

"It was special to be there with my parents who've put all those miles, time, money and energy into me, and my girlfriend who supports me when I am travelling around the world and holds the fort down back home.

"That's the one image that's been in my mind that I'll never forget.

"It lasted for 30 seconds, an amazing speech from KP and suddenly it's run upstairs, stick your pads on, get out there and try and do your job."

England batter Aneurin Donald was part of the T20 squad that won three games against Sri Lanka in September [Getty Images]

Donald had a strike rate of 191, emphasising his role in attacking from the first ball to set the tone for the innings.

He would have liked to have scored more than 46 runs in his three innings - with a top score of 21- although he says he had the full support of captain Harry Brook and coach Brendon McCullum.

"It was a little frustrating," said Donald.

"I could have gone worse and got out for three ducks, so it was better than that.

"I showed a little bit of a glimpse of what I can do and the way I want to play.

"Baz (McCullum) and Brookie are supportive of that and that's exactly why I was picked.

"My job is to come out swinging and get the boys ahead of the game.

"I'd like to be sat here with a bigger score under my belt, but I think I have shown I can throw some punches at that level."

Donald says he was not affected by nerves.

"Walking out to bat with Jos Buttler, someone I've idolised, as friends and batting partners is mad and probably still hasn't sunk in yet," he added.

"Oddly I felt pretty calm, it may have been a little bit because I was older and gone through the ups and downs in my career.

"So I didn't feel anywhere near as nervous as I thought. If this was going to be my only crack, I'm going to enjoy.

"It came and went so quickly with three games in five days.

"Hopefully I get a few more opportunities down the line. It is still mad how quickly things have happened these last few months."

Phil Salt, from Bodelwyddan in north Wales, won the 2022 T20 World Cup with England [Getty Images]

Those further opportunities could come in Australia, after he was named in the squad for the five-match series that starts on Saturday.

"If you ask any young cricketer in England and Wales they're probably going to mention touring Australia as pretty high up on the list," said Donald.

"To play at some of those iconic venues, with that first game at the MCG would be a special moment.

"Whether I get a crack or not, it's going to be a different challenge again, an overseas tour in a hostile environment against a strong team."

Donald's chance came when fellow Welshman Phil Salt was injured. With Salt back and Buttler missing because of a hamstring problem, there could be two Welsh batters at the top of the order, with the in-form Tom Banton also in the equation.

"To walk out with Salty, north and south Wales, where we've got a lot of bases covered there, would be a proud moment, not just for us, but for Welsh cricket also," said Donald.

"To show we can produce some players on the world stage and guys who can kick it at any level.

"Ever since making my debut, whether that's domestically or internationally, the support I've had from Welsh cricket and the wider Welsh community has always been incredible."

Donald will stay in Australia after the series because he has picked up a contract with Perth Scorchers in the Big Bash league. He will then join Joburg Super Kings in the Betway SA20 in South Africa, which starts in late January.

"The franchise world has opened all sorts of doors," said Donald.

"To get your foot in the door in one of the top three leagues in the world was a massive moment.

"It was a big feather in my cap to be able to go to the Perth Scorchers."

This is the cricket life Donald is following with stints in leagues in Canada, Netherlands and UAE. The Indian Premier League (IPL) remains the ultimate T20 goal.

"The skill sets in the shorter format are getting better from probably even when I first started 10-15 years ago," said Donald.

"The amount of opportunities out there for T20 cricket, and the lifestyle it gives you where you can travel the world and play with the best, is a special place to be."

He says it "would be silly" currently not to double down on what he is good at, even if he still wants to play the longer form of the game.

"I am desperate to keep playing red ball, certainly in the county game," he added.

"There's very few guys realistically who can cruise around from franchise to franchise and make a living.

"There's always a bit of a balance, but white ball is the forefront for me at the moment."

#2675. Texans run over ineffective Colts for easy 26-3 victory, winning first home game this season

Houston Texans quarterback CJ. Stroud passed for 194 yards and three touchdowns, providing more than enough offense for a defense that shut down the Indianapolis Colts effectively in a 26-3 win on Thursday night.

The Texans won at home for the first time this season after losing their previous five at Reliant Stadium.

Stroud completed 21-of-27 passes with one interception. A second one appeared to be taken away in the second quarter before replay review ruled that Colts safety Cam Bynum didn't catch the ball cleanly.

Nico Collins caught three passes for 58 yards and a touchdown, while Kayshon Boutte followed with two catches for 40 yards and a score. Rookie tight end Marlin Klein caught Stroud's third TD pass.

The Texans' offense also benefited from the return of running back David Montgomery, back after a four-game absence due to a groin injury. The eight-year veteran rushed for 107 yards on 26 carries, keeping several drives moving on the ground. Emari Demercado also ran effectively, gaining 33 yards on five carries.

However, the sharpest thing seen on the field Thursday night may have been the Texans' "Rivalries" alternate uniforms that harkened back to the Oilers' classic look. With the victory, Houston improved to 4-6 and stayed on the fringes of the playoff race in the AFC. The Texans play host to the Baltimore Ravens in Week 12.

On the other side, the Colts could get nothing going with their rushing attack. Jonathan Taylor managed only 21 yards on 11 carries. That put more pressure on Daniel Jones to produce in the passing game, which did not happen.

Jones completed 12-of-27 passes for 144 yards and an interception. He did connect on four passes of 20 yards or more, but that simply wasn't enough to move Indianapolis toward the end zone. He was also tackled for a safety by Will Anderson Jr. in the third quarter after the Colts were pinned at their 5-yard line on a 62-yard punt from Houston's Kai Kroeger.

Anderson now has 11.5 sacks this season, tops in the NFL, after notching a career-high 12 last season.

With just under eight minutes left in the game and the Colts trailing by 23 points, Colts coach Shane Steichen replaced Jones with Anthony Richardson. But he threw two incompletions on his first series, the only action he saw.

Naturally, Steichen was asked if the Colts will make a quarterback change for their next game. "We'll evaluate everything," he said.

Altogether, the Colts generated only 167 yards of total offense. Anthony Gould tallied 48 yards receiving on two receptions, followed by 30 yards and two catches from Ashton Dulin. Taylor had four catches, but only for six yards.

Even kicker Spencer Shrader couldn't provide many points, missing two of his three field-goal attempts. One of those kicks was from 62 yards and was blocked.

Indianapolis has lost six of its past seven games, dropping to 3-8 for the season. Yet four teams have worse records in a subpar AFC. Up next for the Colts is a home matchup with the New York Giants (5-3-1).

#2674. How can Warriors survive Stephen Curry's absence? Yaxel Lendeborg has to step up, but that's not all

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors were riding high with an eight-game winning streak, a breakout rookie in Yaxel Lendeborg and Stephen Curry in MVP form heading into Wednesday's game vs. the Rockets. Then the record cut out at their party when Curry suffered an oblique tear that will cost him at least two weeks and maybe more.

If it is really just a two-week absence, he'll only miss six games and the Warriors will have dodged a bullet. But even that long without Curry is going to be an uphill battle for a team that, its hot start notwithstanding, already has little margin for error.

In general, there are obvious things that need to happen whenever a team loses the superstar that can cover for their mistakes: Limit turnovers (always a problem for the Warriors) and control the glass (Golden State is a relatively good rebounding team and should be able to be even better with some bigger non-Curry lineups; offensive boards go a long way for a team that is now likely to struggle to score for stretches). Winning the possession game will be vital.

You just have to be sharper in general without the ultimate bailout player on the floor. But more specifically, here are three things that probably need to happen for the Warriors to stay afloat without Curry.

After the Houston loss, Draymond Green had this to say about Lendeborg's 25-point, 10-rebound showing that helped fuel a post-Steph-injury surge and kept the Warriors in the game most of the way.

"The thing he's gonna have to learn to understand is, alright, Steph wasn't out there. [Durant] was off the court [for the Rockets]. You look around, you're probably the best player on the floor. Regardless of team. I think there was a point where he realized like, 'Oh, ding ding ding.' And he started attacking, and the game flipped for us.

"I think that's something he's going to have to realize really fast, is like, there will be often times where he could possibly be the best player on the floor regardless of the team. And we need him to show that, and he doesn't have a problem doing it."

This will never be truer than over these next couple of weeks. Lendeborg, a 24-year-old rookie, is now the Warriors' best player, and they need him to play like it. They need aggression. They need the production, from his iso scoring to creation for others to fueling and finishing as many transition attacks as possible.

He's capable of carrying a team. We saw it against the Clippers, when he went for 37 points and six assists with six 3-pointers and just one turnover as the go-to guy with Curry out.

But that was against one of the worst teams in the league (he gets Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs on Friday), and it was a one-night thing when maybe everyone wasn't quite aware of how good he really is. The secret is out now, and Lendeborg's name is going to be the one circled on every opponent's whiteboard moving forward. He'll get the overarching defensive focus. He'll get the double teams. And he'll have the burden of producing big numbers through all that.

There's no question that Lendeborg has looked incredible to start the year. He has the game and confidence to be a No. 1 option even just three weeks into his professional career. He's the Rookie of the Year favorite for a reason, and there has been justified talk about his being a real All-Star candidate. It's too early to be making statements like that, but for as long as Curry is out, Yaxel indeed needs to perform at that kind of level for an offense that doesn't really have anyone else capable of creating consistent advantages.

So far, the Warriors are making 16.5 3-pointers per game at a 39.7% clip. Both of those marks lead the league. A lot of this is Curry, who is making 4.3 triples per game at a truly absurd 45.7% rate given his shot difficulty, but it's not all him.

Give Brandin Podziemski the courtesy of rounding up three-tenths of a percent, and the Warriors have three guys currently making at least two 3s per game with at least a 40% conversion rate.

These are going to be the main gunners, but Golden State has other capable shooters. Georges Niang and Al Horford. LJ Cryer is about to see more time, and he's a 41.7% shooter. Will Richard is at 45.8%. These are all low-volume shooters who now have the green light.

This is how the Warriors stayed competitive against the Rockets: by jacking up 51 3s. They only made 17 of them, but that was still four more than the Rockets. That's a 12-point surplus, and the Warriors can still make plenty of mathematical hay with Curry out.

It won't be easy. His gravity creates a lot of these open looks guys enjoy, and that's where Lendeborg's ability to draw multiple defenders is going to be essential, but if everyone can combine to make just a few more 3s than normal, it can go a long way toward at least partially replacing Curry's 4.3 3s per game in the aggregate.

The Warriors are a top-10 defense (No. 9 if you remove garbage time, per Cleaning the Glass), and though they are giving up almost seven more points per 100 possessions with Curry off the floor, there's some deception in that stat.

Curry is a solid team defender and still better individually than a lot of people think, which is to say he's not going to be the reason your defense is bad. But he's also not the reason this Warriors defense is -- or at least has been -- good, and theoretically they should be just fine without him on that side of the ball. There's even a chance they get better.

De'Anthony Melton will likely start in his place. The Warriors, as mentioned, can play bigger. Curry's juice is infectious and that factors into defensive energy, and the upcoming schedule is a test (San Antonio, Boston and Memphis all register as top-eight offenses), but Green and company know the onus is on the defense to keep Golden State from taking on water without its captain. Are the Warriors up to the challenge?

#2673. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2671. NBA Washed Meter: Which late-30s (and older) stars still got it? And who's on the decline?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're in an age of outliers when it comes to aging superstars. Injuries are as persistent a problem in the NBA as they've ever been, yet the league is somehow also loaded with big names retaining relevance deep into their 30s (and in one notable case, beyond). Remember when the 2024 Olympics was supposed to be the swan song for LeBron James, Stephen Curry and Kevin Durant as the faces of the NBA? They're currently leading teams with a combined record of 27-10.

Some of the old guys very clearly still have it. Others are starting to slip. There are nine former All-NBA players in their age-36 season or later, so let's check in with each of them and measure how much they've had left in the tank thus far this season.

We're choosing to ignore injuries here, though they've obviously become a persistent issue for Curry. When he's been on the court, Curry has been closer to his peak than anyone on this list. Even after leaving Wednesday's loss to the Houston Rockets after five minutes, he's still averaging more than a point per minute. He has a higher effective field goal percentage than he did when he became the NBA's first unanimous MVP in 2016. He's even trimmed his turnover rate to a career-low. He's playing fewer minutes than he used to, but who cares when you're still getting MVP-caliber per-minute production out of him? Curry is our baseline. This is what it looks like for an old guy not to be washed.

He's playing fewer minutes than he once did, and he's getting the line less than he used to, but otherwise, you'd be hard-pressed to find a difference between this George and the version of him that last made an All-Star Team in 2024. If anything, he's been better this year, outscoring, outrebounding and outassisting his 2023-24 self on a per-minute basis. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections per game among those who have played more than twice this season, and as a result, the Boston Celtics went from averaging the second-fewest turnovers per game in the NBA last season to the seventh-most thus far this season. Boston is getting everything it hoped for out of George this season.

He's taking the fewest shots of his career by far -- just 13.2 per game when he's never been below 16 -- but nobody in Houston is complaining. No Rocket is taking 16 shots per game, but five of them are at double-digit shot attempts and Houston has the No. 3 offense in the NBA. This egalitarian approach is working, especially with Alperen Sengun and Jabari Smith playing the best basketball of their careers and Fred VanVleet back in the fold to organize it all.

Still, you'd expect a volume decrease on a great team to lead to improved efficiency (not that there's ever been much room for improvement on that front for Durant), not a decline. Durant simply isn't shooting at his usual standards thus far. He's made up for it with a sharp uptick in free-throw rate (a new career high and it's not especially close), but that's going to be harder to maintain as the season progresses and we reach higher-leverage games. You shouldn't exactly be afraid for Kevin Durant's shooting, but coupled with his decrease in volume, he might be inching into a very slightly different phase of his career. He's still a star. He just may not quite be the NBA's apex shotmaker at 38.

The early returns -- especially in light of his torn Achilles -- have been tremendously positive. He's playing fewer minutes as so many of these players are, but he's scoring at roughly the per-minute rate he did during his two-year tenure with the Milwaukee Bucks. The raw 3-point numbers look worse than they are. We're still in tiny-sample territory, and Lillard shoots at such volume that only a few games could easily take him from the 33.3% figure he's at now up into the high-30s to which he's more accustomed. The eye test is there. Every few games he turns a quarter or two into Dame Time.

His 3-point attempt rate is a preposterous 62%. That's new for him, and welcome in a role meant to support Deni Avdija. He's never getting to the basket anymore, but that's what Avdija is around to do. Like Durant, he's getting to the line far more than one would expect for a player of his age. That likely won't sustain, especially with his drive numbers declining. Still, it'd be hard to ask for more out of a small guard returning from perhaps the most devastating injury in basketball. Box Plus-Minus rates him as a top-20 offensive player thus far this season, and while the other all-in-ones aren't quite as bullish, the overwhelming sentiment is that Portland is getting something relatively close to the standard Lillard experience at a fraction of the cost.

There are 133 players in the NBA averaging at least 26 minutes per game. Green is scoring less than half as many points per game (3.2) as any of them (Myles Turner, in 132nd, averages 6.7). The Warriors don't expect Green to score. They more or less never have. And it's not as though they truly play 4-on-5. Green remains heavily involved in the offense as a passing hub and hitting the offensive glass as much as ever. His defensive value remains through the roof. Even now, he's among the only players in the NBA that can credibly play center and guard -- not just switch, but truly guard -- on the perimeter.

But so much of what he does offensively is based on his tried-and-true two-man dance with Curry, who's now going to miss multiple weeks. Green has only played 28 minutes without Curry this season, but they've gone badly. We're about to find out how cumbersome a total non-scoring threat is to a basketball team that doesn't have the greatest shooter of all time. Green will still be valuable. But we're nearing the point where the offensive limitations he poses might become great enough to really make you wonder about his overall impact, especially with his defensive rebounding fading as well.

Look, your answer here is going to depend on how you're scaling this. When the bar is his legendary chase down block on Andre Iguodala, you'd be justified in watching James himself get chased down by two-way forward Jalen Slawson and saying "it doesn't matter how good he still he is, no player in the NBA has slipped as much as he has simply because of how high his starting point was." That just isn't the only consideration here. He's fallen from a lofty perch, but landed on his feet.

James has been declining gradually for years in subtle but noticeable ways. He drives less. He runs fewer pick and rolls and takes fewer shots out of isolations. Those numbers tick down bit-by-bit each year. He pads his point total with more transition buckets these days. He preserves his energy more carefully defensively, his value manifesting in his IQ and communication more than anything else. The Philadelphia 76ers are still getting plenty out of him. This roster full of ball-handlers needs a connector. James has always been capable of such a reduced role. He perfected it for the Los Angeles Lakers last season.

He's shooting badly from everywhere -- especially 3-point range, a quietly critical issue for Philadelphia considering Joel Embiid's decline on that front. The 76ers don't ask him for high usage, so getting the five or six hard drives he's capable of per night matter more than stacking the volume he once did. You'd rather have a few big plays than a bunch of lesser ones. How much of what we've seen this season is him pacing himself vs. the reality of playing a 24th NBA season won't really be knowable until bigger games come in the spring. For now, LeBron James is firmly a role player. He's a very valuable role player, one who does things, especially as a passer, that no other role player in NBA history has. But he's a role player nonetheless, and for someone as accomplished as James, that represents meaningful decline even if it doesn't constitute the end of the useful portion of his career.

The Miami Heat rank 23rd in 3-point percentage despite Thompson shooting above 40% on over nine attempts per game. That's how dire the offensive situation in Miami is. Andrew Wiggins and Tim Hardaway Jr. have struggled mightily so far. The entire theory of a team running most of its offense through bigs -- as Miami does with Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- rests on having high-level shooters to space the floor. Thompson is really the only trustworthy Heat shooter at this stage, and to his credit, he's holding up his end of the bargain on that front. He's never taken more 3s per minute than he is this year, and he's making plenty of them.

The trade-off here is that Thompson has been among the most vulnerable defensive players in the entire NBA this season, especially among those with real size. Thompson used to be an elite point-of-attack stopper. He transitioned into guarding bigger forwards as injuries and age sapped his mobility. Now, he's having trouble with just about everyone. Opponents are scoring 1.278 points per possession against him in isolation this season, per Synergy Sports. He really struggles to navigate screens at this stage. Late in games especially, Heat opponents are building a lot of their offense around finding and attacking Thompson.

The Heat are an average defense when Thompson sits and a terrible one when he plays. The former might be the problem here. The Heat were supposed to be great defensively with Antetokounmpo and Adebayo in the front court. They were supposed to be able to abide one defensive weak spot when the reality here is that almost everyone on the team has been worse on that end of the floor than Miami needed them to be. Thompson looks bad in part because everyone here does, but without the support we expected him to have, he's stuck out like a sore thumb defensively in ways that are going to prove problematic in the bigger games coming in April and May.

Harden has always been an extremely flawed player. You accepted the defensive issues and the turnovers and the slow, deliberate pace at which he played because he was such a uniquely gifted shot-creator that he remained enormously valuable in spite of those things. That isn't the case anymore. Not even close. Cleveland has been 19 points per 100 possessions better with Harden off the floor this season. As Danny Cunningham noted before their win over the New York Knicks Wednesday, every member of Cleveland's rotation had a worse net rating with Harden on the floor to that point in the season.

So much of Harden's game for the past two decades or so has started with the rim pressure he's generated. That's mostly been gone this season, and with it has been a lot of Harden's value as a passer. Less help means fewer corner 3s to pass into. When bigs aren't scared of him as a scorer, they don't frantically step up to meet him on drives, opening up his lethal lobs. Harden still gets to the line. He still self-creates plenty of 3s. But without that rim pressure, the flaws become less excusable.

Harden had his best game of the season on Wednesday, a 32-point outburst in that win over the Knicks. Maybe the first few weeks are a blip. Maybe he just wasn't in shape -- he's admitted he didn't play much pickup over the summer. But fitness has always been a concern, and at 37, it's possible and perhaps probable that he can't simply play his way back into shape during the season anymore. He looks like a different player, and if he is, whatever hopes Cleveland had of contending this season likely go up in smoke.

Harden and DeRozan are polar opposites as offensive players, but big picture, they're going through a similar process. You put up with DeRozan's antiquated shot-selection and poor defense because he got to the basket, got to the line and made all of his long 2s. Well, he's shooting 39% from mid-range this season, his lowest mark in more than a decade, and you can't live in mid-range on 39%. Now, DeRozan's decline as a finisher sticks out far more, and in turn, the fact that he can't really defend anymore becomes harder and harder to justify with minutes. Denver is getting crushed in all of DeRozan's minutes, with or without Nikola Jokić on the floor.

The Nuggets don't have much of a choice but to keep relying on DeRozan. This roster has a severe ball-handling deficit beyond Jokić and Jamal Murray. Someone else here needs to dribble, and DeRozan at least still manages to get to the line relatively often, and he does so without turning the ball. That's helpful. It's not enough. The entire premise of DeRozan as a valuable player rests on his ability to make shots most players shouldn't take. He isn't this season, and if that's the case, there are just few other ways he can make up for it to remain an impactful player.

#2670. After Thursday's loss, will Colts give Anthony Richardson another real shot?

Down 26-3 to the Houston Texans Thursday night, the Colts made a quarterback change, benching Daniel Jones and bringing in Anthony Richardson for mop-up duty in the blowout loss.

The Colts took this approach late in the 42-7 loss to the Jaguars on Nov. 1, giving Richardson a few token snaps. It wasn't an evaluation; it was a cup of coffee. That was his last appearance prior to Thursday.

Richardson, 24, has been in limbo for a few years now, a gifted talent in a state of arrested development, playing for a team that doesn't appear too jazzed to get a longer re-examination of a player they drafted fourth overall just three years ago.

On Thursday, Richardson entered midway through the fourth quarter and missed his first two throws of the night. There was no second series; the Texans ran out the clock. And it almost feels like the Colts are trying to run out the clock on Richardson, Jones, Riley Leonard — all of it.

Head coach Shane Steichen this week said he takes "everything into account" when it comes to the quarterbacks. He added: "Obviously, the biggest thing is taking care of the football moving forward."

Asked about a potential QB change after Thursday's loss, Steichen said, "we'll evaluate everything."

Steichen previously has been reluctant to put all the blame on Jones, and it's fair to point out that the Colts offloaded two notable talents at the trade deadline in offensive guard Quenton Nelson and wide receiver Josh Downs.

But the problems have been chronic, even when those player were on the roster. Jones hasn't had more touchdowns than interceptions in any game this season. He's thrown picks in 10 of his 11 games. The contract extension he signed in the offseason is looking more painful, on the books for $46.8 million next season, although it's a deal the Colts can get out of as a post-June 1 cut.

Still, if we're already forecasting the potential end of Jones in Indianapolis, and likely another pivot at quarterback for the franchise, why is Richardson not even a provisional option at this point? Is he that far gone in their eyes?

The excuse for not making a change this week was the Thursday game and the shortened schedule. But it's not as if Richardson hasn't been here for a minute. It's hard to imagine Steichen sees a whole lot of upside in Richardson, or the hook would have come sooner for Jones. Heck, it wouldn't be stunning if Steichen gave Leonard a chance, even over Richardson, at some point.

The Colts declined Richardson's fifth-year option, so the writing has been on the wall for a bit. It's hard not to look back at that 2024 game when Richardson reportedly "needed a breather" as a turning point in Steichen's trust in the QB, even if he ended up bringing Richardson back a few weeks later. Whenever that turning point happened, the trust level just hasn't been there for some time.

Steichen has hinted that a QB change could come, even prior to Thursday night. So there could be an opportunity for someone. There are six games remaining, with the Week 13 bye upcoming.

But isn't Steichen worried about his job? The general manager is already gone, and the owner is watching the operation closely. Outside of a narrow home win over the Dolphins, it hasn't looked very pretty lately. Steichen is going to do what he feels he needs to do to keep his job.

Is there any upside to bringing Jones back next week against the Giants? The Colts might not believe in Richardson, but they could end up helping each other out. If the QB can string a few games together, it helps his chances elsewhere next season. And if the Colts can win a few games, maybe everyone won't lose their jobs.

The big picture isn't pretty, and the Colts still don't have a first-round pick next year, but it's hard to imagine they can't try to squeeze something out of a player who at least has made some energy-generating plays with his legs, even if Richardson's passing metrics haven't been terribly defensible.

Beggars can't be choosers. Jones is playing like a guy who's less than a year removed from an Achilles injury, and the Colts' roster has been gutted. Sure, Leonard is the QB who might have the best chance to return next season, but Richardson has the better talent.

Can he get one more shot to do something in Indy?

#2668. MLB rumors: Yankees eye Alec Bohm, Tarik Skubal books more meetings, plus Nationals, Red Sox, Mariners, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22. As for the present moment, the General Manager Meetings in Las Vegas are underway, and since there may not be any Winter Meetings this offseason (thanks to the lockout), the GMs' pow-wow could instead be a locus of activity.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace and the ongoing GM Meetings, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Wednesday's supply just below.

The Red Sox are once again shopping outfielder Jarren Duran, reports the Boston Globe. He has been in trade rumors constantly the last two years or so. Boston has also reportedly shown interest in free agent Seiya Suzuki, the best right-handed bat on the market. With Gold Glover Wilyer Abreu entrenched in right, the Red Sox would presumably use Suzuki in left field or DH.

Duran, 30, has two years of team control remaining and he's a possible buy-low candidate. From 2023-25, he authored a .276/.339/.471 batting line with 17 homers and 32 steals per season. He slipped to .207/.266/.361 in 2026, however, and the Red Sox need to add power and get more right-handed. Moving Duran to clear a spot for Suzuki would address both needs.

The New York Yankees are eyeing an upgrade at third base given the prolonged struggles of Ryan McMahon, and free agent Alec Bohm may be a potential target for GM Brian Cashman, according to the New York Post. Bohm, 30, is coming off a subpar walk year for the Philadelphia Phillies, but he has a career OPS+ of 101 overall. He also fared much better in the second half, and his season-long numbers were dragged down by a terrible April. Bohm is not much of a fielder these days, but the Yankees may be willing to live with that if they determine he can provide an offensive upgrade.

As for McMahon, Cashman already conceded to looking for a replacement.

"He's signed through next year for us, but I definitely know we need to improve production in a lot of different spots on the club if we can," he told reporters on Tuesday. "So we'll be open-minded to finding what we can run into if it's there."

The market for ace Tarik Skubal, far and away the top free agent available this offseason, continues to pick up steam, and it may be that he signs his next contract before the owners lock out the players on Dec. 1. The Los Angeles Dodgers, who traded for Skubal leading up to the deadline, the New York Mets, the Chicago Cubs, and the San Diego Padres are known to have varying levels of interest in Skubal. Now, the New York Post reports, the Toronto Blue Jays have entered the fray and emerged as Skubal suitors.

As for the Dodgers, they indeed plan to meet with Skubal, GM Brandon Gomes said. There could be a twist in their pursuit, though; The Athletic reports that the Dodgers are interested in Skubal on a short-term deal, presumably with a higher AAV like they gave to Kyle Tucker. But given the uncertainty of the CBA, would Skubal be willing to sign a contract that has him back on the market in just a few years?

Mets top executive David Stearns, meanwhile, emphasized on Tuesday that he and the club are willing to offer lengthy contracts to pitchers but that circumstances matter. That, in theory, should allay fears that he's not prepared to make a significant offer.

The San Diego Padres not long ago declined their club option on right-handed starter Nick Pivetta. However, they may not mean a parting of ways for club and player. Padres lead decision-maker AJ Preller on Tuesday told reporters, including Marty Caswell, that the team hopes to work out a new agreement with Pivetta so that he can return to San Diego for the 2027 season and perhaps beyond. Pivetta enjoyed a standout season in 2025, but his 2026, while excellent while on the mound, consisted of just eight regular-season starts because of elbow problems.

Dylan Crews, the 24-year-old outfielder for the Washington Nationals, has yet to reach the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2023. However, that ceiling is still there, and Crews is obviously young enough to realize his promise. Speaking of Crews, the Athletic reports that multiple teams have approached the Nats about Crews' availability in trade and that the Nats have not declared him off-limits. That of course doesn't mean a trade will happen, but a change of scenery for Crews may indeed be a winter possibility.

Outfielder Randy Arozarena was the Seattle Mariners' top player last season, and now he's a free agent. The M's, though, may not be interested in bringing back Arozarena and instead may be targeting fellow free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki, the Seattle Times reports. Each veteran outfielder will be going into his age-32 season in 2027, and each produced at a high level in 2026.

After missing the playoffs in back-to-back seasons and trading away catcher Adley Rutschman leading up to the 2026 deadline, the Baltimore Orioles seem like a teardown candidate on paper. However, president of baseball operations Mike Elias batted down talk of a major roster makeover. "A lot of our key, core players are very unlikely to go anywhere," Elias told the media, including the Baltimore Banner, at the GM Meetings.

That presumably means that coveted shortstop Gunnar Henderson, among other notable names, won't be going anywhere this winter.

#2667. NBA Rookie of the Year race: Three players at top, but don't count out AJ Dybantsa, Darryn Peterson just yet

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

News broke on Thursday that Chicago Bulls forward Caleb Wilson will miss the next four to six weeks after fracturing his right hand. It marks the third separate hand injury Wilson has suffered during the last 11 months. He fractured his left hand and broke his right thumb during his freshman season at North Carolina, with the latter injury causing him to miss the end of the regular season.

Wilson was off to a hot start during his rookie season with the Bulls. The No. 4 overall pick was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.8 steals in his first 10 games and was one of the few bright spots for the 1-9 Bulls.

Missing the next four to six weeks would keep Wilson out until at least mid to late December. Although there is no 65-game minimum requirement to win Rookie of the Year as with other NBA awards, missing an extended period of time will likely see Wilson fall behind in what should be one of the most competitive races in recent memory.

Entering Friday, there appears to be a clear-cut top five in this season's Rookie of the Year race. Warriors forward Yaxel Lendeborg, the No. 11 pick, is the current favorite (+115 at FanDuel). After Lendeborg, Grizzlies forward Cameron Boozer (+290) and Kings guard Darius Acuff Jr. (+320) have the shortest odds.

The top two picks in the draft -- Wizards forward AJ Dybantsa and Jazz guard Darryn Peterson -- are tied for fourth (+1600) in the odds. Wilson is next at +4000, with a steep drop-off after that.

Dybantsa missed the first four games of the season with an ankle sprain, while Peterson got off to a slower start than some of his peers but has looked fantastic for the shorthanded Jazz during the last week and a half.

The current odds for Rookie of the Year (as of Nov. 13) are below.

Less than a month into the NBA season, three players have separated themselves from the rest. Boozer opened the season as the favorite to win Rookie of the Year, with Wilson, Peterson and Dybantsa not far behind in the odds. However, two players outside of the top five picks in a loaded draft class are in position to crash the party. Here is a quick scouting report on what we have seen from Boozer, Acuff and Lendeborg and how they can continue to stay in the race.

The things Boozer did well in college have carried over to the NBA. Since the 2010-11 season, no player in college basketball had a better box plus/minus (18.75) than Boozer. His freshman season at Duke was better than those of Cooper Flagg and Zach Edey, both of whom also won national player of the year honors. It speaks to how Boozer can make an impact on the floor when he isn't scoring. He has a great feel for the game and is already one of the best outlet passers in the league. He crashes the boards hard and is physical on both ends of the floor.

However, one (small) concern was also an issue at times at Duke: rim finishing. Boozer struggled against bigger defenders at times in college, and he's running into the same thing in the NBA, shooting just 46.6% at the rim on 58 attempts, per Synergy. That number has improved over the last few games, but it's something Boozer will have to improve.

Lendeborg has been fantastic and is a major reason why the Warriors are off to an 8-4 start. The pressure will be even greater over the next several weeks while Stephen Curry is out with an injury. He routinely took advantage of mismatches at Michigan, and he's doing the same in the NBA. His all-around game has taken tremendous strides over the last 12 months and he's going to continue to get better.

Of course, the one knock on Lendeborg in the draft was age. He was the oldest player selected in the first round and just turned 24, but he's a perfect fit for Golden State given its win-now timeline. What has been most impressive for Lendeborg is his shooting. He is knocking down 42.6% of his 3-point attempts while taking 5.7 per game. Last season at Michigan, Dusty May told him to shoot more 3-pointers. It paid dividends for his overall game.

He is the most polarizing rookie in this class, and he is being asked to do more than his peers on a nightly basis. Since having a rough shooting night in his NBA debut against the Clippers, his efficiency has been much better. People who don't watch the Kings (how can you blame them?) might not realize that the box score doesn't tell the full story. Yes, Acuff has attempted over 20 shots per game in each of his first 11 games, but he is also 13th in the league in potential assists (12), 12th in assist points created, and 10th in total assists (80). The game is really slowing down for Acuff in a good way.

His passing was an underappreciated skill during his time at Arkansas. People will see the scoring numbers and immediately throw out a bad comparison for Acuff, but the truth is, Acuff is being asked to run the offense, be the primary scorer, and also facilitate. How many 19-year-olds in the NBA are being asked to do that? Right now, the answer is just him. Acuff will continue to put up numbers for a bad Kings team that is waiting for the trade deadline to deal some of the veterans on the roster.

ACUFF JR. JOINS LEBRON 👏In tonight's action, Darius Acuff Jr. (32 PTS, 10 AST) joined LeBron James (3x) as the only teenagers in NBA history to record 30+ points and 10+ assists in multiple games! pic.twitter.com/VmWshWmQZn

The debate surrounding the No. 1 pick was one of the biggest storylines in the lead-up to this year's draft. With Dybantsa going to Washington and Peterson to Utah, they ended up in similar situations on teams with established veterans that seemed ready to take the next step. But for the Jazz, it has been a nightmare season of injuries, with Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen out for extended periods.

With everyone in the lineup, Peterson struggled to find a clear-cut role during his first few games. He finished in single digits in two of his first four games, which included taking just seven shots from the floor in his NBA debut. Coming out of high school, Peterson was best playing on-ball. However, when he got to Kansas, he played more off-ball. Part of that was due to cramping issues that sidelined him for an extended period, but Peterson has shown he can play both roles well.

darryn scored 26 tonight, a new career high #TakeNote presented by @ZionsBank pic.twitter.com/NaCyoa8kQv

The last four games have been excellent for Peterson and showed why he was the projected top pick entering last college basketball season. He has scored over 20 points in those last four, including a 26-point outburst against the Timberwolves. Peterson's shooting from beyond the arc has also been impressive during that stretch.

With so many key veterans out for Utah at the moment, Peterson has been pushed into an expanded role. It's going to be that way for the next several weeks. With Utah's season already looking like a mess, the organization's top priority should be developing Peterson into a primary option. If the last week is any indication, Peterson could get back into a very competitive Rookie of the Year race.

Thursday was a rough shooting night for Dybantsa during the most entertaining Wizards game of the entire season, which ended with a double-overtime loss at home to Detroit. Dybantsa shot just 2 of 10 and finished with five points -- the first time in his career he finished in single digits. However, Dybantsa did hit a clutch mid-range jumper to send the game to double overtime.

Outside of Kyshawn George taking seven shots in 26 minutes due to foul trouble, Dybantsa attempted the second-fewest (10) shots among starters. Dybantsa also didn't get to the free-throw line, which was shocking because one of his greatest strengths is drawing fouls.

Trae Young (23), Anthony Davis (21) and Alex Sarr (14) all attempted more shots against the Pistons. Dybantsa did contribute in other ways (eight rebounds and four assists), but that kind of game underlines why I'm hesitant to put Dybantsa in Tier 1 of the Rookie of the Year conversation. And trust me, it's not because of talent. Dybantsa is awesome.

AJ DYBANTSA FORCES 2OT!IN THE CLUTCH THE #1 PICK COMES THROUGH. pic.twitter.com/lsqG6bGNXX

The concern is that, with Davis and Young on the roster, the volume of shots for Dybantsa might not be there for him to win Rookie of the Year. Acuff is the primary option for the Kings. Lendeborg is now the de facto No. 1 option with Curry set to miss the next month. Peterson has been thrust into a larger role with veterans out. Boozer is putting up numbers on a nightly basis despite having a lower usage rate than Acuff, Wilson and Lendeborg.

Dybantsa is the face and future of Washington's franchise. He should be featured as such. If he isn't, he will likely fall behind the top three players in the race for the majority of the season.

Even outside of the top four names, several other rookies have performed well this season. Although they will likely be longshots to win Rookie of the Year, here are some sleepers and others worthy of recognition.

It's time for the Clippers to start Wagler. The impact he has on the game off the bench is impressive. If he is given more minutes, he will shine. The stat that stands out about Wagler is that he is shooting better from beyond the arc (35.4%) than inside the arc (29.7%). He is shooting 86% from the free-throw line, which is a positive indicator for future shooting success. He will be fine.

Mara was a player I thought could make an immediate impact as a rookie because of his defense and offensive efficiency. Mara is shooting 60.3% from the field and is blocking 1.8 shots per game. Check and check.

The flashes from Brown are must-see TV. It's the same sentiment as during his time at Louisville. If you put together a highlight tape of Brown's best plays, you would think he's the best guard in the class. He has played in just seven games this season and hasn't started because of a minutes restriction.

Flemings has been great in spots off the bench and even as a starter. He is one of the most efficient rookies in the class -- albeit on lower volume than his peers -- and is shooting 52.1% from the field, 42.9% from 3 and 72.7% from the charity stripe.

New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler is the winner of the American League Cy Young Award for 2026. Schlittler was a unanimous selection via the Baseball Writers Association of America balloting, the results of which were announced on Wednesday, beating out Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease and Guardians rookie Parker Messick.

Schlittler's win snapped the run of free agent Tarik Skubal, who won the last two AL Cy Youngs as a member of the Detroit Tigers.

This past season, the right-handed Schlitter in his age-25 campaign put up dominant numbers:

In addition to the above, Schlitter led AL pitchers in WAR with a mark of 7.0, and his ERA+ of 215 also paced his league. That 215 ERA+, which means that Schlittler's park-adjusted ERA was 115% better than the league average, is a Yankees franchise record. Among Yankee qualifiers, only Ron Guidry's 208 in 1978 comes close. Additionally, Schlittler tied for the AL lead this season with an FIP of 2.56, and he struck out 31.4% of opposing batters, which also ranked second in the AL.

Without Schlittler's top-shelf contributions, the Yankees, without franchise slugger and reigning back-to-back AL MVP Aaron Judge for almost 100 games, might have struggled to make the postseason. Instead, Schlittler's excellence at the front of the rotation helped them win 93 games, post the AL's top run differential, and advance to the ALDS.

"Cam had as dominant a season as a starting pitcher can have from start to finish," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said in a statement. "He's shown an astonishing amount of growth since we drafted him, and his success is no accident. Cam has a tireless appetite for hard work and refinement that has allowed his talents to truly flourish. This Cy Young is richly deserved. Cam was the most dominant pitcher in our league and continues to grow into a foundational player for this franchise."

While Schlittler was outstanding as a rookie in 2025, this past season, he increased usage of his sinker and cutter and improved ride on his 98-mph fastball helped him take the next step and become one of the very pitchers in all of baseball. Since Schlittler doesn't turn 26 until February, continued dominance may be on the way.

Schlittler is now the seventh Yankee to win the Cy Young Award. He joins teammate Gerrit Cole in 2023, Roger Clemens in 2001, Guidry in 1978, Sparky Lyle in 1977, Whitey Ford in 1961, and Bob Turley in 1958.
