#2614. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2613. How have the Heat turned their season around? Giannis and Bam are on fire, but that's not all

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Since opening up 0-4, the Miami Heat have slowly, quietly, been finding their way into the light. It initially came against weaker opponents, with wins over the Pacers, Clippers, Jazz and Kings getting them back near .500. But these back-to-back wins over Cleveland (on Friday) and Detroit (on Saturday) put a real stamp on this stretch. After all the panic, Miami has won seven of nine and is tied for the East's No. 4 seed entering this week.

How have they turned things around? Let's take a look at four major reasons.

Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo have combined for 128 points, 42 rebounds and 17 assists on 72% shooting over these last two wins. The concerns over their offensive fit -- as relative non-shooters who operate largely in the same spots -- have quieted, but also a good bit of this production is coming independent of one another as Erik Spoelstra is staggering their minutes between the start of each half and fourth-quarter closing time.

With shooters all around, Adebayo and Antetokounmpo are free to attack maximum interior space and exploit soft midrange spots, which has been the bread and butter of this run.

Every mid range jumper from Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo against Cleveland last night: pic.twitter.com/jeamVaSLhk

As pointed out by Couper Moorhead of NBA.com, the Heat face more drop-coverage defense (when the big who's guarding the ball screener falls back toward the rim rather than stepping up to the level of the screen or even higher to contest the shooter coming off the screen) than any other offense in the league. That's because nobody fears Miami's pull-up 3-point shooters, and because Giannis and Bam are such forceful attackers of the rim.

The soft spot is in between, outside the restricted circle but inside the 3-point line, or even better inside the free-throw line. It's the dreaded midrange zone, where defenses are happy to, concede shots to players like Giannis and Bam, and right now they are both knocking these supposedly inefficient looks down at ridiculous rates.

These are by far career-high percentages for both guys, and they are coming on career-high frequencies from these zones (over 30% of their total shot attempts in the 3-10 range). Over these last nine games, Giannis is a scorching 22 for 33 from 10-19 feet while Adebayo -- who has also been the best post scorer in the league at 1.26 PPP on 4.8 post-ups per game -- is 30 for 44 from 5-14 feet.

They are absolutely wearing these outer-paint shots out, and if defenses keep with the drop coverage, these shots are likely to remain consistently available. It's not to say they'll keep making them at this rate, of course. But to have established these go-zones is a big step for Miami's half-court offense, because we all know how dangerous they are in the open floor as the highest-frequency and second-highest-scoring transition team.

Now add in the fact that Miami kills teams on the glass with Giannis and Bam on the court (over these last nine, they are grabbing 78.7 percent of all available defensive rebounds and 37.8% of all offensive rebounds, both of which would lead the league), and in the turnover battle, and what you have is a Heat team that is getting a lot more true shot attempts than its opponents (almost 10 more per 100 possessions).

That is everything in today's possession-obsessed NBA. Get up more shots than your opponent by generating second-chance opportunities on the offensive boards and by creating more turnovers than you cough up, and you're in a good spot. Make those extra shots at the rate Miami is right now, and you're almost unbeatable.

Mitchell has gone from a guy perhaps playing to stay in the league, or at least in an NBA rotation, to a current top-three Most Improved Player candidate at FanDuel (+900). He's blowing his previous production away.

The Heat are a low-volume pick-and-roll team for the same reasons they're a prime candidate for drop coverage: They don't have those kinds of pull-up shooters. Mitchell can punish drops with pull-up 3s on occasion (8 for 20 so far, per Synergy), but more importantly he's the one most often hitting Bam and Giannis in those soft-pocket midrange spots we talked about -- in addition to the rim rolls, cuts and kick-out 3s that open up as he breaches the paint, often in transition.

Of Mitchell's 119 assists so far, 55 have gone to Giannis and Bam, and he has directly set up a 3-point make 37 times. Those 9.2 assists per game lead the league among qualified players, and the 257 points his assists have generated rank second only to Trae Young's 260, per PBP Stats. Young is making $49 million this year. Mitchell is making $12 million.

Then there is the shooting. Mitchell has steadily improved from range throughout his career, but this season he's on fire at 43% on catch-and-shoot 3s, per Synergy, as part of Miami's spacing around Bam and Giannis. We saw all of Mitchell's tools in his 22-point/17-assist masterpiece against Cleveland.

Davion Mitchell ABSURD statline vs Cavs: 22 PTS | 5 REB | 17 AST | 7/14 FG | 66 TS% pic.twitter.com/b0d8I1XHDy

Thompson isn't the player he was in his prime. His defense has especially declined, and he's not going to be putting up any more 37-point quarters. But he's still a sniper.

Thompson is splashing 42% on almost 10 3s a game, and his 48 total 3-pointers rank third league-wide, and his 15.3 PPG are the most he's averaged since leaving Golden State. He's been especially hot of late, averaging 20 PPG on 48/45 shooting splits over his last seven games.

Klay Thompson was amazing vs the Pistons26 PTS - 4 AST - 6 3PM - 10/17 FGM Found a new home pic.twitter.com/JvQju9Hais

Over the last seven games, Miami is plus-11.7 with Thompson on the court and minus-3.7 when he's off. That's the best split on the team. The starting lineup of Mitchell, Bam, Giannis, Thompson and Pelle Larsson (who has been big in this turnaround, too, since his promotion to the first five), the Heat are outscoring opponents by 23 points per 100 possessions, and Thompson has been particularly effective playing alongside Giannis. With those two on the court as Bam rests, Miami is drumming teams by 31.6 points per 100, per Databallr.

Miami's defense was expected to be a strength, and when people looked up and saw a bottom-barrel rating, it was jarring. Some of that, if not most of it, could be attributed to inordinately hot shooting by their opponents, which wasn't likely to continue. And indeed it hasn't.

Through the first seven games, Miami opponents were shooting 41.8% from 3 and 50% from the midrange, per Cleaning the Glass. That made for a 58.7 effective field-goal percentage, despite Miami's defense registering a top-three expected eFG% (52.9) based on the shots they were surrendering, per Cleaning the Glass.

Translation: the Heat were, and are, forcing generally inefficient shots, but to start the year those shots were going in at a rate of almost 6% better than expected. That was the worst, or unluckiest, mark in the league, however you want to look at it.

Cut to this four-game win streak, over which opponents are down to 35.2% from 3 with a 53.9 eFG% against an expected 54%, per CTG. That's in part because Miami has cut the number of wide-open 3s (nearest defender at least six feet away) it was allowing to start the year almost in half (to start, they were surrendering 16 wide-open 3s every night, but over this four-game winning streak they are down to 9.1, stingiest in the league). Even better, their opponents have come down from a 45.5% conversion rate on those wide-open 3s to 40%.

All of which is to say, Miami's opponent shooting is coming back to earth. Hot shooting can render any defense helpless, but over time, if you're forcing a team into tough shots from tough spots, the averages are going to swing back your way eventually. Miami is starting to see that happen.

#2612. It wouldn't shock me if ... for Week 11: New WR crashes OROY race, Jared Goff's pesky streak continues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The beauty of the NFL is its unpredictability. It's what keeps us coming back each Sunday, as we never quite know what's going to unfold. We might have a good idea, but more often than not, the consensus outcome fails to actually come to fruition. As difficult as it may be to try and predict what's around the corner in a given week, we've done a pretty good job this season of predicting the unpredictable.

For instance, last week we accurately put you on to both Zach Charbonnet and Josh Downs making waves that far surpassed their over/under gambling odds. We also told you to temper your expectations regarding Fernando Mendoza's first career start, which proved wise. Of course, we're not going to bat a thousand here given the nature of trying to see into the future, and we came up short in our predictions that Brock Purdy would ascend as the MVP favorite, along with Will Anderson Jr. falling two sacks shy of matching his single-game career high.

This go-around, we turn our attention to a couple of individual performances, as well as highlight some developments in the playoff and award races that we wouldn't be shocked to see unfold in Week 11.

All NFL odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook.

Tony Pollard spent the first five seasons of his career in Dallas after the Cowboys selected him in the fourth round out of Memphis in 2019. The veteran back left the organization in 2024, inking a three-year, $21.75 million deal with the Titans. Now, for the first time since leaving the Cowboys, Pollard will face his former team on Sunday.

The 29-year-old has a fantastic opportunity to get one over on his former team, which has struggled immensely to stop the run this season. In fact, the Cowboys are giving up 154.1 rushing yards per game on a 5.2 yards-per-carry clip this season, both the most in the NFL. Dallas is also giving up the third-most receiving yards to running backs and the most receiving touchdowns.

This sets Pollard up for a dominant day out of Tennessee's backfield and continues what has been a white-hot stretch for him. Over his past three games, Pollard has rushed for 279 yards (5.1 yards per carry) and five touchdowns, while catching 14 of his 17 targets for 112 yards and another score.

The way both Pollard and the Cowboys' run defense are trending, it wouldn't surprise us at all if he logs 150 scrimmage yards.

Gambling nuggets to note: Tony Pollard's O/U rushing yards prop for Week 11 is 65.5 (-110 to the Over). Meanwhile, Pollard's O/U rushing + receiving yards prop for Week 11 is 87.5 (-110 to the Over).

The Lions enter Week 11 with a 7-2 record, which is good for first place in the NFC North and slotted in as the No. 2 seed in the conference. Amid the team's five-game winning streak, however, Jared Goff has been a little loose with the football. The Lions quarterback has thrown four interceptions over his last three games, including two last week against the Patriots in Germany.

Goff has thrown an interception in three straight games entering Sunday's contest with the Buccaneers, and it really should be four straight games. Before this streak started, Goff had two interceptions dropped by Packers defenders in Detroit's Week 7 matchup against Green Bay.

Now, Goff faces a Tampa Bay defense that will not only be well rested after being on the bye in Week 10 but has a knack for snatching interceptions. The Buccaneers lead the league with 16 interceptions. Their 72.7 passer rating allowed is also second-best in the NFL and only looking up to the Vikings, so this has the potential to be a tough task for Goff to overcome. It also sets up a strong possibility that this pesky interception streak will continue.

Gambling nugget to note: Jared Goff is +122 to throw at least one interception in Week 11.

The Cleveland Browns get to kick their feet up and watch the action unfold across the league this weekend as they're currently on the bye. Before the break, the club vaulted into the AFC playoff picture and currently sits as the No. 7 seed with a 6-4 record. Even with Cleveland not playing this week, there's a strong opportunity for the franchise's playoff position to strengthen.

Namely, they'll be rooting for the Eagles, who host the Steelers (currently the No. 6 seed). If Philadelphia pulls off the home upset over Pittsburgh (who hasn't won a road game against the Eagles since 1965), the Steelers would draw even with Cleveland with a 6-5 record. Because these teams split the season series, the next tiebreaker would be their record within the AFC North. The Browns (2-1) have a better division record than the Steelers (2-2) at the moment, so they'd leap ahead of them.

On top of the Eagles, if the Panthers and/or Broncos pull off wins against the Ravens and Raiders, respectively, that'd further create some breathing room for Cleveland. By the time they emerge from their bye week and gear up for Week 12, I wouldn't be surprised if the Browns are the No. 6 seed.

Gambling nugget to note: An Eagles, Panthers, Broncos moneyline parlay is +468.

The Vikings have been the talk of the NFL for the bulk of the season thanks to their lethal defense, but they also got a massive boost right before the trade deadline by acquiring Kirk Cousins. The veteran quarterback provided immediate dividends in the club's Week 10 win over the Packers at Lambeau Field, and will try to continue this storybook return to Minnesota when they take on the 49ers in Mexico City. The Vikings are a 3-point underdog in this matchup, but their defense certainly gives them a shot to pull off the upset.

Not to mention that Brock Purdy is 0-2 against the Vikings in his career. In those games, Purdy's teams have averaged just 17 points per game, while he's thrown two touchdowns and committed four turnovers. If Minnesota forces Purdy to look like that once again, they are live to pull out the win.

Provided they do, Minnesota suddenly has an opportunity to leap to the No. 1 seed in the NFC by the end of Sunday. Of course, that result is contingent on other factors playing out over the course of the slate, but it's not out of the realm of possibility. All the Vikings would need is for the Buccaneers to upset the Lions, dropping Detroit to 7-3 on the season. Then, if Minnesota beats the 49ers to move to 8-2, they leap up atop the division and, because of the newly acquired head-to-head tiebreaker, would jump over San Francisco as the top seed in the conference.

Gambling nuggets to note: Vikings are +130 to beat the 49ers. The Buccaneers are +270 to beat the Lions. A Vikings and Buccaneers moneyline parlay is +751. Currently, the Vikings are +450 to finish the season as the No. 1 seed.

The tightest award race in the NFL amongst players is Offensive Rookie of the Year. Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza is the current favorite, and he's started just one game so far this season. While that speaks to the value of the quarterback position, it also highlights just how wide open the race is and how a player can burst onto the scene midseason and make a legitimate run.

In that same vein, folks should start paying attention to Saints rookie wideout Jordyn Tyson.

The No. 8 overall pick at the 2026 NFL Draft had the first half of his rookie season erased due to a hamstring injury he suffered during the summer. However, Tyson returned to the field in Week 9 and has almost instantly started making an impact. Over two games, Tyson has been targeted 18 times and hauled in 15 catches for 110 yards. That includes an 11-catch, 80-yard showing last week against Carolina.

Those receptions are tied for the most in the first two games of a career in Saints history. According to Pro Football Focus, Tyson joined Malik Nabers (2024) and Puka Nacua (2023) as the only receivers since 2020 to have at least 10 receptions in a game within their first two games played.

With New Orleans' running game nonexistent and pass-heavy game scripts projected for the rest of the season, Tyson is set up nicely to put up some eye-popping numbers, especially if he's going to command about nine targets per game. That includes this week, when the Saints are 11.5-point underdogs to the Bears. That suggests they'll be playing from behind and will need to throw the football, which could continue to showcase Tyson.

This might be the time to buy his Offensive Rookie of the Year stock.

Gambling nugget to note: Jordyn Tyson is +1800 to win Offensive Rookie of the Year.

#2611. What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a big-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

Boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

"I'm not going to speak to that right now," he said "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of."

Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

Because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

Hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

The risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

"He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field."

The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

Bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

With Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

One is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

"I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow said. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately."

#2610. Grading NFL quarterbacks on rookie contracts: Caleb Williams, C.J. Stroud kick careers into high gear

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There is nothing more valuable in the NFL than rostering a star quarterback on a rookie contract. The financial flexibility that comes with a highly affordable signal-caller cannot be overstated. That's partly why the New England Patriots made a run to the Super Bowl last year and why the Chicago Bears are poised to do the same in 2026.

To make the most of the opportunity, though, that quarterback must be a legitimate standout. Drake Maye was nearly the league MVP a year ago. Caleb Williams is in contention this season. They and a few others are in line for massive contract extensions when they become eligible.

Teams with slow-developing or underperforming young quarterbacks face the other side of this equation: the frustration of having enough cap space to field stars at other positions while lacking serviceable play at the most important position of all. In many cases, this results in the quarterback's career flaming out and the team looking back to the draft for another swing at finding the face of the franchise. A couple of squads might see that play out in the months to come.

Below are grades for all 12 starting quarterbacks who are on their rookie contracts.

In just his second year as a pro, Maye achieved two feats that no other player on their rookie contract can boast. In fact, in reaching the Super Bowl and finishing one first-place vote shy of the MVP award, Maye stepped closer to glory than most quarterbacks in the league have at any point in their career regardless of contract status. Regression in his third season has come in the form of immense turnover issues (he's tied for second-most through 10 weeks with 13) and a .500 record, but some of that can be attributed to the Patriots roster being depleted by injuries. Speaking of which, Maye's season might be over because of the ankle injury he sustained in Munich in Week 10.

The step backward in 2026 and the ankle issue cast uncertainty over what Maye's next contract will look like if he signs one when he becomes eligible for an extension this offseason. But there is no doubt that he is the locked-in quarterback of the present and future for the Patriots. His proven upside is greater than that of any other signal-caller on a rookie deal.

The blame for the Houston Texans' underwhelming campaign cannot be directed at C.J. Stroud. While his inconsistency in 2024 and 2025 capped the team's success, his performance this year is the only thing keeping the Texans even remotely competitive in the postseason hunt. His return to the tremendous form that made him a standout rookie has been a pleasant development and puts him in line for a massive payday.

When he won the Offensive Rookie of the Year award in 2023, Stroud led the NFL in passing yards per game and interception rate. His numbers this season in both of those categories (273.6 ypg, 0.9 INT%) are almost identical to the ones that put him at the top of the league.

When the Texans inevitably sign Stroud to a lucrative extension, they will bet that the campaigns bookending his four-year career are more indicative of what is to come than the two in the middle.

Through 26 games, it remains unclear whether Cam Ward is a viable long-term starter in this league. The Tennessee Titans will have a tough decision to make at the end of the year: draft another quarterback or add pieces around Ward when they make four selections in the first two rounds? The second-year surge they hoped would come from last year's No. 1 pick has not arrived, so their patience is about to be put to the test.

Given that they are actively deconstructing the roster by trading Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker at the trade deadline, it is clear the Titans prioritize developing their young players over making desperation moves to make the roster competitive as currently constructed. That, along with their willingness to keep Tony Pollard and routinely add talent to the wide receiver group, suggests they want to give Ward every opportunity to improve. The next eight games will go a long way in determining whether Tennessee should stick to that plan or seek another option on draft day.

No team has been more prolific at winning one-possession games since 2025 than the Denver Broncos, and much of the credit goes to Bo Nix. He led the league in game-winning drives last year with seven and leads in both fourth-quarter comebacks (five) and game-winning drives (six) in 2026. Of course, it would be preferable if Nix helped put enough points on the board over the first three quarters that he did not need to pull off heroics in the final minutes, but at least he continues to deliver when his back is against the wall.

This season is thus far the least productive of Nix's three-year career by completion rate, success rate, yards per game, and passer rating. Some of that regression might be attributable to the offensive coordinator change, which prompted Sean Payton to reclaim play-calling duties in Week 5. What is promising is that Nix's last three games were arguably his best of the campaign, so he might be rounding back into form just in time for the stretch run.

Even with a slow start to the year, Nix has been everything the Broncos need since he joined them in 2024. And if not for his ankle injury last postseason, he might have played in the Super Bowl. There is no reason to think Denver will not invest in him when the time comes.

It will take more time to accurately gauge Fernando Mendoza's outlook as an NFL starter. His debut, as should be expected, had its ups and downs. He took six sacks, completed a modest 17 of 29 passes, but scored his first touchdown on a 10-yard run to the end zone. In all, it was a milquetoast showing against a daunting Seattle Seahawks defense.

The Las Vegas Raiders need to bolster their wide receiver group in the months to come in order to give Mendoza the requisite weapons to succeed. The tight end tandem of Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer should help the No. 1 pick get his feet wet, though.

J.J. McCarthy might be saving his career in real-time. The inability to stay healthy and the lackluster play when he was on the field during his first two seasons with the Minnesota Vikings made him an undeniable bust -- so much so that the Vikings demoted him to the No. 3 line on their depth chart and moved on from him for pennies on the dollar when the New York Giants came calling for a trade earlier this year. With the change in scenery, however, has come marked improvement.

McCarthy's Giants debut was astounding: A 243-yard fourth quarter. Since he earned the starting job, he has completed 66.3% of his passes for 224 yards per game with a touchdown and an interception. He went 2-1 in those starts. That is not half bad for someone who joined the team five weeks into the season. There are still obvious flaws in his game, but McCarthy has helped the Giants maintain their lead in the NFC East so far, and that is about all they could have asked for when they traded for him.

The best-case outcome for McCarthy the rest of the way is that he proves himself as a starting-caliber talent and latches on somewhere else in 2027. This is Jaxson Dart's team when he returns to full strength next year. Perhaps the most likely scenario is for McCarthy to settle in as his backup, continue to develop and cement himself as one of the NFL's best No. 2s. That would still be a disappointment considering he is a former No. 10 overall pick, but it would be a step forward from where he began the year.

Elbow dislocations and a couple of minor lower-body injuries halted Jayden Daniels' momentum in the wake of a remarkable rookie season in which he won Offensive Rookie of the Year, finished seventh in MVP voting and took the Washington Commanders to the NFC Championship Game. He has been proficient when healthy since then, but he has only played 14 games since 2024, and the Commanders are just 4-9-1 even with him in the lineup over the last two seasons. His career thus far is a mixed bag, including the highest highs for a rookie quarterback and the lows of a middling team.

The elite rushing prowess that helped him lead the NFL in success rate as a rookie has regressed a bit, but he is a more accurate passer who this year paces the league in interception rate and who is on track to set a career high in yards per game. Again, there is give and take.

If the Commanders can upgrade their offensive line and increase their depth behind the injured Terry McLaurin at wide receiver, Daniels would finally have enough help around him to potentially take Washington back to its 2024 heights and solidify himself as a top-tier quarterback. He is not the problem in Washington.

Williams and the Bears are on a steep ascent to the top of the league. Individually, Williams is on a trajectory that may one day lead him to an MVP award. And from a team perspective, his climb into stardom is the catalyst behind the Bears' surge toward the front of the Super Bowl race.

The four-interception debacle in his last outing was an aberration in what has otherwise been a breakout season for the third-year quarterback. Prior to the setback, he showed an increased comfort in Ben Johnson's high-octane offense and took care of the ball about as well as anyone. Even after that showing, this is the best version of Williams the NFL has seen, with his career-best passer rating, uncanny sack avoidance, and 257.7 passing yards per game.

It feels like this is the start of a superstar career.

From Weeks 1-5, Bryce Young emerged as a dark-horse MVP candidate. The second quarter of the season brought him back down to Earth. In totality, this is still by far the best year of his career, and it could not have come at a more crucial time as he approaches a pivotal offseason in which the Carolina Panthers must decide whether to pick up his fifth-year option, sign him to an extension or begin a separation process.

Coach Dave Canales seems to have a deep understanding of Young's abilities and how best to use them. Young has done nothing but improve under his tutelage. His down weeks are still problematic, but when he is on, Young has been the best version of himself this year. Take his yardage numbers, for instance: the 266.3 yards per game the Heisman Trophy winner averages this season are far greater than the 188.2 of his previous career-best campaign.

Young's development has been a slow burn, but it has been linear and remains on the right track. This is a quarterback Carolina can keep building around.

The New Orleans Saints' motto is to air it out, and they have a quarterback who can do that. Coach Kellen Moore put a lot on Tyler Shough's plate over his first 18 starts and, thus far in 2026, tasked him with throwing the third-most passes per game at 38.1. Across that hefty workload, Shough turned in a middle-of-the-pack passer rating, which is commendable for a quarterback in his sophomore professional season.

If the Saints had a better defense, they would probably stand tall atop the NFL's worst division, and the conversation around Shough would be more positive. Instead, he is merely keeping New Orleans somewhat afloat in a division that could feature a sub-.500 champion. As he continues to build a connection with prized rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson and maintains a highly productive link with Chris Olave, it will become clearer whether he is a true franchise quarterback. But over two half-seasons as a starter, his early returns as a second-round pick are quite positive.

The stop-and-start nature of Michael Penix Jr.'s three-year career makes it hard to judge fairly. He cannot be faulted for his torn ACL last year and the Atlanta Falcons' questionable management of the quarterback room the year prior. What is up for grading, though, is what Penix has done on the field, and over 20 starts, it is an average-to-slightly-below-average performance.

With all of the star talent on the Falcons offense, the team needs its quarterback to perform at a high level and get the most out of Bijan Robinson and Drake London. As they enter the prime of their careers, it is paramount that Penix makes strides. The franchise cannot afford to let its two greatest assets go to waste. In that sense, Penix's slow development is a problem. But at the same time, his flashes suggest that there is a franchise quarterback in him. Back-to-back three-touchdown games in October were emblematic of the ceiling that made him worthy of a first-round pick.

The arm strength Carson Beck lacked in his final year of college is back. The further removed he gets from his UCL injury at Georgia, the more he looks capable of playing in the NFL. But that does not mean he will thrive as the Arizona Cardinals' starter in the second half of the season, nor does it mean the team should not draft a quarterback with its 2027 first-round pick. Beck was dreadful in Week 10 in his debut, throwing a pair of interceptions, taking five sacks, and losing 34-6 to the Los Angeles Rams. Then again, what third-round rookie would thrive in his first career start, with a depleted wide receiver group and against a top-10 defense?

Arizona will do its due diligence in the coming weeks to see what it has in Beck. More likely than not, it does not have a franchise quarterback.

#2608. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

Author: “MH” is a young analyst who regularly produces content for Spielverlagerung NextGen and TotalFootballAnalysis. On X, he can be found under Mh_sv5.

#2607. MLB rumors: Mets targeting first-base help; Padres look wide for pitching; new Ketel Marte suitor emerges

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the General Manager Meetings now in the rearview mirror, it sure seems like we're playing out the clock in Major League Baseball news until the CBA expires. That would be Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET. The expectation at this juncture is that the owners will lock the players out and we'll deal with several months of public negotiations. Until then, we can hope to see some player movement, such as the Red Sox signing Jake Bauers.

In the meantime, let's round up the news and rumors for the day.

The Padres are in desperate need of starting pitching, should they wish to continue contending. The rotation right now would be Joe Musgrove, Randy Vásquez, JP Sears, Jhony Brito and a shrugging emoji. Sure enough, they are all over the rumor mill for rotation help.

The San Diego Union-Tribune reports that they've shown interest in "virtually every starting pitcher" in free agency, "from Tarik Skubal on down. From Matthew Boyd to Shota Imanaga to Dustin May to Kaima Taira." Further, ESPN reports that the Padres have a meeting set up with Skubal but have also shown interest in Freddy Peralta, as well as Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez.

Expect them to remain active until they land at least two starters.

It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are open to trading All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. The Blue Jays have been sniffing around, and now the Orioles have emerged as a suitor, per MLB.com.

This one is interesting in that it's not a natural fit. The Orioles have extra infielders and have been said to be shopping infielders in order to land outfield help. Between second and third base, the Orioles have Jackson Holliday, Jordan Westburg, Blaze Alexander, Coby Mayo and Christian Encarnacion-Strand. Presumably, if they are able to swing a deal for Marte, there would be some shuffling with more trades and/or moving someone to the outfield.

The Mets could have an opening at first base as things currently stand and they've checked in on free agent Ty France, according to the New York Post.

Currently, the Mets are looking at Jared Young (coming off a scary head injury), Mark Vientos and Jorge Polanco as options at first base.

France, 32 and probably considered a journeyman at this point, had a big season in 2026 for the Padres. He hit .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 homers, 72 RBI and a career-high 4.5 WAR.

Reliever Jonathan Loáisiga is close to signing with a new team, reports ESPN. The Dodgers are among five teams involved, with the New York Post adding the Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Blue Jays to the mix.

In 67 outings last season for Arizona, Loáisiga pitched to a 2.42 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and had 48 strikeouts in 67 innings.

The Yankees have re-signed left-handed reliever Tim Hill to a one-year, $2.25 million deal with a $2.5 million club option for 2028, per ESPN. Hill, 36, made 67 appearances last season with a 4.60 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 25 strikeouts in 58 ⅔ innings. He held lefties to a .213/.265/.346 line.

#2606. Week 11 Super Bowl stock report: Kirk Cousins raises Vikings' ceiling, Drake Maye injury tanks Patriots

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The first batch of NFL games after the trade deadline offered a first look at the teams that went all-in on a Super Bowl run. Although not all of the newcomers debuted with their squads — like the Jacksonville Jaguars' prized duo of Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III, who got a week off — some were tremendously impactful and proved their front offices right for investing in them.

Chief among those deadline acquisitions was Kirk Cousins. The Minnesota Vikings quarterback showed what is possible for the NFC North leaders when they have a functional offense.

At the same time that teams like the Vikings charged forward in the hunt for a championship, a couple of squads suffered devastating setbacks. In the Munich Game, both the New England Patriots and Detroit Lions suffered costly injuries that could make the difference in whether they can even compete for the Vince Lombardi Trophy.

This week's byes create the lightest slate of the year and give a handful of Super Bowl hopefuls a chance to recharge before the stretch run, but there are still a couple of contests on tap that should further shape the title picture.

Here are the latest trends in the Super Bowl race heading into Week 11.

Maybe the Vikings just have the Green Bay Packers' number this year, and it does not matter who lines up at quarterback. Heck, if Carson Wentz could defeat the division rivals by 17 points in the season opener, then there would have been no excuse for Cousins not to deliver a win, too, in Week 10. But maybe Cousins' arrival represents something far greater. For the first time since that first game of the season, Minnesota actually had life on offense. Its 30-10 win at Lambeau Field marked just its second 30-point game of the season.

If the offense simply stays out of the way, the Vikings are probably good enough to at least make the playoffs. If that unit is more than net neutral, though, this could become the best season in franchise history. The defense is that elite.

Nobody has scored more than 23 points on Brian Flores' defense all year. All Kevin O'Connell is asking of his offense is to score approximately that many of its own. A team that averages 23 points would rank 13th in the NFL in scoring. That is not an especially high bar. Cousins is enough of an upgrade over the situation Minnesota had at quarterback over the first two months of the year that he should be able to deliver that margin of improvement on his own.

A rejuvenated Justin Jefferson is a scary thing for opponents to see, and it is coming. He saw a season-high 13 targets in Cousins' debut and turned them into a 2026-best nine receptions. One that tandem fully rebuilds the connection that was so prolific during Cousins' first stint in Minnesota, teams will have to devote all kinds of resources to stopping him, which will open up other elements of the Vikings offense.

It is not often that a single player arrives as such an obvious savior in a team's pursuit of a championship. Cousins is exactly what the Vikings need.

Injuries already accounted for a dip in Patriots stock prior to last week. The latest devastating one has New England's outlook at a new low.

The extent of Drake Maye's ankle injury is still to be announced, but the Patriots reportedly fear it is season-ending. Frankly, if Maye cannot play, New England's campaign is done. Tommy DeVito is not the caliber of backup who can step into action and shoulder the kind of load last year's MVP runner-up managed as the leader of an already banged-up unit. That much was clear when the offense sputtered in the 35-10 loss to the Lions in Germany.

It was always going to be an uphill battle for the Patriots to get back into the playoffs, let alone surge back to the Super Bowl, with the volume of absences that hit the offense. A.J. Brown's inability to get and stay healthy, Romeo Doubs' injured reserve stint, TreVeyon Henderson's illness, and a host of offensive line ailments forced this team to trudge through the mud even with Maye calling the shots. Losing the best and most important player in the group would be a death blow. And even if his ankle problem does not end his season, the hole he might find himself in when he returns to action will likely be too deep to climb out of.

It is time to go back to the well for this week's top longshot. The flavor of the week in the NFC South tends to land here for one reason: none of the teams in this division are particularly good. Still, one of them has to make the playoffs and, by default, will finish the year no worse than four wins away from the Super Bowl. And since the Carolina Panthers are back in sole possession of first place, they are the pick for Week 11.

Standings aside, the Panthers are the team to back in the NFC South when it comes to projecting a division winner and one that could sneak its way to a win or two in the postseason. They forced the rest of the league to take them seriously last year when they nearly took down the Los Angeles Rams in the Wild Card round and have the upside to do something similar in 2026.

In addition to Bryce Young playing the best football of his career, the Panthers finally committed to Chuba Hubbard as a featured back this year, and the decision is paying dividends. He handled 27 of the team's 32 rushes in last week's critical win over the New Orleans Saints, finishing as the Panthers' leading rusher with 92 yards and two touchdowns and as their top receiver with five catches for 80 yards. His breakout season is a boon to an offense that occasionally shows flashes of excellence.

Perhaps even more important was the return of Jaelan Phillips. The Panthers went 0-3 without the edge rusher as he nursed a hamstring injury, but they are 4-2 with him in the lineup, and his sack and three tackles for loss against the Saints earned him NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors.

The Panthers are more "NFC South good" than "Super Bowl contender good," but as long as they win the division, they will have an opportunity to make noise in the postseason.

Sunday, 8:20 p.m., NBC, stream on Fubo (try for free)

This might be the game of the year in the NFC. The schematic matchup between Kyle Shanahan and Brian Flores is bound to be one for the ages, and, not to be dramatic, but it might help determine how offenses and defenses attack each other in the years to come. Oh, and it is a clash between division leaders. This has "conference championship game preview" written all over it. How will Brock Purdy handle the Vikings' overwhelming pressure? Will Cousins and Jefferson continue to revitalize Minnesota's aerial attack? "Sunday Night Football" will bring answers and perhaps determine which of these teams is the deserving favorite to represent the NFC in the Super Bowl.

Sunday, 4:25 p.m., CBS, stream on Paramount+

Davis and Bates are set to make their Jacksonville debuts. The former will be tasked with containing Cam Skattebo, who has been on fire since his Oct. 18 benching with 243 yards from scrimmage and three total touchdowns in his last two games. The latter faces a New York Giants passing game that has been a pleasant surprise, with J.J. McCarthy outperforming expectations at quarterback. If the Jaguars are for real as the best team in the AFC, this is a game they win. But it is also a chance for the Giants to respond to their disappointing Week 10 loss and start rebuilding their NFC East lead.

Sunday, 1 p.m., Fox, stream on Fubo (try for free)

Aidan Hutchinson is done for the year with a torn ACL, but Kerby Joseph will make his season debut in the Detroit Lions secondary. With one star out and another back in, perhaps the Lions will not skip a beat and will keep humming on a side of the ball that's been improving in the wake of its early-season struggles. The Lions have been quietly solid at stopping the run, a critical trait in a battle against the league's best rushing team. On the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' side of things, this would be a big one in their quest to climb out of an 0-4 hole and reach the postseason.

#2604. 10 most interesting MLB non-tender decisions, including a Red Sox staple and a former Rookie of the Year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This Friday, Nov. 20, is an important date on MLB's offseason calendar. It is the deadline for teams to offer 2027 contracts to their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players. The player does not have to sign by Friday's 5 p.m. ET deadline, but he must be offered a contract. If he's not, the player is considered non-tendered and immediately becomes a free agent.

Dozens of players are non-tendered every offseason when teams determine their production no longer warrants the salary. Adolis García, Nathaniel Lowe, Alek Manoah, and Christopher Morel were among the notable non-tenders last offseason. Go back a few years and big names like Cody Bellinger and Kyle Schwarber were non-tendered.

With that in mind, here are the 10 most interesting non-tender decisions ahead of Friday's deadline, using the arbitration salary projections at the indispensable MLB Trade Rumors. You can be sure these teams will scour the trade market for these players and try to get something back before making the non-tender official.

Projected salary: $11.1 million (team control through 2028)

Duran was a non-tender candidate even before the Jake Bauers signing pushed him out of the everyday lineup. There is no such thing as too many good players, but the Red Sox now have two first basemen (Bauers and Willson Contreras) and four outfielders (Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela). Mickey Gasper and Masataka Yoshida are still around too. That's eight players for five lineup spots (first base, DH, three outfield spots). On any given day, three of those guys will be on the bench. Duran, who got MVP votes in 2024, had a 20-20 season in 2026, but it came with a ballooning strikeout rate and a .266 on-base percentage. He has been on the trade block for close to two years now and the writing is on the wall. If the Red Sox are unable to trade Duran this week, there's a real chance he'll get non-tendered Friday given his hefty salary projection.

Projected salary: $7.7 million (team control through 2028)

Former No. 1 overall draft picks have been non-tendered in the past (Tim Beckham most recently), just not by the team that drafted them. Non-tendering Torkelson would be a tough look for the Tigers even though he has not developed into the impact hitter he was projected to be coming out of Arizona State. Simply put, the salary is beginning to outweigh the production. Torkelson, 27, is a 25-30 homer bat with one of the league's highest strikeout rates, middling on-base percentages, and no secondary value (defense, baserunning, etc.). That said, the Tigers do not have an obvious replacement first baseman ready to step in (Colt Keith was the backup in 2026). That, plus the fact that Torkelson has No. 1 pick pedigree, could keep him in Detroit another year.

Projected salary: $2.3 million (team control through 2029)

The American League Rookie of the Year in 2024, Gil has battled injuries and ineffectiveness in the two seasons since. The swing-and-miss rate on his fastball went from an elite 28.5% in 2024 to a below-average 18.8% in 2025 and 17.4% in 2026. Gil, 28, spent time in Triple-A this past season and the Yankees moved him into the bullpen late in the year, where the results were so-so. The salary projection is a pittance, particularly for a team with New York's payroll, though Gil is now out of minor-league options (he must pass through waivers to go to Triple-A) and doesn't have an obvious role. Because he is a pitcher and breathing, and also has a major award win in the not-too-distant past, the Yankees might be able to find a trade partner this week. If not, Gil is a definite non-tender candidate.

Projected salary: $7.6 million (team control through 2028)

A fan favorite and an All-Star this past season, Clement crashed hard in the second half, and the fact of the matter is he has a .295 on-base percentage in his three full seasons with the Blue Jays. Also, the soon-to-be 31-year-old's defensive numbers tumbled this year. Clement's contact skills are elite and he's a versatile, high-energy player. As a utility guy, he's an ace. As an everyday player, he's stretched. Clement's projected salary is hefty for a utility player, particularly one with limited offensive upside who no longer reliably catches the baseball. My guess is the Blue Jays will keep him and live with the salary, but it's not an obvious decision.

Projected salary: $5.1 million (team control through 2028)

Similar to Torkelson, non-tendering a former No. 1 overall pick would be a tough look for the Twins, but a clean break might be best for all involved at this point. Lewis, 27, has trended down since his boffo second half in 2023, enough that he was sent to Triple-A for a spell this summer. He's also moved down the defensive spectrum from third base to first base. It's not due to a lack of effort; Lewis is a major tinkerer who has tried all sorts of swing adjustments. It just hasn't come together. A fresh start elsewhere, away from the spotlight of former No. 1 pick and face of the franchise, might be best for him. The budget-conscious Twins could then reallocate the projected $5.1 million elsewhere on the roster. Right now, they can't count on Lewis to hit or have a meaningful impact defensively.

Projected salary: $3.4 million (team control through 2028)

In 2023, Gorman slugged 27 home runs and looked like one of baseball's top young power hitters. In the three seasons since, he has not come close to repeating that success. The hope was that moving him to third base, his natural position, would unlock Gorman's offense following the Nolan Arenado trade. That didn't happen, and Gorman spent a big chunk of the summer in Triple-A, where he continued to have a hard time making contact. Now 26, Gorman has a minor-league option remaining and can go to Triple-A again in 2027, but the signs are not subtle. The Cardinals are reportedly seeking a stopgap third baseman until top prospect Jesús Báez is ready, which would likely not be the case if they had any belief in Gorman. That projected $3.4 million salary is a high price for a reclamation project ticketed for the minors.

Projected salary: $6.9 million (team control through 2028)

Right-handed power is in short supply throughout baseball and Burger, 31 in April, has hit at least 28 home runs in three of the last four years. He is a one-tool player, though. The home runs come with low batting averages, low on-base percentages, higher-than-average strikeout rates, and little to no defensive or baserunning value. Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young said his team lacked "grit and toughness," whatever that means, and indicated he wants more hitters who grind out at-bats. That's not Burger, who can hit the ball a mile but is not known for making life tough on pitchers. The $6.9 million projection could be deemed too pricey for a player with such a limited skill set.

Projected salary: $6.6 million (team control through 2027)

Doval went from the Yankees to the Pirates at the trade deadline, then from the Pirates to the Giants on waivers in September. He's a former All-Star who led the National League in saves in 2023, two things that have boosted his arbitration salaries. Since 2023, Doval has been a middle reliever who was on the outside of the Circle of Trust™ more often than not. The 29-year-old righty still throws very hard. There's nothing wrong with his arm. It's hard to believe he gets hit as hard as he does sometimes. Doval earned $6.1 million in 2026 and a player cannot have a salary cut by more than 20% during his team control years. That would set Doval's minimum 2027 salary at $4.88 million. I wonder if the Giants would offer him a pay cut, say $5.5M or so, and tell him it's either that or a non-tender. That happens a few times a year around the league.

Projected salary: $6.5 million (team control through 2027)

A fan favorite in San Diego -- "Ho-ly Sheets!" chants are commonplace during his at-bats at Petco Park -- Sheets has fallen by the wayside a bit with the Padres, so much so that he started just one of their six postseason games this year. The 30-year-old is a platoon player who is good against righties more than great and is a defensive liability at both first base and left field. Realistically, Sheets is a platoon DH, and teams rarely pay well for that role unless they're confident they will get big offensive numbers. In the grand scheme of things, the projected $6.5 million isn't much. It is top-of-the-market dollars for this skill set, however.

Projected salary: $1.4 million (team control through 2029)

Two years ago, Blanco threw a no-hitter in his eighth career start. This year, he was so far out of the picture that he pitched once in Houston's last 12 games (two innings at the end of a 13-2 blowout), and the Astros opted to start Peter Lambert on two days' rest with a postseason spot on the line in Game 162. Blanco, who is older than you may realize (he turned 33 in August), returned from Tommy John surgery this summer and had a rough go of it. The pitching-needy Astros could send him to Triple-A next season, as he has a minor-league option remaining, but his stuff was diminished after surgery, and again, they didn't trust him late in the year. You would be surprised at how many cheap pitchers get non-tendered every year. Blanco could join them this week.

#2603. Grading every trade deadline acquisition's new team debut: Kirk Cousins, two WRs get near 'A'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This year's trade deadline was a wild one. There were five trades on deadline day itself (plus two more that didn't go through, one because of a physical, the other because of a nearly epic blunder) and another four trades the day before.

Of the 10 players who switched teams last Monday or Tuesday, seven debuted for their new teams later in the week. The Jaguars didn't play either of their marquee acquisitions -- defensive tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III were both inactive -- and Ravens offensive lineman Ryan Neuzil suited up but did not get any snaps.

But those who did play made immediate, positive impacts on their new clubs. As such, we hand out grades from their first impressions.

Week 10: 21-for-31, 207 yards, 2 touchdowns, 1 interception, 3 sacks; 3 rushes, 11 yards

It can be hard to grade Kirk Cousins because, in terms of how he actually played, it was quite good but not great. But in terms of how this looked to previous Vikings passing offenses, this was a revelation worthy of an A+++++++++.

So we land somewhere in the middle with an A-.

Cousins showed remarkable understanding of the offense. Yes, he had been in this system before but not since 2023; much had changed for both Minnesota and Cousins since then. Still, Cousins' football IQ showed when he audibled to a screen pass that went for 16 yards on third-and-12. He also delivered a strike downfield to Myles Price for the Vikings' first touchdown of the day and their longest passing touchdown since Week 3.

COUSINS TO MYLES PRICE FOR A TD ON 3RD AND 23MINvsGB on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/jSQvCluTla

The Vikings' offense looked different from a schematic standpoint, too, with more under center and more play action -- staples of Kevin O'Connell's offense that Kyler Murray simply couldn't execute. Cousins also knew where his bread is buttered: Justin Jefferson had nine catches on 13 targets, both season highs. With this sort of quarterbacking, Minnesota is very much a Super Bowl contender.

Week 10: 4 catches, 53 yards, 1 touchdown

It's hard to envision this debut going much better. Josh Downs caught four of his five passes from Patrick Mahomes as the Chiefs throttled the Falcons 35-13.

Mahomes steps up and drops a dime to Josh Downs for a TD!KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dwTMy1qZYC

Downs put up this stat line on just eight routes run. Eight! It makes sense that he hardly played after joining a new system, but his impact on the plays he did play in was immense. The Chiefs have long needed a wide receiver who can beat man coverage, and Downs does that extremely well. As he learns the playbook more, he should evolve into a big-time contributor.

Hundreds of years from now, somewhere, some place, Keenan Allen will be catching passes and converting first downs. In his 49ers debut, Allen caught five balls for 61 yards, with four of his catches going for first downs, including on third-and-12 and third-and-6.

Brock making plays!SFvsDAL on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rSNkFBMeTP

Just days after joining the team, Allen led all 49ers wide receivers in catches and yards while playing 31 snaps. He continues to defy Father Time, and with two more catches, he will pass Cris Carter for seventh all-time. With three more, he will pass Marvin Harrison for sixth.

Amani Hooker played every single snap in the Bills' blowout win over the Jets, and he made a nice impact on three plays in particular. He teamed up with Terrel Bernard on a tackle for loss against a Breece Hall run and assisted T.J. Parker on a 2-yard Hall run. He set a nice edge (though missed the tackle) on a Braelon Allen run that went for 0 yards, too. In coverage, Hooker had a nice pass breakup -- and maybe a should-have-been interception -- on a pass over the middle intended for Isaiah Williams. Overall, Hooker's versatility was very much on display.

The only one of the three Jaguars acquisitions last week to actually play in Week 10, Davon Godchaux played 17 snaps and registered a tackle on a 5-yard Tony Pollard run. He also had a nice move against Atonio Mafi on the pass rush. Godchaux has always been more of a run-plugging interior defender rather than a pass-rushing one, and that appears to be his role in Jacksonville.

He certainly came away happy with the win after leaving the struggling Saints.

Safe to say Davon Godchaux is happy to be a member of #DUUUVAL #Jaguars @BrentASJax pic.twitter.com/Fyjj7rDsCH

Andre Cisco played a handful of defensive snaps and a handful of special teams snaps for the Lions. He is mostly a depth piece on defense, especially with Kerby Joseph returning.

Andrew Vorhees, part of the package back to Atlanta in the Neuzil trade, played two special teams snaps.
